Chemistry

 Home
OurBigBook.com Words: 60k Articles: 822
Chemistry connects the composition and structure of chemical substances to their properties and transformations. Its central surprise is that rearranging the same chemical atoms can produce a different substance: molecular hydrogen and molecular oxygen can become water without changing which chemical elements are present. Chemical bonds explain the connections; chemical reactions describe the transformations; stoichiometry makes quantitative predictions from the bookkeeping.
This gives a useful route from an invisible world to measurable quantities. A molecule has a definite composition, such as two hydrogen chemical atoms and one oxygen chemical atom in water. A sample contains an enormous number of such molecules. Counting them through amount of substance, measured in moles, lets the same small-number ratios describe a macroscopic sample. The beauty is that the bookkeeping survives this huge change of scale.

Radical (chemistry)

Words: 1k Articles: 9
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
A radical has one or more unpaired Electrons. In a simple atomic orbital or molecular orbital occupancy picture, an unpaired Electron occupies a spatial orbital without an opposite-spin partner in that orbital. A dot such as H∙ marks this electronic property; it does not mean a missing Electron or positive electric charge. Free radicals can be neutral or charged. Terminology also has a boundary: metal ions exhibiting paramagnetism are not normally called free radicals just because they have unpaired Electrons.[ref]
Compare three species containing the same single proton. The hydrogen atom H∙ has one Electron in its 1s atomic orbital, and is a neutral radical. The hydrogen cation H+ has no Electrons, so no unpaired Electron. The hydrogen anion H− has two Electrons paired in its 1s atomic orbital. It is charged but is not a radical in its ground state. With Np​ protons, Ne​ Electrons, and positive elementary charge e, the independent electric charge count is
q=(Np​−Ne​)e;H+:q=+e,H∙:q=0,H−:q=−e.
(1)
The electron pair and electric charge questions require different information. An odd Ne​ ensures that not all Electrons can be paired; an even Ne​ alone does not ensure pairing, as the molecular orbital description of molecular oxygen illustrates.
The distinction matters whenever a chemical reaction mechanism uses dots and charge signs together. Homolysis gives one bonding Electron to each fragment, while heterolysis assigns both to one fragment. A radical chain reaction can pass an unpaired Electron from one species to another without generating net electric charge. Detection then exploits the unpaired Electron's spin and magnetic moment, rather than merely measuring whether the sample carries an electric charge.

Methyl radical (CH3​∙)

Words: 18
Radical (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
The methyl radical is the neutral radical CH3​∙, with an unpaired Electron. It carries the methane chlorination chain between its two propagation steps.

Radical ion

Words: 75 Articles: 2
Radical (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
A radical ion is both a radical and an ion. Removing one Electron from neutral benzene can produce C6​H6​∙+, a radical cation; adding one can produce C6​H6​∙−, a radical anion. These formulae specify net electric charge and an unpaired Electron, without claiming that both reside on one chemical atom.[ref]

Radical ion OurBigBook.com

Radical chain reaction

Words: 253 Articles: 1
Radical (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
A radical chain reaction regenerates a radical during propagation. Initiation supplies free radicals; propagation consumes one and produces another; termination removes chain-carrying free radicals. This explains why one initiating event can lead to many product-forming chemical reactions. The chain-growth polymerization article develops the corresponding growth of polymers.

Methane chlorination chain

Words: 215
Radical chain reaction OurBigBook.com
Light initiates methane chlorination by photodissociation of Cl2​ through homolysis. The elementary bookkeeping is
initiation:propagation:​Cl2​hν​2Cl∙,Cl∙+CH4​⟶HCl+CH3​∙,CH3​∙+Cl2​⟶CH3​Cl+Cl∙.​
(2)
Here hν denotes the photon energy. The first propagation step replaces a chlorine radical with a methyl radical; the second regenerates a chlorine radical. Adding the two propagation equations cancels both free radicals and gives CH4​+Cl2​⟶CH3​Cl+HCl: chloromethane and hydrogen chloride are made while the chain carrier is regenerated.[ref]
For example, recombination 2CH3​∙⟶C2​H6​ of methyl radicals makes ethane and a covalent bond from two unpaired Electrons, removing two carriers. Recombination of two Cl∙ also terminates carriers; in the gas phase, stabilization of the product requires disposal of released energy, for example to a third collision partner. The figure omits that partner. Termination competes with propagation, and further chlorination can consume chloromethane, so this cycle alone does not predict a pure product or a measured reaction rate.[ref]

Stable radical

Words: 509 Articles: 2
Radical (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
An unpaired Electron does not set a universal reaction rate. A stable radical can retain radical character during isolation and storage under specified conditions; a persistent radical survives long enough under specified conditions to be observed. These descriptions concern lifetime and handling, rather than immunity to every possible chemical reaction. DPPH is a practical counterexample to the claim that all free radicals react immediately.
Two mechanisms help explain persistence. Spreading electronic character over several chemical atoms, represented by chemical resonance, can lower the energy relative to a localized description. Bulky surrounding groups can impede approach to a reactive site and slow recombination. Lower energy and slower chemical kinetics are different advantages: neither alone guarantees a long lifetime. A primary computational study explicitly separates these effects, using electronic and geometric descriptors; it does not directly measure every predicted lifetime.[ref]

2,2-Diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl

Words: 351 Articles: 1
Stable radical OurBigBook.com
DPPH is a neutral organic radical used as a spin reference in electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), also called electron spin resonance (ESR). Its unpaired Electron remains bound within the chemical species: “free radical” does not mean a freely moving Electron. The DPPH electron spin resonance experiment makes its magnetic moment observable.
DPPH electron spin resonance experiment
Words: 312
2,2-Diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl OurBigBook.com
The University of Iowa's Electron Spin Resonance, University of Iowa laboratory protocol (revised July 2007, Experiment and Resonance Data Analysis, printed pp. 2–6) specifies DPPH on cotton in a tube inside an RF coil, between Helmholtz coils. A bridge monitors RF absorption; an oscilloscope records this output and the voltage across a 1Ω current-monitor resistor. Sweeping the coil current passes through the resonant magnetic field. The protocol describes two dips when the sweep revisits resonance; these are repeated crossings, not two distinct spectral lines.
Its calibration replaces the sample with a Hall effect probe, maps the magnetic field in 2mm steps, and accounts for sample dimensions. At least four RF frequencies test the resonance relation. Sweep speed is adjusted to obtain comparable passages. Only a local peak-plus-background fit is prescribed, because the full shape is not Gaussian. The protocol also flags unexplained trailing spikes and possible electronics contributions. These controls constrain field and sweep errors; an empty-tube/cotton blank would be an additional background control, not a reported measurement in this protocol.[ref]
For an isolated effective spin one-half with dimensionless positive factor g, the basic resonance model is
ΔE=gμB​∣B∣=hν,g=μB​∣Bres​∣hν​.
(3)
Here μB​ is the Bohr magneton, h is the Planck constant, ν is the applied frequency, and Bres​ is the calibrated resonant magnetic field. A change in frequency should shift the resonance field proportionally in this model. The factor g describes the electronic magnetic moment coupling, not the species' net electric charge.
A resonance supports the presence of detectable paramagnetism. It does not, by itself, identify an unknown radical: other species exhibiting paramagnetism, impurities, overlapping responses, and interactions with atomic nuclei can complicate interpretation. Conversely, absence of a detectable resonance need not mean absence of free radicals; a low concentration, a short lifetime, or an unsuitable measurement range can conceal them. The occupancy and chain diagrams are original bookkeeping illustrations; neither is a measured or simulated DPPH spectrum.

Molecule

Words: 4k Articles: 31
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
A molecule consists of two or more chemical atoms joined by chemical bonds, with zero net electric charge. This follows the terminology of the [ref]. The continuum approximation uses bulk fields in place of individual molecular positions and motions.

Molecular rotation

Words: 1k Articles: 9
Molecule OurBigBook.com
Molecular rotation changes a molecule's orientation. Its rotational kinetic energy depends on the arrangement and masses of its chemical atoms. A rigid rotor freezes internal distances to isolate this motion; rotational spectroscopy tests the resulting energy eigenvalues through transitions between quantum states. The molecular beam electric resonance experiment provides a complementary probe of the coupling to an electric field.

Rigid rotor

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Molecular rotation OurBigBook.com
A rigid rotor models rotational motion with fixed internal separations. Its use in the synthetic Stark effect figure omits vibrational motion and additional interactions in real molecules.
Rigidity fixes the molecular geometry, not the orientation, and does not require a spherical mass distribution. Remove motion of the centre of mass, choose principal axes of the inertia tensor, and write the classical rotational kinetic energy as
Trot​=21​(Ia​ωa2​+Ib​ωb2​+Ic​ωc2​)=2Ia​La2​​+2Ib​Lb2​​+2Ic​Lc2​​.
(4)
Here Ia​,Ib​,Ic​ are the principal moments of inertia, ωa​,ωb​,ωc​ components of angular velocity, and La​,Lb​,Lc​ components of angular momentum. Quantization replaces these last components by angular momentum operators. Different principal moments of inertia produce different spectra: the single-constant linear rigid rotor is a special case, not a formula for every molecule.[ref]
Linear rigid rotor (EJ​=ℏ2J(J+1)/(2I))
Words: 702 Articles: 3
Rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
For a diatomic molecule, let m1​,m2​ be the two masses and r their fixed separation. The distances from the centre of mass are r1​=m2​r/(m1​+m2​) and r2​=m1​r/(m1​+m2​). A perpendicular axis through the centre of mass therefore has moment of inertia
I=m1​r12​+m2​r22​=μr2,μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​.
(5)
The reduced mass μ here is not the electric dipole moment, for which we use d. For a longer linear molecule, replace μr2 by ∑i​mi​ρi2​, where ρi​ is each distance along the axis from the centre of mass. In the point-mass idealization, the axial moment of inertia is zero; turning about that axis changes no nuclear positions, so no independent axial rotational degree of freedom is included.
For the field-free linear rigid rotor, assume a fixed internal quantum state with no electronic angular momentum or electronic spin, and omit couplings to nuclear spin. The rotational Hamiltonian is Hrot​=L2/(2I). Its orientation wavefunctions are spherical harmonics YJM​, and its angular momentum eigenstates satisfy
L2YJM​=ℏ2J(J+1)YJM​,Lz​YJM​=ℏMYJM​,EJ​=2Iℏ2​J(J+1)=hBJ(J+1),
(6)
where J=0,1,2,… and M=−J,−J+1,…,J. Each EJ​ belongs to 2J+1 angular momentum eigenstates distinguished by the magnetic quantum number M, an instance of degenerate energy levels. The Planck constant is h=2πℏ; B is the frequency-valued rotational constant. Notice that the energy eigenvalues scale as J(J+1), not J2.
Subtracting consecutive energy eigenvalues gives
νJ→J+1​=hEJ+1​−EJ​​=2B(J+1).
(7)
Thus increasing level gaps produce a regularly spaced series of lines at 2B,4B,6B,…, with spacing 2B. Allowed positions do not guarantee that every line is visible: electric-dipole selection rules, occupation of the initial quantum state, and instrument response also matter.
Rotational constant (B=h/(8π2I))
Words: 102
Linear rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
In this article the rotational constant is a frequency,
B=8π2Ih​.
(8)
Its dimensions are s−1, since the Planck constant has dimensions kgm2s−1 and a moment of inertia has dimensions kgm2. Some authors instead call hB=ℏ2/(2I) the energy-valued rotational constant; this is the convention in the earlier synthetic molecular beam electric resonance diagram. A third convention uses the spectroscopic wavenumber B=B/c, with c the speed of light. Always check units before using ν=2B(J+1).
If B is known and the two masses are specified, the rigid two-atom model gives the bond length r=h/(8π2μB)​. This is why rotational spectroscopy can constrain molecular geometry. A real fitted constant can depend on molecular vibration, so this inference alone does not establish an equilibrium bond length.
Pure rotational electric-dipole selection rules (ΔJ=±1)
Words: 126
Linear rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
For the field-free, spin-free linear rigid rotor in one fixed internal quantum state, the electric-dipole interaction is −d⋅E(t). A nonzero permanent electric dipole moment along the molecular axis allows pure rotational photon absorption with ΔJ=+1 and photon emission with ΔJ=−1. The matrix element between initial and final quantum states must be nonzero: the existence of an energy gap alone is insufficient. Relative to a chosen z axis, polarization of an electromagnetic wave along z selects ΔM=0; transverse polarization of an electromagnetic wave permits ΔM=±1.[ref]
Hydrogen chloride and carbon monoxide are examples with a permanent electric dipole moment. By symmetry, molecular hydrogen and carbon dioxide have no permanent electric dipole moment in the ideal symmetric internal state. They still rotate and have rotational energy eigenvalues, but the simple permanent-electric dipole spectrum described here is absent. This restriction concerns this interaction and these assumptions, not every possible way of detecting molecular rotation.
Isotope shift of a linear rotor
Words: 213
Linear rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
Changing an isotope changes a mass and therefore the moment of inertia. If the bond length is held fixed, B∝1/μ and every corresponding transition shifts by the same fractional amount. This leading inverse-reduced mass scaling is also used in the more complete diatomic formulation.[ref]
For a deliberately stipulated carbon monoxide example, take m12​=12u, m13​=13u, m16​=16u, u=1.66053906660×10−27kg, r=1.13×10−10m for both isotopic forms, and h=6.62607015×10−34Js. The integer masses are simplifying inputs, not accurate isotopic atomic masses; the shared bond length is an imposed model assumption. Calculation gives
μ12,16​μ13,16​​=748​u,=29208​u,​I12,16​I13,16​​≈1.45395×10−46kgm2,≈1.52080×10−46kgm2,​B12,16​B13,16​​≈57.7188GHz,≈55.1817GHz.​
(9)
In particular,
B12,16​B13,16​​=μ13,16​μ12,16​​=9187​≈0.956044.
(10)
The heavier form's calculated J=0→1 line is 110.363GHz rather than 115.438GHz, a decrease of about 4.396%. These are model predictions from the stated inputs, not published measured frequencies. An isotope changes the spacing as well as the first line; the shift is not a fixed additive offset for the whole spectrum.
Centrifugal distortion (EJ​/h=BJ(J+1)−D[J(J+1)]2+⋯)
Words: 234
Rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
Real chemical bonds can stretch as molecular rotation increases. The resulting larger moment of inertia lowers the energy eigenvalues relative to a rigid rotor. Within one vibrational quantum state, a leading effective correction is
hEJ​​=Bv​J(J+1)−Dv​[J(J+1)]2+⋯,νJ→J+1​=2Bv​(J+1)−4Dv​(J+1)3+⋯.
(11)
Both Bv​ and Dv​ are in frequency units here; v labels the vibrational quantum state. For positive Dv​, the adjacent-line spacing becomes
νJ+1→J+2​−νJ→J+1​=2Bv​−4Dv​(3J2+9J+7),
(12)
so the departures grow with J. Molecular vibration also changes the effective rotational constant: even the lowest vibrational quantum state does not have motionless atomic nuclei.[ref]
The quartic correction is a limited expansion, not a model to extrapolate to arbitrary J. It is small relative to the rigid contribution only while (Dv​/Bv​)J(J+1)≪1; eventually higher terms, changed internal motion, or chemical bond breaking matter. In the synthetic plot, the largest upper-state label is J=5, giving a stipulated correction ratio of 0.03. No universal maximum valid J follows without a particular molecule and precision target.
The quantum numbers also have limits of meaning. Here J describes spin-free rotation. In a molecule with electronic spin, rotation alone is commonly labelled N, while J includes electronic angular momentum; including nuclear spin introduces additional total-angular momentum labels and resolved splittings. An applied electric field can mix different field-free J states through the Stark effect. For identical atomic nuclei, the Pauli exclusion principle can restrict combinations of rotational and nuclear-spin states. The simple 2J+1 degeneracy and every-integer-J ladder therefore describe the stated idealization, not all observed sublevels.[ref]

Rotational spectroscopy

Words: 363 Articles: 2
Molecular rotation OurBigBook.com
Rotational spectroscopy probes transitions between molecular rotation quantum states. In the simple linear rigid rotor, line spacing determines a moment of inertia, while an isotope shift of a linear rotor tests the mass dependence. More general molecular geometry requires several principal moments of inertia and more complicated assignments. The combination makes spectra sensitive fingerprints of both composition and shape.
Fourier transform microwave spectroscopy
Words: 324 Articles: 1
Rotational spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
Fourier transform microwave spectroscopy excites gaseous molecules with a pulse of electromagnetic radiation, then records the emitted time-dependent electric field. A Fourier transform extracts transition frequencies from the decaying signal. In a cavity implementation, two facing mirrors form a resonator; tuned excitation, receiver electronics and digitization replace the molecule-counting readout of molecular beam electric resonance. The pulsed radiation prepares quantum coherence between rotational quantum states; it does not set the whole gas spinning at one classical angular velocity.
For documented laboratory context, Evolution of Microwave Spectroscopy at the National Bureau of Standards (NBS) and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) by F. J. Lovas and others (§5, printed pp. 280–282) describes the NIST cavity instrument, phase-locked sources, mirror tuning and detector-mixer modifications. That account explains one instrument family; it does not establish the electronics of every later commercial spectrometer.
Rotational monitoring of deuterium exchange
Words: 226
Fourier transform microwave spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
A distinct experiment in An Automated, Highly Selective Reaction Monitoring Instrument Using Molecular Rotational Resonance Spectroscopy by Ann Adele Byars and others (Figure 1 and Figure 3) tracked exchange of hydrogen for deuterium in ethyl acetoacetate mixed with deuterated methanol. A pump circulated chemical solution through a valve; a calibrated loop injected aliquots into a temperature-controlled inlet, held at room temperature for this exchange experiment. Neon carried the vaporized sample to a cavity spectrometer. Separately recorded broadband spectra and fitted rotational Hamiltonians identified transitions for the four isotopic forms before targeted monitoring.[ref]
The readout was each assigned line's signal over reaction time, normalized by the sum of the four signals. Transitions with the same quantum numbers reduced response-factor differences. A solvent wash addressed observed sample carryover. The signals distinguished the unsubstituted, two singly substituted, and doubly substituted forms. Only one gas-phase structural form was detected; the authors explicitly caution that their readout does not recover the structural chemical equilibrium in chemical solution.[ref]
This example uses nonlinear molecules, so neither the single-constant linear rigid rotor nor the synthetic comb above is a fit to its spectrum. Its connection to the model is the sensitivity of moments of inertia to isotope placement. Line position helps assign a species; signal size additionally depends on sample transfer, initial quantum state populations and instrument response. Matching quantum numbers is a useful control, not a proof of identical response factors. These distinctions explain why resolving species and determining their concentrations are separate inference steps.

Linear molecule

Molecule OurBigBook.com
A linear molecule has collinear atomic nuclei in its idealized molecular geometry. Both a diatomic molecule and carbon dioxide can supply linear rigid rotor examples, although their electric-dipole selection rules need not give an observable permanent-electric dipole spectrum.

Diatomic molecule

Words: 15
Linear molecule OurBigBook.com
A diatomic molecule contains two chemical atoms; hydrogen chloride and carbon monoxide are examples. Their fixed-separation moment of inertia is I=μr2 in the linear rigid rotor model.

Molecular vibration

Words: 22
Molecule OurBigBook.com
Molecular vibration changes internal separations and bond angles, unlike the fixed internal molecular geometry of a rigid rotor. Its coupling to molecular rotation makes measured rotational constants depend on the vibrational quantum state.

Molecular geometry

Words: 2k Articles: 5
Molecule OurBigBook.com
Why do methane, ammonia, and water have different shapes when each central chemical atom is surrounded by eight valence electrons? The answer separates the positions of atomic nuclei from the electron domains used in a VSEPR model.
Molecular geometry describes the three-dimensional arrangement of the atomic nuclei in a molecule, including bond lengths and bond angles. For a larger molecule, a shape name often describes just the neighbours of one central chemical atom. A Lewis structure records connections and electron bookkeeping; its flat layout does not fix molecular geometry.
In the VSEPR model, electron pair geometry includes both bonding electron domains and lone pairs, whereas molecular geometry counts only the chemical atoms. In methane, four bond pairs and no lone pairs give tetrahedral molecular geometry. In ammonia, three bond pairs and one lone pair give trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry. In water, two bond pairs and two lone pairs give bent molecular geometry. All three use the same ideal tetrahedral electron pair geometry; this does not make their actual bond angles equal. See Flowers, Theopold, Langley and Robinson, Chemistry 2e, §7.6: electron-pair and molecular geometries.
A static drawing also needs a physical interpretation. The atomic nuclei undergo oscillations; an arrangement at a minimum of potential energy and an experimentally averaged arrangement need not have identical bond lengths or bond angles. This distinction matters when comparing measurements with quantum mechanics calculations; see the IUPAC Gold Book: experimental bond-length conventions. Gas electron diffraction gives a concrete route from a laboratory signal to molecular geometry rather than inferring shape from a drawing alone.

Bond angle (θ)

Words: 176
Molecular geometry OurBigBook.com
A bond angle is the angle between two chemical bonds sharing a central chemical atom. In H–O–H, the middle symbol identifies the vertex: the angle is at oxygen. Let u and v be the nonzero displacement vectors from that atomic nucleus to the two neighbours. The actual three-dimensional bond angle satisfies
cosθ=∥u∥∥v∥u⋅v​,0≤θ≤π,
(13)
using the dot product and Euclidean norm. Rotating the whole molecule preserves this expression; projecting it onto a page generally does not.
There is another useful way to find a bond angle. If the two bond lengths are a,b and the distance between the outer atomic nuclei is d, the law of cosines gives
d2=a2+b2−2abcosθ.
(14)
For equal bond lengths a=b, this becomes d=2bsin(θ/2). Thus a measured outer-atom separation contains information about a bond angle even though those outer chemical atoms are not directly joined by a chemical bond.
For a stipulated rigid, equal-bond length model using water's 104.4776∘ equilibrium bond angle, d/b≈1.5811, whereas a straight H–O–H arrangement would give d/b=2. These are calculated geometric ratios, not new measured distances. Gas electron diffraction illustrates how pair-distance information can constrain molecular geometry. Substituting independently averaged distances into the rigid triangle formula does not automatically recover an equilibrium bond angle, because averaging and this nonlinear calculation need not commute.

Tetrahedral molecular geometry

Words: 186
Molecular geometry OurBigBook.com
In tetrahedral molecular geometry, four neighbouring chemical atoms surround a central chemical atom in the directions of the vertices of a tetrahedron. In the regular idealization, the central atomic nucleus lies at the centre of a regular tetrahedron, and every pair of chemical bonds makes the same bond angle. Methane, CH4​, provides the standard example: its carbon has four bonding electron domains and no lone pair. See Chemistry 2e, §7.6: tetrahedral methane.
The exact ideal bond angle follows from four directions proportional to (1,1,1), (1,−1,−1), (−1,1,−1), and (−1,−1,1). Each has squared Euclidean norm 3, and each distinct pair has dot product −1. Hence
θ=arccos(−1/3)≈109.4712∘.
(15)
This is a statement about a regular tetrahedron, rather than a universal exact value for every molecule labelled tetrahedral. It also explains why a cross-shaped flat drawing with 90∘ gaps is misleading: four equal directions can spread out more evenly in three dimensions.
The same vectors sum to zero. Consequently, four equal bond-dipole contributions along those directions cancel. The symmetric methane molecule is nonpolar, but a tetrahedral shape alone does not imply a nonpolar molecule: replacing one neighbour can make the electronic distribution and bond contributions unequal. Chemical polarity depends on both molecular geometry and electron density. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, §2.2: molecular dipoles and methane.

Trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry

Words: 191
Molecular geometry OurBigBook.com
In trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry, three neighbouring chemical atoms form a triangular base and the central chemical atom lies outside its plane. The pyramid has four atomic nuclei; its central chemical atom is the apex, not the centre of the base. Ammonia, NH3​, has this arrangement. The [ref] lists an H–N–H bond angle of 106.67∘, commonly rounded to 106.7∘ or about 107∘.
The Lewis structure of ammonia allocates eight valence electrons as three bond pairs and one lone pair. Four electron domains therefore suggest tetrahedral electron pair geometry; removing the lone pair marker leaves three hydrogen chemical atoms below nitrogen. The VSEPR model treats the lone pair as more space-demanding and predicts compression relative to 109.4712∘, but it does not calculate the precise 106.67∘ value. See Chemistry 2e, §7.6: lone-pair effects.
Three equal bond-dipole contributions in this pyramid cancel sideways, but retain a component along its axis. By contrast, three equal contributions lying in one plane at 120∘ would cancel completely. This shows how a small change in molecular geometry can permit a permanent electric dipole moment. Ammonia is a polar molecule; NIST lists a measured magnitude of about 1.476 debye in the same [ref]. The vector argument predicts allowed direction and cancellation, not the full measured magnitude.

Bent molecular geometry

Words: 192
Molecular geometry OurBigBook.com
In bent molecular geometry, two neighbours and their central chemical atom form a noncollinear triangle, with an interior bond angle strictly between 0∘ and 180∘. Water, H2​O, is the standard example. The NIST CCCBDB experimental water entry, internal coordinates, citing Hoy and Bunker (1979) gives the equilibrium H–O–H bond angle as 104.4776∘ with quoted uncertainty 0.0019∘, usually rounded to 104.5∘.
The oxygen in water has two bonding electron domains and two lone pairs. Its ideal electron pair geometry is tetrahedral, while the three atomic nuclei give bent molecular geometry. Three points always lie in a plane; this does not make the four-domain scaffold planar. Nor does the word bent by itself determine an electron domain count: the same atomic shape can arise from other domain arrangements.
In an illustrative model with two equal bond-dipole contributions of magnitude p separated by bond angle θ, their sum of vectors points along the bisector and has magnitude 2pcos(θ/2). At 180∘ it vanishes; at 104.4776∘ it is approximately 1.2247p. This ratio is a geometric calculation, not a prediction of water's measured electric dipole moment. The entire electron density, including contributions represented by lone pairs, matters. Water is a polar molecule; chemical polarity helps explain its interactions with other polar molecules. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, §2.2: water, lone-pair contributions, and polarity.

Gas electron diffraction

Words: 561
Molecular geometry OurBigBook.com
Gas electron diffraction infers molecular geometry from the diffraction of Electrons by a gaseous sample. It makes a useful experimental test of shape: distances between both bonded and nonbonded atomic nuclei affect the signal, so a proposed straight arrangement and a bent arrangement can be distinguished through their pair separations.
A concrete modern apparatus is the Bielefeld instrument described by [ref]. A hot cathode supplies Electrons; apertures and magnetic lenses shape the beam. A temperature-controlled nozzle injects sample vapour across it inside a vacuum chamber. Pumps and a cold trap reduce unwanted residual gas. A central beam stop catches the strong unscattered beam; off-axis scattered Electrons expose imaging plates. A rotating sector can attenuate the intense small-angle region to accommodate detector range. The authors checked both the spatial scale of the plate scanner and its response to electron dose. These checks matter because an error in detector position or intensity calibration can masquerade as a structural difference.
What is measured is detector signal as a function of position, converted to scattering angle using the sample-to-detector distance. Randomly oriented molecules give radial information. After extracting the molecular intensity, compare it with predictions from a candidate arrangement and adjust the bond lengths and bond angles to improve the fit. The Wann Electron Diffraction Group's account of time-averaged GED, experiment and theory describes radial averaging and this refinement. The apparatus does not photograph one molecule with labelled atomic nuclei.
Why can distances survive random orientation? In a simplified rigid pair model with separation r, write s for the magnitude of the difference between incident and scattered wave vectors. Averaging the interference factor over uniformly distributed directions gives
21​∫−11​cos(srt)dt=srsin(sr)​,
(16)
with limiting value one at sr=0. This follows by integrating the cosine; t is the cosine of the angle between the pair and the scattering direction. The oscillations depend on r, although the orientation has disappeared. A real calculation weights many pairs by their scattering amplitudes and includes nuclear motion. The wave interference explanation and superposed pair-distance contributions are discussed in the same [ref].
Once a consistent structural model supplies two equal bond lengths b and an outer-atom separation d, the law of cosines converts these to a bond angle. For example, the illustrative d/b=1.5811 corresponds to approximately 104.5∘, while d/b=2 is straight. This geometric step explains what a shape measurement is trying to establish; it is not a new water measurement.
There are two essential limits. First, recovering labelled three-dimensional positions from a summed radial signal is an inverse problem: composition, candidate connectivity, and other structural information can be needed to distinguish competing fits. Karle's authored review Structure determination of gaseous and amorphous substances by diffraction methods (1977), abstract explains why too few independent observations make supplementary structural information indispensable. A good fit alone does not prove that the proposed arrangement is unique. Second, atomic nuclei are moving. Distances inferred by gas electron diffraction are motion-dependent averages; corrections are required before identifying them with a minimum-potential energy arrangement. For experimental distance conventions, see the IUPAC Gold Book: bond length. These limitations explain why model assumptions and the averaging convention must accompany a precise bond angle.

A nucleoside combines a nucleobase with a sugar, without the phosphate groups of a nucleotide. Adenosine is the nucleoside built from adenine and ribose. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: nucleosides and nucleotides.

Nucleoside OurBigBook.com
Adenosine consists of adenine joined to ribose. Adding one, two, or three phosphate groups at the ribose's 5′ position gives AMP, ADP, or ATP, respectively. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: the components of nucleotides.

Nucleotide

Molecule OurBigBook.com
A nucleotide contains a nucleobase, a sugar, and one or more phosphate groups. In DNA and RNA, linked nucleotides form a polymer whose nucleotide sequence carries information. The sugar is deoxyribose in DNA and ribose in RNA. See NHGRI: nucleotide.

Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)

Words: 521
Nucleotide OurBigBook.com
ATP is a nucleotide consisting of adenosine, itself adenine joined to ribose, carrying three phosphate groups. From the ribose outward, these groups are labelled α, β, and γ. ATP connects energy-supplying processes to energy coupling for synthesis and active transport; the same carrier can be regenerated and reused. [ref].
The net hydrolysis commonly used in energy coupling is
ATP+H2​O⟶ADP+Pi​.
(17)
Here Pi​ denotes inorganic phosphate. At buffered pH 7, this biochemical shorthand groups the appropriate protonation states into pools and leaves proton exchange with the buffer solution implicit. An explicit, charge-balanced choice is ATP4−+H2​O⟶ADP3−+HPO4​2−+H+, without implying these are the only chemical species present. See the IUBMB recommendations for biochemical thermodynamics.
The quoted textbook biochemical standard state value is approximately
ΔG∘′=−30.5kJmol−1.
(18)
This convention uses fixed pH 7, temperature 298.15K (25∘C), reference pressure 100kPa (1bar), unit reference thermodynamic activities for dissolved reactants and reaction products, and water thermodynamic activity approximated by one. The prime indicates the fixed-pH biochemical convention. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.4: standard ATP hydrolysis value and Biology 2e, 6.2: biochemical standard conditions. This is a reference value, rather than a universal value inside a biological cell; precise tables must also specify chemical solution conditions and any magnesium ion binding convention. Different reference conventions and data treatments give different tabulated values, as discussed in Li et al., 2010: a database of thermodynamic quantities for biochemical reactions.
An exergonic reaction has a negative change in Gibbs free energy, so the overall ATP hydrolysis is favourable under those reference conditions. Breaking a chemical bond by itself costs energy; forming new chemical bonds can release energy. The net change compares all reactants with all reaction products, including their interactions with water and the entropy contribution. Calling the phosphate connection a "high-energy bond" describes a large favourable change in Gibbs free energy on hydrolysis, rather than energy released by bond breaking alone. See 7.5 Strengths of Ionic and Covalent Bonds and Cooper, The Cell: ATP and metabolic energy.
Composition changes the driving force. At the same fixed pH, temperature, pressure, and binding convention, write the molar reaction change as
ΔG=ΔG∘′+RTlnQ,Q=aATP​aADP​aPi​​​.
(19)
Here R is the molar gas constant, T the absolute temperature, and a a dimensionless thermodynamic activity for a biochemical pool. Constant water thermodynamic activity is absorbed into the reference term; fixed pH accounts for buffered protons. The shorthand ΔG means transformed molar reaction Gibbs free energy change, Δr​G′, rather than a finite sample's total change. The natural logarithm acts on a dimensionless reaction quotient, never on concentrations with units. See the IUBMB biochemical thermodynamics recommendations and the general equilibrium constant relation.
For a stipulated ideal dilute chemical solution, let ai​=[i]/c∘, with c∘=1molL−1. Choose [ATP]=5mmolL−1, [ADP]=0.5mmolL−1, and [Pi​]=1mmolL−1, ignoring activity coefficient corrections and magnesium binding. These are illustrative inputs, not a claim about a particular biological cell. Then
Q=0.005(0.0005)(0.001)​=10−4,RT=(0.008314462618)(298.15)=2.47895703kJmol−1,
(20)
and
ΔG=−30.5+2.47895703ln(10−4)≈−53.332kJmol−1.
(21)
Increasing Q tenfold raises ΔG by RTln10≈5.708kJmol−1 at this temperature. Thus the ATP to ADP ratio and available inorganic phosphate matter, even with the same standard state value. These are local molar predictions at the stipulated composition, rather than a constant total yield as an isolated sample reacts.

Adenosine diphosphate (ADP)

Words: 136
Nucleotide OurBigBook.com
ADP contains the same adenosine unit as ATP, with two phosphate groups instead of three. One ATP converted by the stated hydrolysis gives one ADP and one inorganic phosphate: 3=2+1 accounts for the phosphate groups while adenine and ribose are retained. ADP is therefore a reusable material carrier, rather than ATP with its entire structure discarded.
Regeneration reverses the net chemical reaction:
ADP+Pi​⟶ATP+H2​O.
(22)
At the same stipulated reference conditions its ΔG∘′ is +30.5kJmol−1, the negative of the hydrolysis value. It is an endergonic reaction and requires energy input through energy coupling; a catalyst alone cannot supply that input. Recycling the material carrier does not recycle the expended driving energy. Cellular respiration and light-dependent reactions supply routes for regeneration. See Cooper, The Cell: ATP generation and energy coupling.
ADP is a nucleotide with two phosphate groups. Formation of ATP from ADP and phosphate couples to energy supply in light-dependent reactions; the Calvin cycle returns ADP after using ATP. [ref].

AMP is adenosine carrying one phosphate group at the ribose's 5′ position. The count distinguishes AMP from ADP with two and ATP with three; adenosine itself has none. See Cooper, The Cell: ATP, ADP, and AMP.

Electron density (n(r))

Words: 39
Quantum chemistry OurBigBook.com
The electron density describes the expected number of Electrons per unit volume at position r. For a system with a fixed number N of Electrons, ∫n(r)d3r=N. A Lewis structure allocates electron counts without specifying this spatial density.

Electron configuration

Words: 135 Articles: 2
Quantum chemistry OurBigBook.com
An electron configuration records the occupation of electron shells and electron subshells by Electrons. For neutral sodium in its ground state, 1s22s22p63s1 gives 2+2+6+1=11 Electrons; adding the occupations within each electron shell gives (2,8,1). A superscript counts Electrons, rather than multiplying the preceding labels. Removing the outer Electron gives the sodium ion Na+ with 1s22s22p6, or (2,8). See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, electron configurations of atoms and ions.

Electron shell (n)

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Electron configuration OurBigBook.com
An electron shell collects the allowed electronic quantum states sharing a principal quantum number n. Its occupancy is the number of Electrons assigned to those states in an electron configuration. An electron shell is not a material surface or a prescribed orbit.
Electron subshell
Words: 43
Electron shell OurBigBook.com
An electron subshell groups the allowed electronic quantum states within an electron shell by their orbital angular momentum quantum number ℓ. Labels s and p mean ℓ=0 and ℓ=1, respectively; their capacities are two and six Electrons. The leading number in 2p identifies the electron shell, while p identifies the electron subshell.

Atomic orbital (ϕnℓm​(r))

Words: 94
Quantum chemistry OurBigBook.com
An atomic orbital is a one-Electron spatial wavefunction used to describe an Electron's state in a chemical atom. For a one-electron hydrogen atom, orbitals can be exact energy eigenstates; descriptions of many-electron atoms instead use an orbital approximation. A normalized atomic orbital has ∫∣ϕ∣2d3r=1, and the Born rule gives the position probability density ∣ϕ∣2. It is a function extending through space, not a prescribed classical orbit. [ref]
The linear combination of atomic orbitals combines these single-centre functions to approximate a molecular orbital. The orbital overlap measures their inner product, and their relative quantum phase controls the interference shown in molecular orbital theory.

Molecular orbital theory

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Quantum chemistry OurBigBook.com
Molecular orbital theory describes the electronic arrangement of a molecule using molecular orbitals: one-Electron spatial wavefunctions extending over the combined atomic nuclei. Filling bonding molecular orbitals can stabilize a chemical bond; filling antibonding molecular orbitals opposes that stabilization. A molecular orbital is a building block of a many-Electron description, rather than the entire many-Electron wavefunction. See Robert W. Field, MIT 5.61, lecture 24, pp. 1–4: molecular orbitals and the LCAO approximation.
First make the interference visible with an exactly normalized one-dimensional toy. Replace the three-dimensional 1s atomic orbitals of the hydrogen atom by two Gaussian functions centred at x=±a, with dimensionless x and a>0:
ϕA​(x)=π−1/4e−(x+a)2/2,ϕB​(x)=π−1/4e−(x−a)2/2,S=∫−∞∞​ϕA​ϕB​dx=e−a2.
(23)
The normalized sum and difference are ψ±​=(ϕA​±ϕB​)/2(1±S)​, following the same linear combination of atomic orbitals algebra. At a=1, the orbital overlap is S=e−1≈0.367879. At the midpoint, ϕA​(0)=ϕB​(0)≈0.455581, giving
ψ+​(0)≈0.550879,∣ψ+​(0)∣2≈0.303468,ψ−​(0)=∣ψ−​(0)∣2=0.
(24)
Both probability densities have total integral one: interference redistributes probability, rather than creating an extra Electron. These are toy wavefunctions, not actual hydrogen atom orbitals or predictions of molecular hydrogen energies.
Now fill the two 1s-derived molecular orbitals in the minimal model. The lower bonding molecular orbital is labelled σg​; the upper antibonding molecular orbital is σu∗​. The Pauli exclusion principle permits at most two Electrons in each spatial molecular orbital, with opposite spin projections along a chosen axis. For the lowest electron configuration in this model, fill σg​ first. The subscripts g and u denote even and odd behaviour under inversion through the midpoint; the star marks an antibonding molecular orbital. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, 8.4: occupancy and bond order and Field, MIT 5.61, lecture 25, pp. 1–3: bonding, antibonding, and symmetry labels.
With Nb​ Electrons in bonding molecular orbitals and Na​ in antibonding molecular orbitals, the model's bond order is b=(Nb​−Na​)/2. The three elementary counts are:
  • Molecular hydrogen, H2​: two Electrons give (σg​)2 and b=(2−0)/2=1.
  • The hydrogen molecular ion H2+​: one Electron gives (σg​)1 and b=(1−0)/2=1/2.
  • Two neutral helium chemical atoms, He2​: four Electrons give (σg​)2(σu∗​)2 and b=(2−2)/2=0 in this minimal 1s model.
The zero bond order says this minimal model gives no net covalent bond for He2​. It does not rule out every bound pair of helium chemical atoms: a very weak Van der Waals force can bind a neutral helium dimer, which has been observed experimentally. See Zeller et al., Imaging the He2 quantum halo state using a free electron laser, PNAS 113, 14651–14655 (2016), p. 14651: van der Waals binding and Luo et al., The weakest bond: Experimental observation of helium dimer, Journal of Chemical Physics 98, 3564–3567 (1993). The bond order count does not include that weak binding mechanism.
The useful surprise is that sharing alone does not determine a chemical bond: the relative quantum phase and the occupancy matter together. The same two shapes explain why adding an Electron to a bonding molecular orbital increases the model's bond order, while adding one to an antibonding molecular orbital decreases it. Molecular orbital theory also accounts for the unpaired Electrons and paramagnetism of molecular oxygen, which its all-paired Lewis structure misses. See Chemistry 2e, 8.4: the molecular orbital description of oxygen.

Molecular orbital (ψ(r))

Words: 313 Articles: 2
Molecular orbital theory OurBigBook.com
A molecular orbital is a one-Electron spatial wavefunction for the combined atomic nuclei of a molecule. For a normalized molecular orbital, the Born rule gives the position probability density ∣ψ(r)∣2, with ∫R3​∣ψ∣2d3r=1. The molecular orbital is the amplitude, rather than its squared modulus or a classical trajectory.
In the independent-orbital approximation, a doubly occupied molecular orbital contributes 2∣ψ∣2 to the Electron number density, whose integral is two. An empty molecular orbital contributes zero, even though its shape is still part of the model. The molecular hydrogen example therefore uses one occupied spatial molecular orbital for two Electrons, distinguished by their spins. A negative real probability amplitude means a relative quantum phase of π, not positive electric charge; multiplying the whole wavefunction by −1 changes only its global phase.
Bonding orbital (σg​)
Words: 92
Molecular orbital OurBigBook.com
Occupying a bonding molecular orbital favours a chemical bond. For the two equivalent 1s atomic orbitals of the hydrogen atom, the sum σg​=σ+​ has constructive interference between the protons. The resulting Electron density in that region helps stabilize the combined system. Its lower energy in this model follows from the Quantum Hamiltonian, not from the plus sign alone; see Field, MIT 5.61, lecture 25, pp. 1–2.
For example, (σg​)2 in molecular hydrogen supplies Nb​=2, hence bond order one when Na​=0. The sum in the molecular orbital theory toy has midpoint probability density 0.303468, whereas the difference has zero there. The normalization factors must be included in this comparison.
Antibonding orbital (σu∗​)
Words: 117
Molecular orbital OurBigBook.com
Occupying an antibonding molecular orbital opposes a chemical bond. For equivalent 1s atomic orbitals of the hydrogen atom, the difference σu∗​=σ−​ vanishes on the plane halfway between the protons: every point there is equally far from both centres, so the amplitudes cancel. This nodal plane removes the contribution of this molecular orbital to Electron density on that plane; it does not make an entire finite region empty. The 1s-derived antibonding molecular orbital lies above its bonding molecular orbital partner in energy. See Field, MIT 5.61, lecture 25, pp. 1–2.
In the He2​ minimal model, (σu∗​)2 adds Na​=2 and cancels the bond order contribution of (σg​)2. Opposite signs on the two lobes describe probability amplitudes, while both lobes have nonnegative probability density after squaring. The star is an orbital label, not an extra Electron or an electric charge.

Linear combination of atomic orbitals

Words: 195 Articles: 1
Molecular orbital theory OurBigBook.com
The LCAO approximation builds a molecular orbital as a linear combination of single-centre atomic orbitals. For two equivalent normalized real 1s functions ϕA​ and ϕB​, choose their signs positive and define their orbital overlap S. At nonzero separation, 0<S<1, and the normalized combinations are
σ±​(r)=2(1±S)​ϕA​(r)±ϕB​(r)​,S=∫R3​ϕA​(r)ϕB​(r)d3r.
(25)
Here σ+​=σg​ and σ−​=σu∗​. Equal coefficients use the equivalence of the two centres; a general LCAO need not have equal coefficients. See Field, MIT 5.61, lecture 24, pp. 3–6: LCAO coefficients and overlap integrals.
For the Gaussian function toy's a=1, the two denominators are 2(1+S)​≈1.654013 and 2(1−S)​≈1.124385. To check wavefunction normalization, expand the square: ∫(ϕA​±ϕB​)2=1+1±2S. Dividing by 2(1±S) gives one. The local probability density is
∣σ±​∣2=2(1±S)ϕA2​+ϕB2​±2ϕA​ϕB​​.
(26)
The cross term is the interference; adding the separate densities first would lose it. These formulas normalize the chosen linear combination exactly, while the restricted choice of atomic orbitals remains an approximation to an actual molecular orbital.
Orbital overlap (S)
Words: 47
Linear combination of atomic orbitals OurBigBook.com
The orbital overlap of normalized real atomic orbitals is their inner product S=∫ϕA​ϕB​. It is a dimensionless measure of their common amplitude, not an Electron count. For the Gaussian function toy, increasing a from 1 to 2 reduces S from e−1≈0.367879 to e−4≈0.018316. As S tends to zero, both LCAO normalization denominators tend to 2​.

Bond order (b=(Nb​−Na​)/2)

Words: 74
Molecular orbital theory OurBigBook.com
In the elementary molecular orbital theory count, bond order is half the excess of Electrons in bonding molecular orbitals over those in antibonding molecular orbitals. Thus adding one Electron to a bonding molecular orbital raises b by 1/2, while adding one to an antibonding molecular orbital lowers it by 1/2. The configurations drawn above give 1, 1/2, and 0. This count summarizes net covalent bond occupancy; it is neither a measured energy nor a universal test for every kind of binding. See Chemistry 2e, 8.4: molecular orbital bond order.

Chemical bond

Words: 14k Articles: 87
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
A chemical bond associates chemical atoms or groups of chemical atoms into a sufficiently stable structure to treat it as a distinct entity. The concept covers connections within molecules and in extended solids; see the IUPAC Gold Book, chemical bond. It is useful because composition alone does not specify how the chemical atoms are connected, and those connections help determine a chemical substance's properties and possible chemical reactions.
In a covalent bond, Electrons are shared between chemical atoms. Two hydrogen chemical atoms can form a molecular hydrogen molecule, with its Electrons interacting with both atomic nuclei. In the usual description of this diatomic molecule, the potential energy as a function of nuclear separation has a minimum: moving the nuclei too close or too far raises the energy. See 7.2 Covalent Bonding.
Separating bonded chemical atoms requires energy; forming the corresponding chemical bonds releases energy. Whether an overall chemical reaction releases energy depends on both the chemical bonds broken and those formed. The lines in the stoichiometry diagram indicate connections schematically, rather than literal rods or a sequence of microscopic events.

Bond-dissociation energy (D)

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Chemical bond OurBigBook.com
A bond-dissociation energy specifies the energy needed for a stated dissociation into separated fragments. An energy from the lowest vibrational state, an energy from the bottom of a potential energy well, and a finite-temperature molar dissociation enthalpy require different conventions; do not silently mix them in an electronegativity formula.
Which fragments, in which quantum states, and at which temperature? For a neutral gaseous molecule with a specified two-electron covalent bond, the usual thermochemical convention is homolysis,
A−B(g)⟶A∙(g)+B∙(g).
(27)
Each fragment receives one of the two bonding Electrons; the dots denote unpaired Electrons. The final fragments are isolated from each other, with their own relaxed molecular geometry and specified electronic quantum states. The energy cost includes this relaxation, rather than merely stretching the initial chemical bond while freezing everything else. For a neutral parent, heterolysis instead produces A+(g)+B−(g), or the opposite assignment of electric charges; those are different final states and different energies. A value for gaseous neutral fragments cannot be transferred to ions, a chemical solution, or a solid without accounting for those changed conditions.[ref]
The distinction is useful beyond terminology. Pauling electronegativity compares consistently defined bond-dissociation energies; photodissociation can reveal a specified ground-state threshold; a thermal chemical reaction balance requires compatible enthalpies. A threshold is also different from an activation energy: it compares initial and final quantum states, whereas a barrier can obstruct the path between them.

Bond potential-well depth (De​)

Bond-dissociation energy OurBigBook.com
For a diatomic molecule, let V(r) be the electronic potential energy at bond length r, with the atomic nuclei treated as fixed while finding the electronic energy. Choose zero at infinitely separated chemical atoms in the specified electronic quantum states. If the minimum occurs at re​, the bond potential-well depth is
De​=V(∞)−V(re​)=−V(re​).
(28)
The bottom of this curve describes an equilibrium bond length, not an attainable motionless vibrational quantum state. Changing the zero of potential energy shifts both endpoints equally and leaves De​ unchanged. A quantum harmonic oscillator approximates the curve near its minimum but rises without limit, so that local approximation alone cannot supply a dissociation asymptote. A Morse potential supplies both a minimum and a finite separated-fragment limit.[ref]

Ground-state dissociation energy (D0​)

Words: 146
Bond-dissociation energy OurBigBook.com
The ground-state dissociation energy starts at the lowest vibrational quantum state, with the lowest allowed rotational quantum state and the fragment states explicitly specified. For a diatomic molecule whose fragments are ground-state chemical atoms, omitting any additional rotational correction,
D0​=De​−EZP​,
(29)
where EZP​ is the vibrational zero-point energy measured upward from the well minimum. The initial molecule already has this energy, so less additional energy is needed to reach the same final limit.[ref]
For fragments that are themselves molecules, include their zero-point energies too. Define De​ as the electronic energy difference between separately relaxed products and reactant; then, with consistent rotational conventions,
D0​=De​+∑fragments​EZP​−EZP,parent​.
(30)
Thus “subtract the parent's zero-point energy” is sufficient for atomic products but generally incomplete for molecular products. An excited final quantum state raises its channel threshold by its excitation energy; that threshold does not become the ground-product D0​ just because a detector selects it.

A bond-dissociation enthalpy is the molar enthalpy change for the specified homolysis at temperature T, with reactant and products in specified standard states. Its usual units are kJmol−1. The superscript ∘ specifies standard states; it does not fix T to room temperature.[ref]

Δdiss​H∘(T)=NA​D0​+δhA​(T)+δhB​(T)−δhAB​(T).

Here NA​ is the Avogadro constant. The thermal increments include translational kinetic energy, molecular rotation, thermally excited molecular vibration and electronic states when populated, and the pV contribution to enthalpy. They are additional to the zero-point energies already included in D0​. If values of standard enthalpy of formation at the same T are available, Hess's law gives the same quantity as Δf​H∘(A)+Δf​H∘(B)−Δf​H∘(AB).
Units alone do not identify the convention. Multiplying either De​ or D0​ by the Avogadro constant gives molar energy, but does not add thermal enthalpy. One electronvolt per dissociation corresponds to 96.485332kJmol−1. A spectroscopic wavenumber ν represents energy hcν, using the Planck constant h and speed of light c; 1cm−1 corresponds to 0.011962657kJmol−1.[ref]

Homolysis splits a covalent bond with one bonding Electron assigned to each fragment. A neutral closed-shell molecule thereby produces fragments with unpaired Electrons, each a radical. The usual bond-dissociation enthalpy uses this product convention.

Internal excitation energies here are relative to the parent and product ground states used to define D0​; Erecoil​ is the total product translational kinetic energy in the parent's centre of mass frame. Measuring one product's kinetic energy is insufficient by itself. For two fragments of masses mA​,mB​, conservation of momentum gives Erecoil​=EA​(mA​+mB​)/mB​ when A is detected. Unknown product excitation can conceal part of the available energy.

Opposed vacuum-ultraviolet laser pulses excited selected molecular levels and, about 10ns later, selectively ionized excited nitrogen fragments. A microchannel plate detector, phosphor screen and camera recorded radii.[ref]
The measured squared radii were fitted against molecular excitation energies, referenced to the parent ground state:
Ej​=D0,channel​+κRj2​.

A wavemeter monitored the excitation source; scanning the probe covered the recoil Doppler shift. Subtracting the atomic excitation energies converted the intercept to ground-product D0​.[ref]

Agreement of De​ across isotopes after zero-point energy correction tested consistency. The method still requires correctly assigned levels, adequate near-threshold signal and stable imaging; a signal drop alone can reflect another channel or a barrier.[ref]
This measurement determines a state-resolved ground-state dissociation energy. Obtaining a finite-temperature bond-dissociation enthalpy requires the thermal increments above; obtaining a bond potential-well depth requires the zero-point energy correction. Electronegativity (χ)

Words: 3k Articles: 17
Chemical bond OurBigBook.com
Electronegativity describes a chemical atom's tendency to attract electron density towards itself in a chemical bond. It helps answer a useful question: when two different chemical atoms share Electrons, which end of the chemical bond tends to be richer in electron density? For hydrogen chloride, the answer is chlorine: the covalent bond is a polar covalent bond, conventionally written Hδ+−Clδ−. The symbols indicate partial atomic charges, not isolated ions carrying whole elementary electric charges.[ref]
Electronegativity is a comparison scheme, not the number of Electrons on a chemical atom. A partial atomic charge depends on how the electron density is partitioned; formal charge instead follows an integer allocation in a Lewis structure. Neither is numerically equal to electronegativity. Nor is electronegativity identical to electron affinity, which concerns adding an Electron to an isolated species. Different electronegativity scales use different measured inputs and conventions; compare numbers only after specifying the scale.[ref]
For a concrete comparison, the Royal Society of Chemistry lists Pauling electronegativities χP​(H)=2.20 and χP​(Cl)=3.16. Their difference is 0.96, so the electronegativity rule predicts bond polarization towards chlorine in hydrogen chloride. An isolated molecular hydrogen molecule has identical ends and zero electronegativity difference. These examples explain a direction of unequal sharing, not a quantitative partial atomic charge.[ref][ref]
A larger electronegativity difference often suggests stronger bond polarization, but there is no universal numerical boundary where a covalent bond suddenly becomes ionic bonding. Tables of cutoffs are classification aids with exceptions. Hydrogen fluoride, for example, is described by a polar covalent bond even when its electronegativity difference exceeds a textbook's nominal ionic threshold. The actual electron density, physical setting, and chemical substance's structure matter.[ref]
The distinction from ionization energy is equally useful: an ionization energy measures the cost of removing an Electron from a specified isolated species, whereas electronegativity compares attraction for electron density in a bonded environment. Neither the removal cost alone nor the attachment release alone supplies a unique bonded-atom electronegativity. A scale combines selected measured inputs with a model and a convention.[ref]

Electronegativity OurBigBook.com
Pauling electronegativity is a relative, dimensionless scale motivated by bond-dissociation energies. The interesting observation is that a chemical bond between unlike chemical atoms can be stronger than a simple baseline inferred from the corresponding like-atom chemical bonds. An empirical excess energy can then be associated with an electronegativity difference. The 1932 paper The Nature of the Chemical Bond. IV. The Energy of Single Bonds and the Relative Electronegativity of Atoms built such a map; its original coordinates used hydrogen as zero, so those coordinates should not be mistaken for the modern tabulated Pauling electronegativities.[ref]
One arithmetic-baseline version of the Pauling scale relation is
ΔD​=DAB​−2DAA​+DBB​​,∣χP​(A)−χP​(B)∣≈1eVΔD​​​.
(39)
Here DAB​, DAA​ and DBB​ are consistently defined bond-dissociation energies per molecule, and the arithmetic mean is the chosen baseline. With molar energies instead, write ΔD​/(96.485kJmol−1)​, approximately 0.102ΔD​/(1kJmol−1)​. The denominator makes the result dimensionless; the factor 0.102 is not a unit-independent magic constant. This is an empirical relation with a specified baseline, not a definition valid for every chemical bond.[ref]
For an explicitly synthetic example, suppose DAA​=DBB​=300kJmol−1 and DAB​=396.485kJmol−1 with the same temperature and dissociation convention. Then ΔD​=96.485kJmol−1 and the model gives an electronegativity difference of 1. Replacing DAB​ by 300kJmol−1 gives zero; a negative excess would make this real square-root model inapplicable, not produce a negative electronegativity difference. These invented inputs illustrate the formula and are not measurements of named chemical substances.
Only differences appear, so adding the same constant to every Pauling electronegativity leaves this relation unchanged. A reference value must fix the origin. The bond-dissociation energies alone also do not tell which endpoint attracts electron density more strongly, because interchanging A and B leaves the formula unchanged. Chemical comparisons fix that direction. Thus Pauling electronegativity is useful as a compact ordering, while the underlying measured energies and approximations remain essential.

A Pauling bond-energy excess subtracts a chosen like-atom baseline from the unlike-atom bond-dissociation energy. For an unequal-input arithmetic example, stipulate DAA​=200, DBB​=450 and DAB​=421.485kJmol−1, all with one dissociation convention. The arithmetic mean baseline and excess are

The arithmetic-baseline Pauling scale model therefore gives ∣χP​(A)−χP​(B)∣=96.485/96.485​=1. The bond-dissociation energy 421.485 is not itself the excess: subtracting the baseline is essential. All three numbers are stipulated, not experimental values for named chemical elements.
Changing the baseline changes the model. For the same stipulated inputs, a geometric mean baseline would be 200×450​=300kJmol−1, yielding an excess of 121.485kJmol−1 and a difference of approximately 1.122. It is a different construction, even though both start from the same bond-dissociation energies. State which baseline is used before comparing electronegativity differences.
The arithmetic-baseline Pauling scale also has a useful inverse: a difference of 0.5 corresponds to an excess of 24.12125kJmol−1, and a difference of 2 corresponds to 385.94kJmol−1. Doubling the electronegativity difference quadruples the modeled excess. Interchanging the endpoint labels changes neither quantity; the square root alone cannot choose the direction of bond polarization.
In The Nature of the Chemical Bond. IV. The Energy of Single Bonds and the Relative Electronegativity of Atoms (printed pp. 3576–3578, Table II and equation (1)), Linus Pauling organized excess energies for chemical bonds into an approximately additive map of their square roots. He also identified a limitation: his H–F map separation of 2 predicted an excess of 4.00eV, exceeding his table's value by 1.23eV. Those are historical values and a historical model discrepancy, not modern recommended inputs.[ref]

If attachment is instead tabulated as the signed energy change ΔEattach​=E(X−)−E(X), the same expression is (I−ΔEattach​)/2. Stating the sign convention prevents adding the wrong quantities. The 1934 original treated suitable valence states, which are not automatically the ground states used in this example.[ref]

For hydrogen, the RSC ground-state inputs are I=1312.05 and Aea​=72.769kJmol−1, giving χM​=692.4095kJmol−1≈7.176eV per chemical atom. An electron affinity is neither an electronegativity nor a lattice energy. The first describes a specified isolated-species energy difference, electronegativity compares attraction for electron density in a chemical bond, and lattice energy refers to an entire ionic crystal and separated gaseous ions. A stable anion can therefore help explain ionic bonding without describing the full energy balance for making a salt.

Dipole evidence for bond polarization

Words: 512 Articles: 2
Electronegativity OurBigBook.com
A permanent electric dipole moment gives evidence of separated positive and negative electric charge in an overall neutral molecule. This is a more direct probe of chemical polarity than an electronegativity table. For hydrogen chloride, NIST lists about 1.109 debye for the lowest vibrational state and 1.093 debye for the equilibrium value. They describe different averaging conventions, not two contradictory measurements. The NIST WebBook traces the vibrational value 1.1085 debye to molecular-beam electric-resonance measurements in 1970.[ref][ref]
How does molecular beam electric resonance reveal an electric dipole moment? A source and apertures form a beam of molecules in vacuum. A first nonuniform electric field, A, selects quantum states through their different Stark effects. In a central region, C, electrodes supply a nearly uniform electric field and applied radiation drives transitions at selected frequencies. A second nonuniform electric field, B, analyzes the outgoing quantum states; a detector measures the rate of arriving molecules. In a transmission-loss arrangement, resonant radiation transfers some molecules to a quantum state rejected by B, so the measured arrival rate dips. The observable is a change in detected molecules as the radiation frequency is scanned, rather than light absorption itself. This general apparatus description is documented in a later experimental thesis; it is not a reconstruction of the exact 1970 HCl instrument.[ref]
The inference comes from how transition frequencies change with the known electric field. The interaction −μ⋅E couples the electric dipole moment to the electric field; fitting the quantum mechanics of the relevant rotational states extracts its magnitude. A free rotating molecule need not show a first-order shift proportional to ∣E∣: the weak-field Stark effect can be quadratic. The diagram uses a simplified rigid rotor, with B an energy constant, to illustrate this behavior. It omits the fine details of actual spectra.
Useful controls include scans with the radiation off to measure the baseline arrival rate, repeated scans at several calibrated electric fields, and agreement between independently assigned transitions. These are methodological checks, not claims about undocumented steps of the 1970 experiment. Field calibration and state assignment limit the inferred electric dipole moment. The published 1970 abstract confirms analysis of HCl and DCl beam-resonance spectra and combination with infrared spectroscopy intensities to obtain a distance-dependent electric dipole moment; its full apparatus and calibration record were unavailable here.[ref]
Even an accurately measured electric dipole moment is not an absolute partial atomic charge. Replacing a hydrogen chloride molecule by two point electric charges ±q separated by bond length r gives ∣μ∣=∣q∣r. Using 1.109 debye and r=1.27455×10−10m gives ∣q∣≈0.181 times the elementary electric charge. This is an effective two-point model, combining a vibrationally averaged electric dipole moment with an equilibrium bond length, not a unique partition of the actual electron density or a measured “18.1 percent ionic bond”.[ref]
For a molecule with several chemical bonds, molecular geometry can cancel opposing contributions to the total electric dipole moment. Carbon dioxide illustrates why an overall nonpolar molecule need not have unpolarized individual chemical bonds. An electronegativity comparison helps anticipate local bond polarization; the measured molecular electric dipole moment tests the entire electric charge distribution.

Ionic bonding binds oppositely charged ions through attraction governed by electrostatics. A conductivity experiment on salt solutions tests this transport picture, rather than simply asserting that charged constituents must make every material conductive.

Solvation is stabilization through interactions between a solute and its solvent. It involves both the solute's surroundings and reorganization of the solvent: neighbors move, orientations change, and existing interactions compete with new ones. Electric forces, Van der Waals forces, and specific interactions such as hydrogen bonds can contribute. Solvation can also occur at groups on an insoluble material, so it does not require complete dissolution.[ref]
Solvation by water is called hydration. Hydration of ions is the charged special case, but neutral molecules such as sucrose can also interact with water without becoming ions. Dissolution, desolvation, and ionization describe different changes, as the examples below show.[ref][ref]
The useful question is therefore not just whether a solute attracts a solvent, but how much the whole system gains after paying for the rearrangements. A hydrogen bond is an attractive association involving a hydrogen attached to another chemical atom, and an accepting atom or group. In the IUPAC 2011 definition, the atom X in X−H is more electronegative than hydrogen, and evidence of bond formation is required. The familiar strong examples use O–H or N–H groups, but restricting the concept to only nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine misses weaker cases. A short distance alone is not the entire definition.[ref]
In the depicted water pair, one O–H group is the hydrogen bond donor; the other oxygen supplies the hydrogen bond acceptor. The solid O–H line denotes a covalent bond within a water molecule; the dotted H···O line denotes the hydrogen bond between them. One water molecule can play both roles in a larger arrangement because it has O–H groups and lone pairs.
This makes hydrogen bonds useful for understanding organization beyond a single molecular formula. They connect water molecules and contribute to protein folding and recognition between molecules. The same types of chemical atoms can support different associations depending on which donor and acceptor sites are exposed and how they are oriented. Alberts and colleagues discuss these noncovalent interactions in Molecular Biology of the Cell, the chemical components of a cell.
Hydrogen bonds are often directional, with an approximately straight donor–H–acceptor arrangement favourable in familiar cases; strength and preferred geometry depend on the system. The IUPAC definition uses converging experimental or theoretical evidence rather than one universal distance threshold. The author-hosted 2009 task-group draft, §§3.1–3.3 explains the definition and typical criteria leading to the recommendation.

Hydrogen bond donor (X−H)

Words: 296
Hydrogen bond OurBigBook.com
A hydrogen bond donor is the X−H group supplying the attached hydrogen in a hydrogen bond X−H⋯Y. The donor atom X, or the whole molecule containing it, may also be called the donor. The terminology does not imply transfer of a free proton: in the ordinary water pair, the O–H covalent bond remains. Familiar donors include O–H groups in water and N–H groups in ammonia. See Andrew Glasfeld, Intermolecular Attraction, pp. 12–13: donor and acceptor roles.
The attached hydrogen is essential to this role. At the nitrogen site, an unprotonated amine R3​N can be a hydrogen bond acceptor, but has no N–H hydrogen bond donor. Protonation gives R3​NH+: the new N–H group can donate, while that nitrogen no longer has the accepting lone pair. This is a change of chemical form, not a permanent label attached to a chemical element. Here R denotes a group attached through carbon; the statement concerns the nitrogen site and does not rule out weaker C–H associations elsewhere. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, 24.3: amine protonation and Glasfeld: protonated amines as donors.
An amide with an N–H covalent bond can donate even though its nitrogen is ordinarily not an accepting site. For example, in R−C(=O)−NH−R′, N–H is a hydrogen bond donor and the carbonyl group's oxygen is a hydrogen bond acceptor. Replacing the remaining N–H by another group attached through carbon removes this N–H donor without removing the accepting oxygen. The analogous division of roles in a peptide bond helps explain protein structure. See Glasfeld: amide roles and biological interactions. The useful question is therefore which site supplies the hydrogen, rather than whether the whole substance is simply “hydrogen bonding”.

Hydrogen bond acceptor

Words: 391
Hydrogen bond OurBigBook.com
A hydrogen bond acceptor supplies the electron-rich atom or group Y interacting with the attached hydrogen of a hydrogen bond donor in X−H⋯Y. An oxygen lone pair in water is the familiar example. Acceptance describes the association, not necessarily acquisition of a proton. A single molecule, such as water or ammonia, can offer both hydrogen bond donor and hydrogen bond acceptor sites. See Glasfeld: water and nitrogen-containing accepting sites.
A lone pair drawn in a Lewis structure is a useful clue, not a universal test. At an ordinary neutral amide nitrogen, the nominal lone pair participates in chemical resonance with the carbonyl group, so this nitrogen is ordinarily excluded from lists of hydrogen bond acceptors; the carbonyl group's oxygen remains an accepting site. Protonation changes the test again: NH4+​ has four N–H covalent bonds and no nitrogen lone pair, whereas ammonia has three and one. These distinctions follow the actual chemical form, and accepting ability also depends on the partner and whether it can approach the site. See McMurry: amide resonance and protonation and Glasfeld: limitations of nitrogen accepting sites.
Conversely, an accepting group need not supply an atom-centred lone pair. The following phenol–benzene experiment probes an O–H donor interacting with the ring's distributed π electron density.
Saggu, Levinson and Boxer (2011) used infrared spectroscopy to compare 200mmolL−1 phenol in different solvents. The O–H stretching peak was at 3611cm−1 in CCl4​ and 3555.9cm−1 in benzene. To distinguish association from a general solvent effect, they diluted the ring-containing chemical solutions with CCl4​: two peaks appeared, with the free peak nearly fixed while the associated peak depended on the partner. Replacing the O–H hydrogen with deuterium reproduced the ordering of shifts for different partners. Thus the perturbed O–H group identifies the hydrogen bond donor; the ring supplies the hydrogen bond acceptor. A peak shift alone does not specify a unique molecular geometry. [ref]
The roles make recognition between molecules intelligible: exposed hydrogen bond donors need compatible hydrogen bond acceptors in reachable positions. A count of sites is a starting description, not a prediction of binding strength. In water, forming a contact between two partners can also replace their existing hydrogen bonds to water; the Gibbs free energy of association concerns the whole change. See Glasfeld, pp. 15–16: competition with solvent interactions.
