Covalent bond

Words: 5k Articles: 13
Chemical bond OurBigBook.com
A covalent bond joins chemical atoms through shared Electrons. In the familiar two-centre description, one bond pair contributes to a connection between two atomic nuclei. Sharing means that the Electrons belong to the combined arrangement and interact with both atomic nuclei; it does not mean that identifiable dots shuttle along drawn paths. The [ref] emphasizes the concentration of Electrons between atomic nuclei and the resulting attraction and characteristic separation. The pair picture is especially useful for simple molecules, but is not a universal description of every covalent bond.
A Lewis structure turns this picture into practical bookkeeping. Count the valence electrons, indicate which chemical atoms are connected, and allocate two Electrons to each line. A bond pair is shared; a lone pair is assigned to one chemical atom without connecting it to another. A double line represents two bond pairs. Dots and lines record allocations, rather than positions, trajectories, or a measured three-dimensional arrangement. [ref]
For molecular hydrogen, H2​, each neutral hydrogen chemical atom supplies one valence electron. Thus 1+1=2 valence electrons make one bond pair, represented by H−H, with no lone pairs. Each hydrogen counts the same shared pair when checking its two-electron arrangement. The molecule still contains two Electrons, not four: counting a pair around both endpoints does not create extra Electrons.
For water, H2​O, neutral oxygen supplies six valence electrons and the two hydrogen chemical atoms supply one each: 6+1+1=8. Two O–H connections consume four Electrons as two bond pairs. The remaining 8−4=4 Electrons form two lone pairs on oxygen. Around oxygen, the two bond pairs and two lone pairs count as eight Electrons; each hydrogen counts two. The whole water molecule has ten Electrons, because two additional oxygen Electrons are omitted from this valence electron drawing.
For ammonia, NH3​, the total is 5+3×1=8 valence electrons: five from nitrogen and three from hydrogen. Three N–H connections use six Electrons as three bond pairs, leaving two Electrons as one lone pair on nitrogen. Thus water and ammonia have the same total of eight valence electrons but different allocations: two plus two pairs versus three plus one. This small calculation already distinguishes their connectivity without a detailed quantum mechanics calculation.
For molecular oxygen, O2​, 6+6=12 valence electrons give the conventional O=O Lewis structure. Its two bond pairs use four Electrons, leaving eight as four lone pairs, two on each oxygen. Each oxygen consequently counts eight Electrons locally. However, actual molecular oxygen has two unpaired Electrons and exhibits paramagnetism: it is attracted into a stronger magnetic field. The all-paired Lewis structure cannot capture this observation. Molecular orbital theory describes the unpaired Electrons; the successful counting diagram alone is insufficient. [ref]
Why does sharing produce a stable separation? For molecular hydrogen, the electronic arrangement responds as the atomic nuclei approach. Their interactions can lower the energy, but pushing them too close raises it. A curve of potential energy against separation therefore has a local minimum, rather than falling forever. Attraction and repulsion balance there. This is a statement about the combined system, not a claim that stationary Electrons sit between otherwise motionless atomic nuclei. [ref]
The following Morse potential makes those features calculable. Set x=r/re​, where r is separation and re​ its equilibrium value, and let D be the well depth. With the self-chosen parameter a=2, define the dimensionless quantities
u(x)=DV(r)​=(1−e−2(x−1))2−1,f(x)=DF(r)re​​=−dxdu​=4(e−4(x−1)−e−2(x−1)).
(62)
Here F=−dV/dr is the net separating force, obtained from the derivative of the potential energy. Positive f pushes the chemical atoms apart; negative f draws them together. These are illustrative curves with re​=D=1 in chosen units, not measured molecular hydrogen data or fitted parameters.
At x=1, u=−1 and f=0. The second derivative is u′′(1)=8>0, confirming a local minimum. At x=0.5, u=(1−e)2−1≈1.9525; at x=1.5, u=(1−e−1)2−1≈−0.6004. As x increases without bound, u approaches zero from below. Thus moving from the well bottom to separated chemical atoms requires an increase of D in this model's potential energy. An actual quantum mechanics dissociation threshold also depends on the initial motion of the atomic nuclei, so the well depth alone is not every measured dissociation energy.
The force panel separates f into a positive term 4e−4(x−1) and a negative term −4e−2(x−1). At x=1 they are +4 and −4, cancelling exactly; nearer separations favour the positive term. These are algebraic components of the chosen Morse potential, not separately measured microscopic forces. Their usefulness is to show how a balance arises from the slope of one energy curve.
The beauty of the pair picture is its economy: a few marks summarize connectivity and constrain what a proposed molecule can contain. Its historical anchor is Gilbert N. Lewis's 1916 paper [ref], also available as an [ref]. Lewis structures remain useful because they answer counting questions quickly; quantum mechanics supplies the richer account when energy, shape, or unpaired Electrons matter.

Covalent bond OurBigBook.com
A phosphodiester bond connects two groups through a phosphate diester. In a nucleic acid backbone, the bridging phosphate is connected through oxygen to the 3′ carbon position of one sugar and the 5′ carbon position of another. These covalent bonds connect successive nucleotides along a strand; they are distinct from the hydrogen bonds between paired nucleobases.

Disulfide bond (S−S)

Words: 1k
Covalent bond OurBigBook.com
A disulfide bond is the single covalent bond between the two adjacent sulfur chemical atoms in a disulfide, conventionally written R−S−S−R′. Here R and R′ stand for the attached organic groups; they may belong to the same molecule or to initially separate molecules. A disulfide bond is a chemical bridge, rather than a hydrogen bond or a mere contact between nearby groups. Two thiols, R−SH and R′−SH, can supply its two sulfur endpoints. [ref]
The stoichiometry of forming a disulfide bond is especially revealing. Written as an oxidation half-reaction, it is
R−SH+R′−SH⟶R−S−S−R′+2H++2e−.
(63)
The reverse reduction half-reaction consumes two Electrons and two hydrogen ions to restore two thiols. Both sides contain two sulfur chemical atoms; the two hydrogen chemical atoms have moved into the two hydrogen ions, and the net electric charge remains zero because +2−2=0. Thus one disulfide bond corresponds to two thiol groups and two transferred Electrons. These half-reactions describe redox bookkeeping, not a complete standalone chemical reaction: an accompanying reactant must accept or supply the Electrons, and pH affects the actual protonation of the groups. Mercaptoethanol can promote reduction through exchange of disulfide bonds, but adequate excess and appropriate conditions are needed; adding it does not by itself prove complete reduction. [ref]
In a protein disulfide bond, the endpoints are normally the amino acid side chains of two cysteine amino acid residues. An intrachain protein disulfide bond closes an intramolecular bridge within one polypeptide chain; an interchain protein disulfide bond connects different polypeptide chains, and can arise by intermolecular crosslinking of initially separate molecules. Forming or reducing these bridges changes covalent bond connectivity and can change protein structure, while preserving the order of amino acid residues and the peptide bonds in the protein backbone. A complete chemical account of protein primary structure includes crosslinks as well as sequence, so preservation of sequence does not imply preservation of every covalent bond. Mature insulin has two interchain protein disulfide bonds and one intrachain protein disulfide bond. [ref]
A bridge is useful because it constrains which parts of a polypeptide chain can move apart without breaking a covalent bond. Its placement therefore matters as well as its presence. The ribonuclease A refolding experiment provides the existing experimental example: breaking and reforming four protein disulfide bonds can accompany loss and recovery of function. Counting four bridges alone cannot tell whether their endpoints have the native pairing. This is an attractive connection between simple chemical counting and the richer problem of protein folding.
How can an experiment reveal an initially hidden disulfide bond? Ellman's reagent, also called DTNB, measures free thiols by producing a yellow absorbing species. Its reactive disulfide bond undergoes exchange with the conjugate base R−S− of a thiol, producing a mixed disulfide attached to R and one released 2-nitro-5-thiobenzoate species, abbreviated TNB. At the assay pH, the strongly colored form is the dianion TNB2−: one negative charge is on sulfur and the other is on the carboxylic acid-derived COO− group. With excess DTNB and complete reaction, one released TNB reports one reacted thiol. George L. Ellman's 1959 paper introduced the tissue assay; it was subsequently reexamined quantitatively. [ref] [ref]
The modern apparatus can be simple: tubes, pipettes, a buffer solution, cysteine standards, DTNB, and an instrument that measures absorbance through a cuvette at wavelength 412nm. The Pierce protocol uses 50μL of a 4mgmL−1 DTNB stock, 2.50mL of buffer solution, and 250μL of sample. Its buffer solution is 0.1molL−1 sodium phosphate at pH 8.0 with a metal-binding additive. After 15 minutes at room temperature, measure absorbance against a buffer solution plus DTNB blank; run known cysteine concentrations in parallel. The observable is increased yellow color and increased blank-corrected absorbance as more accessible thiols react, rather than direct imaging of disulfide bonds. These are published protocol conditions, not measurements performed for this article. [ref]
For a before/after test, split a purified protein sample into matched aliquots. Measure accessible free thiols in one aliquot; subject the other to complete reduction of its disulfide bonds, remove the reducing reagent, then measure the resulting thiols with fresh DTNB. Process the unreduced aliquot through a matching cleanup. Normalize to recovered protein and known dilution, since cleanup can change both. To estimate all reducible protein disulfide bonds, expose buried groups using matching protein denaturation conditions in both aliquots and calibrate in that same chemical solution; a native-accessibility measurement answers a different question. A larger corrected reading after reduction supports conversion of previously unreactive groups into detectable thiols. Attribution to disulfide bonds requires excluding other reducible sulfur modifications. This is a proposed comparison based on the detection principles, not a reconstruction of Ellman's original tissue measurements. [ref]
Under the Beer-Lambert law, the blank-corrected absorbance is A=εlc, where l is the cuvette path length, c is the released TNB concentration, and ε is its molar absorption coefficient. Riddles, Blakeley and Zerner measured ε412​=14150Lmol−1cm−1 in dilute aqueous salt chemical solutions, confirming the value independently using cysteine. It must not be applied indiscriminately to other solvents or protein denaturation mixtures. [ref] For aliquots compared on the same final volume and protein concentration basis, the ideal estimate is
cS−S​=2cSH,after​−cSH,before​​=2εlAafter​−Abefore​​,nˉS−S​=cprotein​cS−S​​.
(64)
The factor of two follows from the reduction stoichiometry; nˉS−S​ is the number of disulfide bonds per protein molecule, or an average for a mixed population. If the aliquots have different dilutions or recoveries, convert each reading to a common sample basis before subtracting.
As a hypothetical calculation, choose cprotein​=10μmolL−1 in each final cuvette, two free thiols and two disulfide bonds per protein molecule, and l=1cm. Before reduction, cSH​=20μmolL−1 gives A=0.283; complete reduction adds four thiols per protein molecule, so cSH​=60μmolL−1 gives A=0.849. The difference 0.566 gives cS−S​=20μmolL−1 and nˉS−S​=2. The published tube volumes imply a dilution factor 2.80/0.250=11.2; reversing that dilution multiplies both thiol and protein concentrations by 11.2 and leaves the bridge count per protein molecule unchanged.
Controls determine whether that arithmetic has chemical meaning. Use fresh cysteine standards and a processed blank without protein to detect color generated by residual reducing reagent. Even a reducing reagent containing no thiols can interfere: Han and Han showed that tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine, abbreviated TCEP, reduces DTNB to two TNB equivalents per TCEP. [ref] In the hypothetical model, 5μmolL−1 residual TCEP in only the reduced cuvette would add A=0.1415 and falsely add 0.5 bridge per protein molecule. A stable endpoint and agreement after a further reduction treatment help check completion. A sample without DTNB checks its own color; cloudy samples can also attenuate light without producing TNB. Match pH, temperature, accessibility and calibration chemical solution, and minimize delay that permits reoxidation. If two already-free but buried thiols become accessible only in the reduced aliquot, they mimic one new disulfide bond per protein molecule. Finally, bulk absorbance supplies a count under these assumptions: it does not locate the cysteine endpoints, distinguish intrachain from interchain bridges, or establish the native pairing of a protein disulfide bond.

Lewis structure

Words: 3k Articles: 10
Covalent bond OurBigBook.com
Before calculating electronic energy, ask a simpler question: where can the available valence electrons go? A Lewis structure makes that budget visible, and nitrate shows why a correct budget can still require several resonance structures.
A Lewis structure records which chemical atoms are connected in a molecule or ion and how its valence electrons are allocated. One line represents one bond pair, two lines two bond pairs, and three lines three bond pairs; two dots beside a chemical atom represent one lone pair. The marks are a counting language, rather than measured Electron positions. See the IUPAC Gold Book, Lewis formula.
For water, H2​O, the budget is 6+2×1=8 valence electrons. Two O–H lines use four Electrons; the other four form two lone pairs on oxygen. For ammonia, NH3​, 5+3×1=8 valence electrons give three N–H lines and one lone pair on nitrogen. Both molecules contain four electron pairs, but their allocations differ. Each shared bond pair is counted once in the total budget, even though both endpoints count it when checking the octet rule.
A practical construction method is:
  • Add the neutral chemical atoms' valence electron counts. Add one Electron for each unit of negative electric charge, or subtract one for each unit of positive electric charge.
  • Choose candidate connections and put one bond pair on each. Hydrogen normally has one connection in these simple Lewis structures.
  • Place remaining Electrons as lone pairs, checking the octet rule. If an endpoint has eight Electrons but the central chemical atom lacks them, try converting an endpoint lone pair into an additional bond pair, keeping the total budget fixed.
  • Compute every formal charge and check its sum against the net electric charge. Compare reasonable candidates, including chemical resonance when several allocations share the same connections.
For carbon dioxide, 4+2×6=16 valence electrons. Starting with two single C–O connections leaves twelve Electrons, enough for three lone pairs on each oxygen, but only four Electrons around carbon. Converting one lone pair from each oxygen into a second bond pair gives O=C=O. Eight Electrons are in the four bond pairs, and eight are in four lone pairs, two on each oxygen. Carbon has no lone pair; all three chemical atoms satisfy the octet rule, and all three formal charges vanish.
For the nitrate ion, NO3−​, the valence electron budget is
5+3×6+1=24.
(65)
Nitrogen contributes five, the three oxygen chemical atoms contribute eighteen, and the negative electric charge adds one Electron. Start with nitrogen connected to each oxygen by one bond pair: those three lines use six Electrons. Put the remaining eighteen Electrons into three lone pairs on each oxygen. Each oxygen now satisfies the octet rule, but nitrogen counts only six Electrons. Reassign one oxygen lone pair as a second bond pair on its N–O connection. This changes the allocation without adding an Electron; it applies the construction procedure in Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, 7.3: drawing Lewis structures.
The resulting nitrate Lewis structure has one N=O connection and two N–O connections. Its four bond pairs use eight Electrons, and its eight lone pairs use sixteen: 8+16=24. The doubly connected oxygen has two lone pairs; each singly connected oxygen has three; nitrogen has none. All four chemical atoms satisfy the octet rule. Any of the three oxygen chemical atoms can supply the additional bond pair, giving the three equivalent resonance structures below.
Why not draw three N=O connections to make the ion look symmetric? With two lone pairs on each oxygen, that drawing still spends 12+12=24 Electrons and has the right total formal charge, but places twelve Electrons around nitrogen. It fails the octet rule for this second-period chemical element. Three equivalent resonance structures express the symmetry without that invalid local count.
The economy is beautiful: a handful of dots and lines rules out many impossible counts and identifies lone pairs that can participate in acid-base chemistry. A Lewis structure helps choose rational candidate connections before a detailed quantum chemistry calculation. It does not specify a complete many-Electron wavefunction, actual electron density, or molecular geometry. Adding the separate VSEPR model, described in Chemistry 2e, 7.6: molecular structure and polarity, predicts bent water and pyramidal ammonia; the layouts above alone make no such prediction. Molecular orbital theory supplies a richer electronic description, including the unpaired Electrons of molecular oxygen that an all-paired Lewis structure misses.
In 1916 Gilbert N. Lewis proposed two-dot notation for the shared Electrons of a chemical bond and fuller dot formulae for the outer Electrons, explicitly relating a shared pair to the existing single-line notation. See Lewis, The Atom and the Molecule, JACS 38, 762–785 (1916), pp. 777–778, available as an [ref]; the relevant passage is also readable in a [ref]. The modern quantum mechanics interpretation should be distinguished from his historical model of fixed outer Electrons.
Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory
Words: 340 Articles: 2
Lewis structure OurBigBook.com
The VSEPR model predicts approximate molecular geometry by arranging the electron domains around a central chemical atom to reduce their mutual repulsion. Start with a Lewis structure, count the domains, and then distinguish the resulting electron pair geometry from the positions of the chemical atoms themselves. A lone pair counts as a domain even though it is not another chemical atom.[ref]
Three worked counts have the same total of eight valence electrons. In methane, carbon's four plus the contributions of four hydrogen chemical atoms give 4+4=8: four bond pairs, no lone pairs, and tetrahedral molecular geometry. In ammonia, nitrogen's five plus three from hydrogen give 5+3=8: three bond pairs and one lone pair, producing trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry. In water, oxygen's six plus two from hydrogen give 6+2=8: two bond pairs and two lone pairs, producing bent molecular geometry. All three have four electron domains; their molecular geometries differ.
The regular tetrahedral directions can be represented by the unit vectors
3​1​(1,1,1),3​1​(1,−1,−1),3​1​(−1,1,−1),3​1​(−1,−1,1).
(66)
Each pair has dot product −1/3, so the ideal bond angle is θ=arccos(−1/3)≈109.47∘. This is a geometric calculation, rather than a prediction that every four-domain molecule has that exact bond angle. Lone pairs and different kinds of chemical bonds distort the ideal arrangement; water's H–O–H angle is about 104.5∘.[ref]
The model is attractive because small-number bookkeeping produces a spatial prediction without first solving for every molecular orbital. Shape then helps explain chemical polarity and which hydrogen bond donor or hydrogen bond acceptor sites are accessible. It is a qualitative model, not a full calculation of the electronic energy or a universal solution for every chemical compound. Gillespie and Nyholm's 1957 review [ref] is a historical anchor for its development.
Electron domain

Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory OurBigBook.com
An electron domain is a region of electron density counted around a central chemical atom in the VSEPR model. One lone pair counts as one domain; a bond to one neighbour counts as one domain even when its bond order is two or three. Domain count is therefore different from simply counting electron pairs.
Electron pair geometry
Words: 36
Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory OurBigBook.com
Electron pair geometry describes the arrangement of all electron domains in the VSEPR model, including lone pairs. Molecular geometry instead describes the arrangement of chemical atoms. Four domains have a tetrahedral ideal arrangement, but keeping only the bonded neighbours gives the different molecular geometries of methane, ammonia and water.
Bond pair
Words: 152
Lewis structure OurBigBook.com
A bond pair is an electron pair allocated to a connection between two chemical atoms in a Lewis structure. A single line stands for one bond pair, or two Electrons. A double connection contains two bond pairs, or four Electrons; a triple connection contains three bond pairs, or six Electrons. A bond pair is shared bookkeeping for the combined arrangement, rather than two distinguishable Electrons each permanently owned by one endpoint.
In water, two bond pairs use 2×2=4 of the eight valence electrons. In ammonia, three bond pairs use 3×2=6 of the eight valence electrons. In O=C=O, each C=O connection contains two bond pairs, so there are four bond pairs in the entire carbon dioxide molecule. Counting connections and counting bond pairs therefore give different answers for multiple connections.
The same bond pair is treated differently for different questions: both endpoints count its two Electrons for the octet rule, whereas each endpoint receives just one Electron for formal charge. Neither convention asserts equal physical electron density at the endpoints. For electronic shapes, occupancy, and energy, see molecular orbital theory rather than treating a bond pair line as an entire wavefunction.
Lone pair
Words: 161
Lewis structure OurBigBook.com
A lone pair is an electron pair assigned to one chemical atom without a connecting line to another chemical atom in a Lewis structure. It is usually shown as two dots. Water has two lone pairs on oxygen, accounting for four valence electrons; ammonia has one lone pair on nitrogen, accounting for two. In O=C=O, each oxygen has two lone pairs, and carbon has none.
A lone pair can be reactive. In protonation of ammonia, the nitrogen lone pair becomes a new bond pair to a proton:
NH3​+H+⟶NH4+​.
(67)
The proton supplies no Electron, so the eight valence electrons are retained: three bond pairs plus one lone pair become four bond pairs. The resulting nitrogen has formal charge 5−0−8/2=+1; each hydrogen has formal charge zero. This is why identifying an available lone pair helps explain the chemical base behaviour of ammonia, rather than merely decorating its formula.
Lewis already used the ammonia to NH4+​ example in The Atom and the Molecule (1916), pp. 777–778. In modern terms the dots identify an allocation of Electrons, not two stationary particles or an isolated patch unaffected by the rest of the molecule. A molecular orbital description can spread electronic amplitude over several chemical atoms while a localized Lewis structure remains useful for acid-base chemistry.
Formal charge (FC=v−n−b/2)
Words: 330
Lewis structure OurBigBook.com
The formal charge of a chemical atom in a Lewis structure assigns it all of its nonbonding Electrons and half of the Electrons in its connections:
FC=v−n−2b​.
(68)
Here v is the neutral chemical atom's valence electron count, n is the number of nonbonding Electrons assigned to it, and b is the number of bonding Electrons incident on it. Count Electrons, not electron pairs: two lone pairs mean n=4, and two double connections mean b=8. The number FC gives electric charge in units of the positive elementary charge. Equal splitting is a bookkeeping convention, regardless of the actual electron density. See the IUPAC Gold Book, formal charge.
For O=C=O, each oxygen has v=6, n=4, b=4, giving formal charge 6−4−4/2=0. Carbon has v=4, n=0, b=8, giving formal charge 4−0−8/2=0. For O−−C≡O+, the left oxygen has formal charge 6−6−2/2=−1, carbon still has formal charge zero, and the right oxygen has formal charge 6−2−6/2=+1. The net electric charge is zero in either drawing.
The Lewis structure with no separated formal charges is the dominant contributor in this elementary comparison; the charge-separated drawing is a less important contributor, rather than an equally dominant alternative. This is a qualitative selection rule, not a calculation of energy or numerical chemical resonance weights. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, 7.4: comparing carbon dioxide structures. A zero formal charge does not imply zero partial atomic charge: the latter depends on partitioning the actual electron density, which a Lewis structure does not supply.
As a short consistency derivation, summing n+b/2 over all chemical atoms counts every drawn Electron once: a nonbonding Electron is assigned once, and a bonding Electron contributes half at each of its two endpoints. Thus
∑i​FCi​=∑i​vi​−Nvalence​,
(69)
where Nvalence​ is the total drawn valence electron count. The right side is the net electric charge in units of elementary charge. This catches a wrong budget even when individual octet rule checks look plausible.
Resonance (chemistry)
Words: 733 Articles: 2
Lewis structure OurBigBook.com
A single nitrate Lewis structure singles out one N=O connection, yet the three N–O chemical bonds of the isolated symmetric ion are equivalent. Chemical resonance reconciles that symmetry with the integer electron pair allocations of a Lewis structure. The equal chemical bond lengths in nitrate are discussed in The Open University, Discovering chemistry: resonance structures.
Chemical resonance uses several Lewis structures with the same chemical atom connections and total electric charge to describe electronic structure that one allocation cannot fully express. The chemical atoms stay in place; the positions of bond pairs, lone pairs, and formal charges differ between drawings. A two-headed arrow ↔ connects the drawings and is distinct from a chemical equilibrium arrow ⇌. See the IUPAC Gold Book, resonance form.
In each nitrate resonance structure, use the existing formal charge convention FC=v−n−b/2:
FC(N)FC(singly connected O)FC(doubly connected O)​=5−0−8/2=+1,=6−6−2/2=−1,=6−4−4/2=0.​
(70)
Here v counts neutral-chemical atom valence electrons, n counts nonbonding Electrons, and b counts incident bonding Electrons. The sum is +1−1−1+0=−1, agreeing with the nitrate ion's net electric charge. The formal charge rules and their distinction from actual atomic electric charge are given in Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, 7.4: formal charges and resonance.
Keep one labelled oxygen fixed while reading the three nitrate resonance structures. Its connection is double in one drawing and single in two. Equal weighting within this three-contributor Lewis structure model gives the average bond order
bN−O​=32+1+1​=34​.
(71)
The same calculation applies to all three N–O connections. Averaging the drawn formal charges similarly gives −2/3 per oxygen, while nitrogen retains +1; +1+3(−2/3)=−1. These fractions summarize the chosen contributors. They are not a measurement of partial atomic charge, a literal fraction of an Electron sitting on an oxygen, or time spent in one drawing.
The resonance hybrid has one spatially continuous electron density extending over the ion. None of its N–O chemical bonds is permanently selected as the double connection of one contributor. The dashed marks above are symbols; Electrons do not travel along them or make the marks float between chemical atoms. For isolated symmetric nitrate, symmetry makes the three N–O chemical bonds equivalent; an environment that distinguishes the oxygen sites can remove that equivalence. The fraction 4/3 alone predicts neither a chemical bond length nor a dissociation energy. The general relation between multiple chemical bonds, lengths, and strengths is discussed in 7.5 Strengths of Ionic and Covalent Bonds; its tabulated averages are not a nitrate-specific calibration of 4/3.
Ozone provides a useful two-contributor comparison. Its 3×6=18 valence electrons give three bond pairs and six lone pairs. One resonance structure has a double O–O connection on the left and a single one on the right; the other reverses these allocations while retaining the same chemical atom positions and connections. The central oxygen has one lone pair and formal charge +1; the singly connected terminal oxygen has three lone pairs and formal charge −1; the doubly connected terminal oxygen has two lone pairs and formal charge zero. Thus 6+12=18 Electrons and zero net electric charge are conserved. The equal-contributor bond order count is (2+1)/2=3/2 for either connection. See MIT 5.111, lecture 10, pp. 4–5: ozone resonance structures.
For carbon dioxide, O=C=O and O−−C≡O+ share sixteen valence electrons and the same O–C–O connections. The mirror drawing O+≡C−O− is also possible. The two charge-separated drawings are equivalent to one another for an isolated symmetric carbon dioxide molecule, but neither is equally dominant with O=C=O in the elementary formal charge comparison.
Chemical resonance does not mean that a molecule rapidly flips between drawings, nor that separate molecules at chemical equilibrium carry the individual drawings. The actual electron density belongs to one combined electronic description. In a quantum mechanics treatment, contributors enter a linear combination of many-Electron wavefunctions; a molecular orbital treatment can describe the extended electronic arrangement through molecular orbitals. The drawings alone provide neither a measured density nor numerical weights. Their usefulness is to expose the limitations of one localized allocation without pretending that every algebraically allowed Lewis structure contributes equally.

A resonance structure is one Lewis structure contributing to a chemical resonance description. The contributors retain the same atomic nuclei in the same positions, the same connections, and the same total valence electron count and electric charge; allocations of bond pairs, lone pairs, and formal charges differ. They are alternative representations of one electronic structure, not distinct substances with different atomic arrangements. See Chemistry 2e, 7.4: resonance forms.

A resonance hybrid is the combined electronic description expressed using several resonance structures. The word does not describe a mixture of separate molecules or ions: a nitrate ion has one electron density, rather than three species in chemical equilibrium. Equal weighting is appropriate for the equivalent nitrate contributors in the elementary model; the unequal carbon dioxide contributors illustrate why it is not a general rule. Octet rule
Words: 179
Lewis structure OurBigBook.com
The octet rule is a useful empirical guide: many Lewis structures of chemical compounds containing carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen give each of those chemical atoms eight Electrons when nonbonding Electrons and all incident bonding Electrons are counted. Hydrogen instead normally counts two Electrons. These are local counts, not independent budgets: a shared bond pair counts at both endpoints but only once in the molecule's valence electron total.
In water, oxygen counts 4+4=8 Electrons; in ammonia, nitrogen counts 2+6=8; in O=C=O, carbon counts 0+8=8 and each oxygen counts 4+4=8. The charge-separated carbon dioxide drawing also satisfies the octet rule, so the octet rule alone cannot select the dominant contributor. Formal charge provides another check.
The octet rule is a heuristic rather than a theorem about every chemical bond. Odd valence electron totals cannot be partitioned entirely into electron pairs, and some valid Lewis structures have fewer or more than eight Electrons around a chemical atom. See Chemistry 2e, 7.3: exceptions to the octet rule. The capacity of the s and p electron subshells, 2+6=8, helps motivate the guide for these chemical elements, but does not prove universal compliance. Lewis discussed a stable outer group of eight, together with a two-Electron arrangement for hydrogen, in The Atom and the Molecule (1916), pp. 768 and 774.

Valence electron

Words: 147
Chemical bond OurBigBook.com
A valence electron belongs to the electronic arrangement used to describe a chemical atom's chemical bonds and ordinary chemical reactions. For the neutral hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen chemical atoms used here, the valence electrons occupy the outermost occupied electron shell. Their respective electron configurations are 1s1, 1s22s22p2, 1s22s22p3, and 1s22s22p4, giving one, four, five, and six valence electrons. See Chemistry 2e, 6.4: electron configurations and valence electrons.
Lewis structures show these valence electrons while omitting the inner Electrons. Consequently, eight drawn valence electrons in water do not mean eight total Electrons: neutral water has ten, with two inner oxygen Electrons omitted. Neutral ammonia likewise has ten total Electrons but eight valence electrons; neutral carbon dioxide has twenty-two total Electrons but sixteen valence electrons.
This distinction makes the small counts useful: connections and possible lone pairs can be organized without representing every Electron or solving the entire many-Electron wavefunction. The outermost-electron shell shortcut applies to the examples above, rather than serving as a universal definition for all chemical elements; the electronic arrangement relevant to chemical bonds can also involve other electron subshells.

Polymer

Chemistry OurBigBook.com
A polymer is a large molecular chain or network built from many chemically linked repeating units. Statistical chain models idealize its microscopic structure by segment vectors and describe its conformation through distributions, correlations and scattering. A freely jointed chain fixes each segment length while allowing independent orientations; a Gaussian chain replaces the segment or coarse-grained displacement distribution by a Gaussian distribution. These ideal models neglect excluded-volume and other segment interactions.

Polymer OurBigBook.com
The Flory approximation balances the entropic cost of expanding an ideal chain against a mean-field excluded volume interaction. For N segments of length b in d spatial dimensions, minimizing R2/(Nb2)+vN2/Rd gives Rd+2∼vN3b2. This yields the scaling exponents 3/5 in three dimensions and 3/4 in two dimensions. It is a scaling approximation, not an exact numerical free energy or proof of critical exponents; confinement replaces Rd by the accessible coil volume.

Polymerization

Polymer OurBigBook.com
Polymerization converts a monomer, or a mixture of monomers, into a polymer: repeated chemical reactions establish a connected molecular chain or network. The central question is how connections form, not merely whether a material becomes solid. Joining small molecules can produce a thread that can be handled, while the individual molecules remain invisible. See IUPAC, Basic Definitions of Terms Relating to Polymers, definition 2.2.
In step-growth polymerization, complementary reactive groups on monomers and on shorter or longer chains can react with one another. A two-unit chain can join a three-unit chain to make a five-unit chain; growth does not require a specially active end to add only free monomers. An example is the Nylon 6,10 reaction of H2​N(CH2​)6​NH2​ with ClC(=O)(CH2​)8​C(=O)Cl: each amine end can form an amide connection with an acid-chloride end, with formal elimination of HCl. Both reactants have two suitable ends, allowing repeated joining. See Paula Hammond, MIT 10.569 lecture 2: step-growth joining and Hammond, lecture 5, p. 4: acid chloride–amine reaction.
In chain-growth polymerization, a monomer reacts with an active site on a growing chain, and the growth step regenerates an active site. Schematically, Pj∗​+M⟶Pj+1∗​, where j counts incorporated monomeric units and the star denotes reactivity rather than a particular electric charge. Ethene forming polyethylene is an example: the double chemical bond is converted into single chemical bonds as the carbon backbone grows. Initiation creates the active chains; subsequent reactions can deactivate them or transfer reactivity to another molecule. See IUPAC: chain polymerization and John McMurry, Organic Chemistry, 31.1: chain growth. Whether growth is stepwise or carried by an active site is a different question from whether small byproducts are released: chain-growth polymerization can also release them.
A motivating experiment: drawing nylon from a liquid interface. Feldwinn's UCSB demonstration places 25mL of an aqueous chemical solution of hexamethylenediamine, H2​N(CH2​)6​NH2​, in a 100mL beaker, then gently adds 25mL of sebacoyl chloride, ClC(=O)(CH2​)8​C(=O)Cl, in an organic solvent. The procedure specifies hexane; other parts of that handout list cyclohexane. The layers remain separate. The instructor catches material at their interface with tweezers and winds it slowly onto a glass rod; the handout reports continued spooling of Nylon 6,10. It specifies freshly prepared acid-chloride chemical solution and washing the thread before touching it. These are observations and conditions of a supervised laboratory demonstration, not measurements of chain lengths. See Feldwinn, UCSB Demonstration Library, Demo 044, pp. 1–3.
The mechanistic interpretation is that the monomers encounter one another near the interface, where amide connections produce the film; withdrawing it exposes a region where more material can form. An authored research demonstration independently reports a rapidly formed interfacial film collapsing into a thread on withdrawal, using cyclohexane and an aqueous chemical solution containing potassium hydroxide. See Polymer Day: Outreach Experiments for High School Students, Journal of Chemical Education (2017), nylon demonstration. This is the striking observation: a thread much longer than the beaker can emerge because material is continually supplied to the formation region, rather than because a pre-existing thread was hidden in the liquid.
Useful proposed controls, not results reported in those demonstrations, omit one monomer at a time while retaining the same solvents, liquid amounts, and pulling procedure. The prediction is loss of a renewable drawable Nylon 6,10 film; merely finding cloudiness would not establish polymerization, since other chemical reactions, including acid-chloride hydrolysis, can occur. See McMurry, 21.4: competing acid-chloride hydrolysis. Stopping and restarting withdrawal would probe renewal at the interface. Even successful drawing does not measure the degree of polymerization, establish a chain-length probability distribution, or prove the entire growth mechanism. Chemical identification and a molecular-size measurement would be needed for those stronger conclusions. These controls and limits are inferences from the setup, not invented experimental data.
Why almost complete reaction matters in step growth. For ideal linear step-growth polymerization, assume exactly two reactive groups per starting molecule, equal numbers of complementary groups, only joining of different chains, no rings, no branching, and no loss of chain material. Let N0​ count starting monomer molecules, including both reactant species, and let p be the fraction of either type of reactive group consumed. There are initially N0​ groups of each type, so pN0​ connections reduce the number of chain-bearing molecules to N=N0​(1−p); the count excludes small byproducts but includes unreacted monomers. The number-average degree of polymerization, measured in monomeric units, is therefore
Xn​=NN0​​=1−p1​.
(72)
Thus p=0.90, 0.99, and 0.999 give Xn​=10, 100, and 1000. Losing the last fraction of unreacted groups matters enormously. See Hammond, lecture 3: balanced step-growth conversion. This counts residues of both feed species; a Nylon 6,10 interior constitutional repeating unit contains two such monomeric units.
For an AA+BB feed with A0​≤B0​ initial reactive-group counts, put r=A0​/B0​ and now let p denote the fraction of the limiting A groups consumed. Under the same linear, no-ring assumptions, N0​=(A0​+B0​)/2 and N=N0​−pA0​, giving
Xn​=1+r−2rp1+r​.
(73)
For r=0.98, even complete consumption of A gives Xn​=(1.98)/(0.02)=99. Stoichiometry controls chain length as well as yield. See Hammond, lecture 2, pp. 2–3: stoichiometric imbalance. The liquid-interface demonstration is not a homogeneous, balanced reactor, so its thread length cannot be inserted into this formula as a molecular chain length.
A contrasting chain count. In ideal living polymerization, assume no chain termination or irreversible chain transfer, all chains initiated before the counted growth, one chain per effective initiator, a fixed chain count C, and every consumed monomer molecule incorporated into those chains. If M0​ is the initial number of feed monomer molecules and q their incorporated fraction, conservation gives Xn​=qM0​/C=qR in monomeric units, excluding initiator fragments. For R=200, incorporating half the feed gives Xn​=100. If initiation consumes one monomer molecule per chain, the fixed-chain interval starts at q=1/R, rather than q=0. See Hammond, lecture 21, p. 1: ideal living-chain count. The mean does not imply identical chain lengths. Living polymerization does not require reversible loss of monomers; the defining absence of chain termination and irreversible chain transfer is explained in Devon Shipp, IUPAC Polymer Education workshop, Radical Polymerizations II, slide 50. Ordinary chain-growth polymerization with new chains, termination, or transfer need not follow the straight line.
The useful connection is between local chemistry and a macroscopic material: selecting reactive ends and their proportions controls connectivity, while the resulting polymer's conformation is a separate problem described by models such as the freely jointed chain or Gaussian chain. Formation of chemical bonds, the count of monomeric units, and the count of statistical segments must be kept distinct.

Polymerization OurBigBook.com
In step-growth polymerization, suitable reactive groups on molecules of different chain lengths can join. The linear count and its assumptions are given in polymerization.
A one-unit monomer, a two-unit chain, and a twenty-unit chain can all be joining partners if their functional groups are compatible and accessible. Schematically, Pj​+Pk​⟶Pj+k​: the subscripts count monomeric units, and end-group chemistry is suppressed. In chain-growth propagation, by contrast, Pj∗​+M⟶Pj+1∗​ requires a free monomer and a polymerization-active site. An arbitrary pair of existing chains is not a propagation pair in that mechanism. The practical consequence of step-growth polymerization is that most monomers can have joined something while the average chain is still short.
Whether a joining step releases a small molecule is a separate question. Polycondensation releases small products during the joining chemistry, as in the Nylon 6,10 demonstration in polymerization. Polyaddition joins suitable chains without that elimination: reacting a diol with a molecule bearing two isocyanate groups can build a polyurethane. Thus step-growth polymerization and polycondensation are not synonyms.[ref]

Use an ideal feed in which every starting molecule has exactly two suitable functional groups: either one A and one B, or two A groups mixed with two B groups. Only an A–B pairing can form a joining chemical bond. Assume no loss of feed-derived material, no splitting of chains, no competing consumption of the counted functional groups, no branching, and no cyclization in step-growth polymerization. Linear here describes connectivity; a chain can bend in space. Small byproducts of polycondensation do not enter the chain-bearing molecule count.
Let N0​ count all initial feed molecules, J the number of intermolecular joins, and N all remaining chain-bearing molecules, including unreacted monomers. Each join turns two molecules into one, so N=N0​−J exactly. If chain i contains ji​ feed-derived monomeric units, conservation gives ∑i=1N​ji​=N0​. Consequently the number-average degree of polymerization is
Xn​=N∑i=1N​ji​​=N0​−JN0​​.

This is a count of both feed species' monomeric units, rather than a count of interior constitutional repeating units. For AA+BB chemistry an interior repeat often contains two feed-derived units, as explained in monomer. Equal functional group reactivities are not needed for this bookkeeping at a specified J; predicting a time course or a chain-length probability distribution requires additional assumptions.
For the figure's eight AB feed molecules, three joins can give lengths (2,3,1,1,1), so N=5 and Xn​=8/5. Joining the first two chains gives (5,1,1,1): the incorporated total stays eight, N becomes four, and Xn​=2. A graph makes the bookkeeping visible: each starting monomer molecule is a vertex of a graph, and each intermolecular joining chemical bond connects two previously distinct connected components of a graph. The connected pieces are the counted molecules.

In a balanced bifunctional feed there are initially N0​ A groups and N0​ B groups. Define the functional-group conversion in step growth by p=J/N0​: the reacted fraction of either group type. Each join consumes one of each. Therefore N=N0​(1−p). In the eight-AB example, three joins give p=3/8 and four give p=1/2. In the latter state only three of eight starting monomer molecules remain isolated: their disappearance fraction is 5/8, different from p=1/2. Neither this group-based p nor disappearance of isolated monomers is the incorporated-feed fraction in the ideal living polymerization count.
With unequal initial counts A0​≤B0​, this article always uses p=J/A0​, the conversion of the limiting A groups. The reacted fraction of B groups is J/B0​=rp, where r=A0​/B0​. The fraction of all initial functional groups consumed is 2J/(A0​+B0​)=2rp/(1+r). At nonzero conversion these three fractions coincide only at r=1. Naming the measured group type prevents an apparently correct equation from using the wrong conversion.

Xn​=1−p1​.

For an original balanced feed of 2000 monomer molecules, 1900, 1960, and 1990 intermolecular joins give p=0.95, 0.98, and 0.995. In chain-growth polymerization, each growth step joins a monomer to a reactive site on a polymer chain and regenerates that reactive site. This is the precise mechanistic restriction in IUPAC's definition: growth occurs exclusively through these monomer–chain-site reactions. The word chain refers to the succession of site-regenerating chemical reactions. It does not merely mean that the product looks like a long chain. Chain-growth initiation starts this succession; chain-growth propagation continues it; chain-growth termination and chain transfer in chain polymerization can change its fate.[ref]
The contrast with step-growth polymerization concerns the permitted joining partners. There, suitable reactive groups can join two existing chains, for example a two-unit chain and a three-unit chain. In chain-growth propagation, a free monomer adds to a polymerization-active site. Release of a small byproduct is a separate classification question: IUPAC explicitly allows condensative chain polymerization.[ref] The useful consequence is that a few growing chains can incorporate many monomer molecules while much of the feed remains unreacted. Their degree of polymerization depends on how those units are shared among chains, as finite chain-growth bookkeeping makes explicit.

Stipulate six further additions to each chain, obtaining (10,10,10,10). Other allocations with the same total also satisfy Xn​=10: living does not mean identical lengths.
Alternatively, stipulate that the first two length-four chains undergo chain-growth termination without joining, while the other two each receive twelve more monomer molecules. The final lengths are (4,4,16,16), with (C,A,S)=(4,2,40). The mean degree of polymerization is still 10, but two chains have stopped and two carry the remaining growth. The population variance of lengths is 36, compared with zero in the deliberately equal living allocation. These are synthetic populations, not measured molecular distributions and not a claim that all terminating processes are broader than all living processes. Indeed, assigning all twenty-four remaining additions to one still-active chain gives the living allocation (28,4,4,4), with the same mean but variance 108. Comparable start times and opportunities for chain-growth propagation are extra assumptions behind an expectation of more uniform lengths.
If the two terminated length-four chains instead join, their inactive product has length eight; with the same remaining additions the final lengths are (8,16,16). Now C=3, A=2, S=40 and Xn​=40/3. Thus chain-growth termination can change both which chains grow and which chains enter the denominator. Continuing chain-growth initiation, inefficient initiation, chain transfer in chain polymerization, and reactivation require their own counts. Predicting an entire length distribution additionally needs a specified reaction mechanism and growth statistics. A measured mean alone cannot establish living polymerization.

Chain-growth polymerization OurBigBook.com
NMR monitoring of chain polymerization uses nuclear magnetic resonance signals to follow monomer and other distinguishable chemical species. In a proton experiment, suitable signal integrals can track changes in their relative amounts. Disappearance of a monomer signal is a consumption readout; it is not a direct count of polymerization-active sites. Overlapping signals, baseline errors and competing chemical reactions can obstruct the inference. A pre-reaction reference and independent product characterization make the consumption interpretation stronger.
Size-exclusion characterization of chain polymers
Words: 72
Chain-growth polymerization OurBigBook.com
Size-exclusion characterization of chain polymers separates dissolved chains using porous columns and records an elution signal. Calibrating that separation against appropriate standards supplies a size-related estimate of molecular masses. Detector response and calibration must accompany any claimed molecular distribution: an elution trace is not automatically a histogram of molecule counts or degree of polymerization. Similar signals can conceal chemically different chain populations, while a shift toward larger apparent size alone does not show that every chain retained a polymerization-active site.
Monitoring chain polymerization in a sealed tube
Words: 352
Chain-growth polymerization OurBigBook.com
A simple route to deuterated polystyrene block copolymers by reverse iodine transfer polymerisation by Trevor Gavin Wright and Harald Pasch (2015, Experimental section, pp. 3237–3238) provides a concrete study of consumption and chain products. The authors used a valve-sealed J Young tube, freeze–pump–thaw preparation and argon. NMR monitoring of chain polymerization compared a 25∘C reference with spectra acquired at 70∘C every fifteen minutes for twenty-four hours. Their formulation contained an azo initiating reagent, molecular iodine and a vinyl monomer. Companion flask syntheses used stirring and a heated silicone-oil bath.
The authors followed initiating and transfer-agent signals; Figure 3 reports a transfer-agent signal rising during induction and then falling as polymerization proceeds. Their size-exclusion characterization of chain polymers used porous columns, refractive-index detection and polystyrene calibration. These distinct consumption and size readouts concern transfer-mediated chemistry; they do not establish strict living polymerization. [ref]
Useful proposed controls, rather than reported measurements, are a matched mixture omitting the initiating reagent, an unheated mixture, and a repeat of the complete formulation. Keep monomer amount, solvent, tube preparation and acquisition conditions matched where possible. The unheated comparison needs a readout that does not itself initiate polymerization; placing it in the hot probe would defeat that control. A mixture omitting iodine asks a different question: it changes chain transfer in chain polymerization and induction chemistry, so it is not necessarily a no-polymerization control. Record the pre-reaction baseline and compare crude material with isolated product; isolation can selectively remove shorter chains. These comparisons help separate initiation-dependent monomer consumption from signal drift and unrelated chemical reactions.
The mechanistic inference is deliberately limited. Consumption plus independently characterized larger chain products supports polymerization; evidence of an induction stage helps test a proposed reaction mechanism. Neither readout directly counts stars in Pj∗​, proves the absence of chain-growth termination, nor recovers every chain length. A chain-extension test would probe retained growth capability, but even a successful extension would not by itself establish that all original chains extended. No measured molecular distribution is reconstructed here. IUPAC cautions that reversible deactivation can produce living-like behaviour even when some termination occurs.[ref]

Monomer

Words: 432 Articles: 3
Polymer OurBigBook.com
A monomer is a chemical substance whose molecules can undergo polymerization and contribute units to the essential structure of a polymer. A monomer molecule is the individual reactant; its incorporated monomeric unit is the portion identifiable as derived from that reactant. Incorporation can change chemical bonds and release small byproducts, so the unit in the chain need not have the complete molecular formula of the feed molecule. See IUPAC: monomer molecule and IUPAC, A brief guide to polymer terminology: monomeric units.
Three different counts answer three different questions. Monomer molecules describe the feed; monomeric units trace that feed's contributions to the product; a constitutional repeating unit describes the smallest chemical pattern repeating along a regular chain. In Nylon 6,10, two different monomers supply one interior constitutional repeating unit,
−NH−(CH2​)6​−NH−C(=O)−(CH2​)8​−C(=O)−.
(82)
Its molecular formula is C16​H30​N2​O2​. The diamine feed is C6​H16​N2​, and the diacid-chloride feed is C10​H16​Cl2​O2​; subtracting two HCl gives the interior-repeat budget. For a finite linear chain made from n of each reactant, there are 2n−1 joining connections, hence 2n−1 formal HCl eliminations, rather than 2n. One amine end and one acid-chloride end remain in that ideal unmodified chain. This is a stoichiometry check on the depicted reaction, not a claim that the washed experimental thread retains those ends. The reacting end-group chemistry is documented in Hammond, lecture 5, p. 4; the specified Nylon 6,10 reactant pair is reported in Polymer Day, nylon demonstration.
Ethene shows the reverse counting mismatch. One CH2​=CH2​ monomer molecule contributes a two-carbon −CH2​−CH2​− monomeric unit to ideal linear polyethylene, without a small byproduct in that growth step. But the smallest constitutional repeating unit of its uniform backbone is just −CH2​−: a chain containing m incorporated ethene monomeric units contains 2m such interior one-carbon repeats. End groups are additional bookkeeping. The frequently drawn [−CH2​−CH2​−]m​ is useful for tracing the feed, although it is not the smallest constitutional repeat. The minimum-pattern definition is given in IUPAC: constitutional repeating unit; the ethene growth chemistry is described by [ref].
A segment of a freely jointed chain or Gaussian chain instead belongs to a statistical model. It can represent many chemical bonds and several constitutional repeating units; its length and the segment count are chosen to describe chain conformation at the intended scale. The three-repeats-per-segment drawing in Figure 34. "From two liquid layers to a Nylon 6,10 thread: monomers, a constitutional repeating unit, and statistical segments" is a deliberately arbitrary coarse-graining example, not a measured Kuhn length. Always state the counting convention before substituting a segment count for a degree of polymerization. This separation lets chemistry track which chemical atoms entered the material while statistical models track how the material bends and extends.

Nucleic acid

Words: 2k Articles: 13
Polymer OurBigBook.com
A nucleic acid is a polymer built from linked nucleotides. The two principal kinds are DNA and RNA. Each nucleotide contributes a sugar, a nucleobase, and phosphate to the chain; the nucleobase is only the letter-bearing component, not the entire nucleotide. DNA uses deoxyribose, whereas RNA uses ribose. A chain of six nucleotides is therefore not six free nucleobases placed beside one another. See NHGRI: nucleic acids.
The chemical scaffold and the variable lettering do different jobs. Covalent bonds maintain the sugar–phosphate backbone, while the order of attached nucleobases specifies the nucleic acid sequence. A phosphodiester bond links the 3′ position of one sugar to the 5′ position of the next through phosphate. These position numbers refer to carbon chemical atoms in the sugar; they define a strand's direction even when it bends or forms a circle. See Brown, Genomes, 2nd edition: the human genome.
This division is useful: the backbone supplies a connected physical record, and base pairing allows its letters to recognize partners. DNA replication copies that record, and transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA. RNA can also fold into functional shapes through base pairing within one chain; a nucleic acid sequence specifies chemical order, not a requirement for a straight shape. The beauty is that the same kind of polymer can carry a message and form a structure that acts on messages.

Nucleic acid sequence

Words: 255 Articles: 1
Nucleic acid OurBigBook.com
A nucleic acid sequence records the ordered nucleobases of a nucleic acid strand, conventionally read from 5′ to 3′. The standard DNA alphabet is adenine A, cytosine C, guanine G, and thymine T; the standard RNA alphabet uses uracil U in place of thymine T. Each letter denotes the nucleobase attached to one nucleotide, so the six-letter DNA nucleic acid sequence 5′-ACGTAC-3′ describes six linked nucleotides. See NHGRI: representing DNA by a sequence of letters.
Order carries information that composition loses. Both ACGTAC and AACCGT contain two adenine, two cytosine, one guanine, and one thymine nucleobase, but their nucleic acid sequences differ at positions 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. At position 2, for example, the first has cytosine and the second adenine. Reporting only the four counts cannot reconstruct either ordered record.
To obtain the partner of 5′-ACGTAC-3′, apply the DNA base pairing rules position by position: A selects T, C selects G, G selects C, T selects A, A selects T, and C selects G. Alignment gives 3′-TGCATG-5′. Its opposite end labels matter because the two are antiparallel nucleic acid strands. Reading the partner from its own 5′ end reverses the aligned lettering and yields the reverse complement, 5′-GTACGT-3′.
Reversal alone gives CATGCA; complementation alone gives aligned TGCATG. Neither operation alone gives the partner written in the usual 5′-to-3′ convention. Applying the reverse complement operation twice returns ACGTAC: GTACGT complements to CATGCA, which reverses to ACGTAC. This convention makes a single reported strand sufficient to specify an ideally complementary DNA duplex, provided its direction is known.
Reverse complement
Words: 14
Nucleic acid sequence OurBigBook.com
A nucleotide sequence obtained by reversing the order and complementing each nucleobase according to the appropriate base pairing rules.

Base pair (bp)

Words: 328 Articles: 1
Nucleic acid OurBigBook.com
A base pair is an association of two nucleobases through hydrogen bonds in a compatible arrangement. It commonly joins opposite strands of a nucleic acid double helix, but can also join two regions of one folded RNA strand. Canonical Watson–Crick DNA base pairs match adenine with thymine and guanine with cytosine; canonical RNA base pairs use adenine with uracil instead. The nucleobases belong to complete nucleotides, including their attached sugars and backbone phosphate. See NHGRI: base pair.
The abbreviation bp also measures the length of a paired region. Our ACGTAC/TGCATG duplex has six base pairs, containing twelve nucleotides altogether. Its upper strand contains two adenine, two cytosine, one guanine, and one thymine nucleobase; the lower contains one, one, two, and two respectively. Combined, the counts are three of each nucleobase. Equality of total adenine and thymine, or of total guanine and cytosine, need not hold within either individual strand.
Base pairing
Words: 205
Base pair OurBigBook.com
Base pairing is the recognition and association of compatible nucleobases. In canonical Watson–Crick geometry, an adenine–thymine base pair has two hydrogen bonds, while a guanine–cytosine base pair has three. These counts refer to those specific geometries and usual chemical forms; they are not a definition of every possible base pair. RNA can also contain other pairings, and canonical adenine–uracil pairing replaces adenine–thymine pairing. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: DNA structure.
For this illustrative duplex, the six base pairs are A–T, C–G, G–C, T–A, A–T, and C–G. Thus three contribute two hydrogen bonds each and three contribute three each:
3×2+3×3=15.
(83)
Each dotted connector in the diagram counts one hydrogen bond; coloured boxes denote whole nucleobases, not individual chemical atoms. The solid rails denote the covalent bond scaffold. Separating the two strands disrupts base pairing and base stacking without requiring the backbone to be cut.
The count of fifteen hydrogen bonds is not fifteen identical contributions to a duplex's Gibbs free energy. Base stacking, interactions with water and ions, temperature, and the order of neighbouring base pairs also matter. Knowing the fraction of guanine–cytosine base pairs alone does not fix a nucleic acid double helix's shape or stability. See Brown, Genomes: pairing and stacking interactions. What makes base pairing especially useful is its selectivity: an exposed DNA strand constrains the partner's nucleic acid sequence, giving DNA replication a chemical recognition rule.

Nucleic acid double helix

Words: 368 Articles: 2
Nucleic acid OurBigBook.com
A nucleic acid double helix consists of two nucleic acid strands winding around a common axis. In the familiar DNA arrangement, sugar–phosphate backbones lie outside and paired nucleobases lie inside, stacked along the axis. The strands are antiparallel nucleic acid strands. The flattened base pairing ladder above displays partners and direction; winding that ladder into a helix adds spatial organization. RNA can also form double-helical paired regions, so the geometry is not exclusive to DNA. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: DNA structure.
The useful surprise is that a structure explains a copying principle. Complementary base pairs allow each DNA strand to specify the other's nucleic acid sequence; separate strands can each act as templates in DNA replication. This is a structural constraint, while the enzymes and stages of DNA replication supply the actual process. A nucleic acid sequence specifies letter order without, by itself, giving every detail of the three-dimensional helix.
On 25 April 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick published a model with two oppositely directed chains, outside phosphate groups, and specific base pairs. Their short paper explicitly connected this pairing to a possible copying mechanism, while describing the model as requiring further experimental tests. See the original [ref], with an accessible [ref].
Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling's paper in the same issue had a different role: it presented X-ray diffraction evidence from DNA fibres and its structural interpretation, including the helical character of the wetter B form and evidence for phosphate groups on the outside. They distinguished forms produced at different water contents and assessed compatibility with the Watson–Crick model. Read their original [ref]. The model and the experimental analysis are distinct contributions; a diffraction pattern is evidence constraining a molecular geometry, rather than a direct picture of letter-by-letter base pairing.
Antiparallel nucleic acid strands

Nucleic acid double helix OurBigBook.com
Two nucleic acid strands with opposite directional alignment: a 5′-to-3′ direction on one is aligned with the 3′-to-5′ direction on the other.
Base stacking

Nucleic acid double helix OurBigBook.com
Base stacking is the close arrangement and interaction of neighbouring nucleobases with their approximately planar faces above one another. Along a nucleic acid double helix, neighbouring base pairs stack successively; base pairing instead associates partners across the two strands. Both affect duplex stability, and the interactions depend on the identities and arrangement of neighbouring nucleobases. See Brown, Genomes: base pairing and base stacking.

Deoxyribonucleic acid

Words: 453
Nucleic acid OurBigBook.com
Deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA, is a nucleotide polymer that stores biological information in its nucleotide sequence. The crucial variable is order: two DNA molecules can contain the same numbers of each nucleobase yet carry different nucleotide sequences. This makes a physical molecule an inheritable record, rather than merely a mixture of ingredients. Genes are functional regions of that record; the whole DNA nucleotide sequence is not one long gene. See NHGRI: DNA fact sheet.
Each DNA strand has a backbone of alternating deoxyribose sugars and phosphate groups joined through covalent bonds. Attached nucleobases supply the familiar four-letter alphabet: adenine A, thymine T, guanine G, and cytosine C. In ordinary double-stranded DNA, base pairing matches A with T and G with C. The backbone connects successive nucleotides along a strand; base pairing connects partners across strands. Keeping these two connections distinct explains how strands can separate while each retains its own nucleotide sequence.
The two backbones have directions, conventionally labelled 5′ and 3′ after numbered carbon chemical atoms in deoxyribose. They form antiparallel nucleic acid strands: following one from 5′ to 3′ takes you opposite to the other's 5′-to-3′ direction. For the chosen DNA nucleotide sequence 5′-ATGCC-3′, write its partner directly underneath as 3′-TACGG-5′. Now read that partner from its own 5′ end: its reverse complement is 5′-GGCAT-3′. Complementing letters and reversing their order are separate operations. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: the structure and function of DNA.
The diagram's rails represent sugar–phosphate backbones and its coloured blocks represent nucleobases, not individual chemical atoms. Reading left to right gives five matched positions: A–T, T–A, G–C, C–G, C–G. There are two A–T-type base pairs and three G–C-type base pairs; the complete two-strand example contains ten nucleotides. Reversing the bottom row changes the reading convention, not the physical partners. Real double-stranded DNA winds into a nucleic acid double helix; the flattened ladder emphasizes base pairing and direction without pretending to show its three-dimensional geometry.
The motivating consequence is copying by a template. After strands separate, each existing DNA strand specifies which incoming nucleotides should accompany it through base pairing. DNA replication uses enzymes to build complementary strands, allowing the record to persist through successive biological cells. Base pairing supplies a selection rule, while enzymes perform the chemistry: a matching diagram alone is not a complete copying mechanism. The connection between structure and copying was already central to the model published by Watson and Crick on 25 April 1953. See Watson and Crick, Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids, Nature 171, 737–738 (1953).
Stored information needs interpretation. Some DNA regions specify proteins through RNA; others contribute to functional RNA or regulate gene expression, and some have no known function. Non-coding DNA means sequence that does not specify a protein's sequence of amino acids, not automatically useless sequence. Nor does a DNA nucleotide sequence alone determine an organism's fate: phenotypes also depend on biological context and environment. See NHGRI: non-coding DNA. Its double-stranded form is often modeled mechanically as a worm-like chain, with elasticity and effective excluded volume depending on solvent conditions.

Ribonucleic acid

Words: 414 Articles: 3
Nucleic acid OurBigBook.com
Ribonucleic acid, or RNA, is a nucleotide polymer whose nucleotide sequence can both carry information and organize a working molecular shape. Its backbone contains alternating ribose sugars and phosphate groups connected through covalent bonds. Its usual nucleobases are adenine A, uracil U, guanine G, and cytosine C. Thus RNA uses U where DNA uses T; its ribose also differs chemically from DNA's deoxyribose. See NHGRI: RNA.
In transcription, an enzyme uses one DNA strand as a template for RNA. For example, the DNA template 3′-TACGG-5′ specifies 5′-AUGCC-3′ in RNA. The base pairing rules now include A–U rather than A–T, while G–C remains. This RNA matches the other DNA strand's 5′-to-3′ lettering after T is replaced by U. Identifying the template strand matters: replacing T by U in an arbitrarily chosen DNA strand is not a general method for deriving the RNA product. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: from DNA to RNA.
RNA is often a single strand, but single-stranded does not mean straight or entirely unpaired. Complementary regions within one RNA molecule can undergo base pairing, bringing distant positions together. Consider the illustrative twelve-nucleotide nucleotide sequence 5′-GCAUUUUUAUGC-3′. Pair positions 1 with 12, 2 with 11, 3 with 10, and 4 with 9. The resulting stem-loop has four base pairs: G–C, C–G, A–U, U–A. Positions 5–8 remain unpaired in the loop. Both arms belong to the same continuous backbone, and the paired arms have the directions of antiparallel nucleic acid strands.
The diagram proposes a possible pairing pattern, not a prediction that this short RNA must adopt that shape under every condition. Actual RNA folding depends on additional interactions, temperature, ions, and associated proteins; the full three-dimensional arrangement contains more information than the drawn base pairs. The example's purpose is to show how a linear nucleotide sequence can specify contacts within itself.
Different RNA roles make this flexibility useful. Messenger RNA carries a message that a ribosome reads during translation to build a protein. Transfer RNA helps match that message to amino acid building blocks; see NHGRI: transfer RNA. Ribosomal RNA forms structural and catalytic parts of the ribosome. Other RNA participates in gene regulatory networks, changing how strongly genes are expressed. Many RNA molecules therefore function without being translated into proteins; for some genes, functional RNA is the product itself.
Most strikingly, some folded RNA acts as an enzyme: these catalytic RNA molecules are ribozymes. The ribosome's bond-forming active site is built from RNA, although the complete ribosome also contains proteins. Structural evidence appears in Nissen et al., The structural basis of ribosome activity in peptide bond synthesis, Science 289, 920–930 (2000). RNA therefore connects a readable record with physical recognition, regulation, and catalysis: the same kind of polymer can be a message, an adaptor, or part of molecular machinery.

Radius of gyration (Rg2​=2N21​∑m,n​⟨∣Rm​−Rn​∣2⟩)

Polymer OurBigBook.com
For N equally weighted positions, the squared radius of gyration is the average squared distance from the center of mass: Rg2​=N−1∑n​⟨∣Rn​−Rcm​∣2⟩, where Rcm​=N−1∑n​Rn​. Expanding pair differences gives ∑m,n​∣Rm​−Rn​∣2=2N∑n​∣Rn​−Rcm​∣2, and therefore
Rg2​=2N21​∑m,n​⟨∣Rm​−Rn​∣2⟩.
(84)
For a Gaussian chain or freely jointed chain with these N positions and mean squared link length b2, each pair variance is b2∣m−n∣. Summing separations yields Rg2​=b2(N2−1)/(6N)∼Nb2/6. Counting all endpoints of N links instead gives N+1 positions and the corresponding finite-size formula.

Ion (q=ze)

Words: 472 Articles: 9
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
An ion is a chemical atom or a group of chemical atoms with a nonzero net electric charge. A positive ion is a cation; a negative ion is an anion. The whole entity carries the electric charge: a hydronium ion is a group of four chemical atoms with net charge +e. This definition agrees with [ref].
For an ordinary ion containing only atomic nuclei and Electrons, let Np​ count all its protons and Ne​ all its Electrons. Each proton contributes the elementary charge +e, each Electron contributes −e, and neutrons contribute zero. Therefore
q=(Np​−Ne​)e=ze,z=Np​−Ne​.
(85)
The signed integer z is the net electric charge number. Removing an Electron increases z by one; adding an Electron decreases z by one. Changing the Electron count leaves the atomic number, and therefore the identity of the chemical element, unchanged.
For example, a neutral sodium chemical atom has 11 protons and 11 Electrons. Its cation Na+ still has 11 protons, but only 10 Electrons, so q=(11−10)e=+e. A neutral chlorine chemical atom has 17 protons and 17 Electrons; its anion Cl− has 17 protons and 18 Electrons, so q=(17−18)e=−e. These are particle inventories, not pictures of atomic orbitals. See 2.6 Ionic and Molecular Compounds (§2.6: ions and ionic compounds).
One sodium chloride formula unit accounts for one Na+ cation and one Cl− anion, whose net electric charges sum to zero. Ordinary solid sodium chloride is an extended arrangement of ions, rather than discrete NaCl molecules. This is a useful distinction: a neutral material can contain charged constituents, and its chemical formula tells us their ratio without claiming that each pair is a separate molecule.
Ion bookkeeping connects chemistry to electric current: moving ions can transport electric charge, while stationary ions cannot supply a transport current density. In electrochemistry, both signs of ions can contribute to the same conventional current. An ion opposing a fixed electric charge is called a counterion.
