Electrochemistry

Words: 4k Articles: 15
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
Electrochemistry studies how chemical reactions, transport, and chemical equilibrium couple to electric charge and electric potential. In a cell, Electrons travel through the external circuit, while mobile ions carry electric current through the electrolyte. At the electrodes, redox reactions connect these two forms of electric charge transport. This connection makes it possible both to obtain electrical work from a chemical reaction and to use electrical work to drive a chemical reaction.
An anode is an electrode where oxidation occurs; a cathode is an electrode where reduction occurs. These definitions refer to the chemical reactions, rather than universal positive or negative terminal signs. In a galvanic cell delivering electrical work, the anode is negative and the cathode positive. In an electrolytic cell driven by an external source, the anode is positive and the cathode negative. See Pingarrón et al., Terminology of electrochemical methods of analysis (IUPAC Recommendations 2019), §§3.1 and 3.4 and Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §17.2: galvanic cells.
For a worked example, consider an electrolytic cell containing molten sodium chloride, with the anode connected to the positive terminal and the cathode to the negative terminal of an external source. At the cathode, sodium cations gain Electrons; at the anode, chlorine anions lose Electrons:
cathode, reduction:anode, oxidation:overall:​2Na++2e−⟶2Na,2Cl−⟶Cl2​+2e−,2Na++2Cl−⟶2Na+Cl2​.​
(86)
The first line has net electric charge zero on each side; the second has −2e on each side. Adding the lines cancels the transferred Electrons and preserves both chemical atom counts and net electric charge. The sodium product is neutral, and the chlorine product is a diatomic molecule. These equations specify molten sodium chloride; aqueous chemical solutions introduce competing water reactions. See 17.7 Electrolysis (§17.7: electrolysis of molten sodium chloride).
Electrochemistry underlies battery charging and the manufacture of chemicals by electrolysis. Its particularly useful idea is that an Electron inventory in a balanced chemical equation also accounts for transported electric charge. Transport alone is a different question from an electrode chemical reaction: an ion may carry electric current through the electrolyte without itself being consumed at an electrode.
Historically, Michael Faraday introduced the terms electrode, electrolyte, anion, cation, and ion in the terminology section of his 1834 paper, Experimental Researches in Electricity, Seventh Series by Michael Faraday (§§662–667). His §667 explicitly treats the direction assigned to electric current as a convention. His ion language predates the modern Electron and atomic nucleus picture used in the charge-counting example above.
For an electrolyte near chemical equilibrium, a Poisson-Boltzmann equation can approximate the distribution of ions in an electric potential. Such an equilibrium model does not by itself describe a cell carrying sustained electric current.

Electrode

Words: 397 Articles: 2
Electrochemistry OurBigBook.com
An electrode is an electronic electrical conductor in contact with an electrolyte. In a cell carrying sustained redox electric current, chemical reactions at this interface exchange Electrons with chemical species. An electrode can participate in the chemical reaction, as the dissolving zinc anode of a Daniell cell does, or provide a conducting surface without appearing in the net chemical equation. This distinction is illustrated by active and inert electrodes in Flowers, Theopold, Langley and Robinson, Chemistry 2e, §17.2.
The interface connects two kinds of electric charge transport: Electrons in the external electrical circuit and ions in the electrolyte. The same Electron does not travel through the wire, swim through the salt bridge, and complete a circuit! The half-reactions account for how electronic and ionic transport meet. This is the useful idea behind both obtaining electrical work in a galvanic cell and supplying electrical work in an electrolytic cell.
Name an electrode from its net chemical reaction: oxidation means anode, and reduction means cathode. State the operating mode before assigning terminal signs. For a galvanic cell supplying a passive load, the anode is negative and the cathode positive; for an ordinary two-terminal electrolytic cell driven by a source, the anode is positive and the cathode negative. Here positive means higher terminal electric potential than the other electrode, not a claim that the bulk material has a large positive net electric charge. See Pingarrón et al., Terminology of electrochemical methods of analysis (IUPAC Recommendations 2019), §§3.1 and 3.4.

Anode

Words: 97
Electrode OurBigBook.com
The anode is the electrode at which the net electrode chemical reaction is oxidation: the reacting chemical species loses Electrons. This definition is independent of terminal sign. See IUPAC Gold Book: anode.
During Daniell cell discharge, a zinc chemical atom becomes a Zn2+ cation, leaving two Electrons in the electrode; those Electrons leave through the external electrical circuit. The zinc anode is the negative terminal. In an externally driven electrolytic cell, Electrons instead leave the anode through the lead to the source's positive terminal. Conventional current in that lead points toward the anode, opposite to Electron motion. The anode can therefore be positive while still being the site of oxidation. See Daniell cell for the balanced half-reaction and electrode for the operating-mode sign conventions.

Cathode

Words: 98
Electrode OurBigBook.com
The cathode is the electrode at which the net electrode chemical reaction is reduction: the reacting chemical species gains Electrons. This definition is independent of terminal sign. During Daniell cell discharge, Cu2+ cations accept Electrons arriving at the copper cathode and become neutral copper. The cathode is then the positive terminal. In an externally driven electrolytic cell, the source's negative terminal supplies Electrons to the negative cathode. See Pingarrón et al., §3.4: cathode and Daniell cell.
An ion carrying electric current need not undergo reduction at the cathode. For example, in the ideal Daniell cell charge-balance picture, potassium cations arriving from a salt bridge remain dissolved while Cu2+ cations are consumed. Follow the half-reaction to identify the reacting species; follow electric charge conservation to account for the other moving ions.

Galvanic cell

Words: 1k Articles: 2
Electrochemistry OurBigBook.com
A galvanic cell supplies electrical work from a spontaneous redox chemical reaction under the specified conditions. In discharge through a passive load, oxidation occurs at its negative anode and reduction at its positive cathode. Separating the reacting compartments makes the Electrons take an external route, where their transport can deliver useful work. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §17.2: separated reactions and electrical work.
In the metallic external electrical circuit, Electrons move from anode to cathode, while conventional current goes from cathode through the load to anode. Inside the cell, net ionic conventional current closes the loop from the anode compartment toward the cathode compartment. Oppositely moving cations and anions can both contribute to that direction; see electrolyte for the signed current density calculation. A cell can maintain a nonzero terminal electric potential difference near open circuit while delivering almost no power; the Daniell cell voltage and load experiment makes this distinction concrete.

Daniell cell

Words: 978 Articles: 1
Galvanic cell OurBigBook.com
A Daniell cell uses the zinc/Zn2+ and Cu2+/copper pairs. In the separated-compartment teaching version, a zinc electrode contacts an aqueous chemical solution containing Zn2+, and a copper electrode contacts one containing Cu2+. A salt bridge supplies an ionic connection; a wire and load supply an electronic connection. During discharge,
anode, oxidation:cathode, reduction:net:​Zn(s)⟶Zn2+(aq)+2e−,Cu2+(aq)+2e−⟶Cu(s),Zn(s)+Cu2+(aq)⟶Zn2+(aq)+Cu(s).​
(87)
The zinc electrode loses material and copper is deposited at the cathode. Each half-reaction conserves chemical atom counts and electric charge: the first has net charge zero on each side, the second +2e−2e=0 on the left and zero on the right. The net reaction has +2e on both sides, with no Electrons left in its chemical equation. The Zn/Cu teaching cell and these half-reactions are described in Florida State University, Redox Reactions in Voltaic Cells: Construction of a Potential Series, lab background.
Creating one mole of Zn2+ adds 2F of positive electric charge to the anode compartment's ionic inventory; consuming one mole of Cu2+ removes 2F of positive electric charge from the cathode compartment. Here F is the Faraday constant. In an ideal bookkeeping example using a potassium nitrate salt bridge, two moles of nitrate anions entering the anode compartment compensate the first change, and two moles of potassium cations entering the cathode compartment compensate the second. Other ions in the cell can share the actual transport. The two compensating inventory changes do not mean that 4F flowed through the load: the same series electric current transports 2F through each cross-section of the circuit per mole of net reaction. See salt bridge.
Under standard-state conditions near 298K, tabulated reduction potentials give a cell electromotive force of approximately 1.10V. This is a reversible reference value, not a promised loaded reading; actual composition matters through thermodynamic activity. The tabulated copper and zinc values and their subtraction are given in Purdue University, Electrochemical Reactions: standard-state reduction potentials. For the net chemical equation as written, the molar Gibbs free energy change obeys
Δr​G=−2FE.
(88)
Thus E=1.10V corresponds to about −212kJmol−1 of net reaction. At fixed temperature and pressure, −Δr​G is the maximum reversible electrical work per mole for this cell reaction. It is not automatically all the heat released by a finite-current cell. See 17.4 Potential, Free Energy, and Equilibrium (§17.4: cell potential and free energy).
Daniell cell voltage and load experiment
Words: 651
Daniell cell OurBigBook.com
The motivating observation is that a chemical reaction can produce a signed electrical reading even when its reacting materials occupy separate vessels. UC San Diego's teaching demonstration places a copper strip in 0.1molL−1 CuSO4​ and a zinc strip in 0.1molL−1 ZnSO4​, using two 400mL beakers with about 300mL of chemical solution in each. The strips connect to a voltage meter. Initially there is no ionic connection; the demonstration specifies a zero reading. A filter-paper salt bridge containing aqueous Na2​SO4​ then connects the chemical solutions. With the meter's positive lead on copper and negative lead on zinc, its reported readings are about +1.1V; exchanging the leads reverses the reading. These are observations reported by the university, not data generated for this article. See UC San Diego, demonstration 9B: apparatus, bridge control and meter polarity.
The controls answer different questions. Exchanging only the meter leads checks the sign convention; it does not reverse the chemical reaction or swap the anode and cathode. Interrupting only the salt bridge tests the need for an ionic return path. Its absence prevents sustained cell electric current, but a very high-input-resistance meter may still show a transient or unstable reading while interfaces store electric charge. The zero reading specified for the university's apparatus is therefore not a universal theorem for every meter. Reconnecting the same salt bridge distinguishes a reversible interruption from a disconnected wire or exhausted chemical solution. This interpretation follows from electric charge conservation in a model allowing interfacial electric charge storage; see IUPAC Gold Book: integral capacitance of an electrode for the capacitance associated with electrode charge.
To distinguish terminal electric potential difference from delivered power, compare the nearly open-circuit reading with readings across a known resistor load. In the nearly open-circuit condition, a meter with input electrical resistance much larger than the cell's effective internal electrical resistance draws little electric current. With a load, measure its terminal electric potential difference V and infer I=V/R using Ohm's law; track the readings over time and repeat the nearly open-circuit reading afterwards. Keep the temperature, chemical solution compositions, immersed electrode areas, bridge geometry and electrical contacts comparable. This is a model-based extension of the documented demonstration, not a claim that UC San Diego published a load sweep. A finite-current drop can reflect ionic electrical resistance, changes of interfacial reaction rates, or depletion near an electrode; a single voltage reading cannot identify which dominates. The interfacial and composition contributions are distinguished in IUPAC Gold Book: overpotential and [ref].
For a deliberately simplified calculation, model the cell by a constant electromotive force E in series with a constant internal electrical resistance r, and a passive load R>0. Take I positive from the cathode through the load to the anode. Then
I=R+rE​,V=IR=E−Ir,Pload​=IV=I2R.
(89)
The nearly open-circuit limit R→∞ gives V→E but I→0 and Pload​→0. A straight V-versus-I line is a prediction of constant r, not a general law for electrochemistry. See Ling, Sanny and Moebs, University Physics II, §10.1: internal resistance, terminal voltage and load.
For the chosen values, I=5.50mA and V=0.550V. Holding these toy parameters fixed for 600s gives transported electric charge Q=It=3.30C and an extent of reaction ξ=Q/(2F)≃17.1μmol, assuming all the electric current serves the two specified half-reactions. The same ξ counts zinc consumed and copper deposited, rather than equal masses. The energy budget is
EQ=3.630J=1.815J delivered to loadVQ​​+1.815J internal dissipationI2rt​​.
(90)
The load's electrical work also becomes Joule heating when the load is a resistor. Here EQ accounts for the reaction's available reversible electrical work; a full cell thermal budget would also require its thermodynamic entropy contribution. Real measurements need uncertainty estimates, a specified meter input electrical resistance and calibration, and allowance for changing composition and unwanted chemical reactions. The toy value r=100Ω is not a measured property of the university's cell.

Electrolysis

Words: 2k Articles: 2
Electrochemistry OurBigBook.com
Electrolysis uses an external source of electrical work to drive redox chemical reactions at the electrodes of an electrolytic cell. Its characteristic application is forcing a chemical reaction in a direction that is nonspontaneous under the specified conditions: a discharging galvanic cell supplies electrical work, whereas electrolysis consumes electrical work. This makes electrolysis useful for producing otherwise difficult-to-obtain chemical substances, charging a rechargeable battery, and depositing a metal coating on a conducting object.[ref]
Always identify the anode by oxidation and the cathode by reduction. In ordinary driven two-terminal operation, the source withdraws Electrons from the positive anode and delivers Electrons to the negative cathode. In a discharging galvanic cell, the anode is negative and the cathode positive. Thus terminal signs change with operating mode, while the reaction definitions remain valid. Through the electrolyte, ions transport electric charge; they need not all be consumed at an electrode. The electrolyte and electrolytic cell articles explain this transport and its conventional current direction.
For a net chemical equation transferring z Electrons per reaction event, the molar reaction Gibbs free energy obeys
Δr​G=−zFEchem​,
(91)
where F is the Faraday constant and Echem​ is the reversible cell electromotive force for the reaction in the written direction. A nonspontaneous direction has Δr​G>0 and Echem​<0 at fixed temperature and pressure. The ideal opposing voltage magnitude is Δr​G/(zF); sustaining a finite electric current generally needs additional drive because of electrical resistance and finite electrode reaction rates. This thermodynamic voltage concerns the actual composition, rather than necessarily standard conditions.[ref] Not every use of electrolysis increases bulk chemical Gibbs free energy: transferring copper between equivalent surfaces can have zero bulk Δr​G while the source still supplies dissipated electrical work. See the existing electrolytic cell example.
A particularly revealing experiment measures copper transfer instead of merely looking for a coating. Two separated copper electrodes stand in aqueous CuSO4​ electrolyte in a vessel, with insulated leads to a regulated direct-current power supply, a series ammeter and a switch. A balance reads each electrode's mass before and after a timed run. The Institute of Physics describes copper cells with ammeters, adjustable current and removable cathodes; its comparison uses three similar cells at 1A for ten minutes, 0.5A for ten minutes, and 0.5A for twenty minutes. The specified observation to test is that deposited copper mass is proportional to electric current times time. These are documented experimental settings, not measurements generated here.[ref]
The ideal half-reactions are
anode, oxidation:cathode, reduction:​Cu(s)⟶Cu2+(aq)+2e−,Cu2+(aq)+2e−⟶Cu(s).​
(92)
Each deposited copper chemical atom requires two Electrons, so z=2. The anode loses copper and the cathode gains it; ideally their mass changes have equal magnitudes, and the bulk copper cation inventory stays constant. Local concentrations near the electrodes can nevertheless differ. The sulfate anions participate in ionic transport without appearing in these net half-reactions; electronic electric current in the wires becomes ionic electric current in the electrolyte through the two interfaces.[ref]
Clean, rinse, dry and identify the electrodes before their initial weighing. After interrupting the electric current, rinse away adhering electrolyte, dry again and weigh without rubbing off the deposit. KIT's university practical explicitly calls for distilled-water rinsing, careful drying and weighing both electrodes; it warns that loose copper grains can be lost during handling.[ref] Useful additional controls are repeated drying and weighing until the reading stabilizes, and a matched unpowered immersion followed by the same rinse/dry cycle. These controls test retained liquid, residual dissolved salts, handling loss and chemical changes unrelated to passed electric charge; they are proposed checks, not additional observations reported by KIT. Keep immersed electrode area, spacing, electrolyte composition and temperature comparable across runs, and keep the electrodes from touching.
Record the electric current as a function of time, together with the exact switch-on and switch-off times. Taking I(t)≥0 in the chosen deposition direction, the transported electric charge is
Q=∫t0​t1​​I(t)dt.
(93)
For constant electric current, Q=I(t1​−t0​); with sampled readings, use numerical integration rather than assuming that one ammeter reading remained constant. The two equal-charge Institute of Physics settings each give 600C, while its shorter 0.5A setting gives 300C. With MCu​=63.546gmol−1, the mass per amount of substance tabulated by KIT, and F≈96485.33212Cmol−1, ideal Faraday's laws of electrolysis predict
mCu​=2FMCu​Q​≈{0.09879g,0.19758g,​Q=300C,Q=600C.​
(94)
These are calculated predictions for complete conversion of the measured electric charge into retained copper, not experimental results. For a stable process, doubling the electric charge doubles the deposited mass; equal electric charge gives equal deposited mass even when the electric current and duration differ.
The balance reading is a test of the whole model. Competing reduction of water or other chemical species can divert electric current from copper deposition; transient electrode capacitance can also consume part of a short pulse without producing copper. A fragile deposit can detach even when its formation used the expected electric charge. Conversely, retained electrolyte or salts can increase an apparent mass gain. Comparing anode loss with cathode gain helps detect such problems but does not identify every cause. A slope below MCu​/(2F) alone cannot distinguish competing chemical reactions from lost deposit. Current efficiency measures the fraction of transported electric charge assigned to a specified electrode reaction, rather than the fraction of electrical energy stored chemically.[ref]
The beautiful connection is that an electrical measurement counts chemical events: integrating electric current and reading a balance provide two ways of following the same Electron stoichiometry. This makes electrolysis useful for controlling coating quantity and for testing a charge-to-amount of substance relation. It does not determine coating uniformity, adhesion or the required voltage, which depend on transport and electrode chemical kinetics as well.

Faraday's laws of electrolysis (m=MQ/(zF))

Words: 320
Electrolysis OurBigBook.com
Faraday's laws of electrolysis state that the mass of material formed or consumed by a specified electrode reaction is proportional to the transported electric charge, and that equal electric charge produces masses proportional to M/z for different reactions. Here M is the product's mass per mole, and z is the positive number of Electrons transferred per product entity. For complete use of the electric charge in that reaction,
ne−​=FQ​,nproduct​=zFQ​,m=zFMQ​.
(95)
The first relation uses the Faraday constant; the second uses half-reaction stoichiometry; the third converts amount of substance to mass. For equal transported electric charge in two ideal cells,
m2​m1​​=M2​/z2​M1​/z1​​.
(96)
The number z belongs to the balanced half-reaction, rather than to the metal's name alone: copper deposited from Cu2+ needs z=2. These modern forms of both laws are given in KIT's practical.[ref]
If other same-direction electrode reactions share the measured electric current, define an integrated current efficiency η=Qproduct​/Q. Provided the product is neither subsequently consumed nor lost, the retained mass is
m=ηzFMQ​,η=∫I(t)dt∫Iproduct​(t)dt​.
(97)
Here 0≤η≤1 follows from the specified same-direction partition of electric current. It is not a universal bound on every signed partial-current convention: IUPAC notes that simultaneous oxidation and reduction at one electrode can produce a current-efficiency ratio above one.[ref] When efficiency varies during a run, use the charge-weighted ratio above, rather than an unweighted average over time. If deposition removes material from a multicomponent chemical solution, specify which chemical species is being counted and balance its half-reaction before choosing z.
Michael Faraday's accessible 1834 paper, Experimental Researches in Electricity, Seventh Series, §783 states proportionality between chemical action and the quantity of electricity passed. In §§789–791 he describes connecting a molten tin-chloride cell in series with a water-decomposition charge indicator, weighing the receiving electrode before and after, and comparing the deposited metal with the indicator's gas readout. The common series electric current makes these two readouts comparable. This was a quantitative test of chemical equivalents, rather than merely an observation that a deposit appeared. It is historical evidence, not a suggested classroom procedure; the modern Electron-counting derivation above uses concepts unavailable to Faraday.[ref]

Electrolytic cell

Words: 316
Electrolysis OurBigBook.com
An electrolytic cell uses an external source of electrical work to drive electrode chemical reactions. In the ordinary two-terminal driven mode, its positive anode supports oxidation and its negative cathode supports reduction. The source removes Electrons from the anode and supplies Electrons to the cathode; through the electrolyte, net conventional current goes from anode toward cathode. Terminal signs refer to the driven cell's terminals relative to each other. The source supplies electrical power to the cell. See 17.7 Electrolysis (§17.7: electrolysis and electroplating).
For example, transferring copper from a soluble copper anode onto a conducting object at the cathode has the ideal half-reactions
positive anode:negative cathode:​Cu(s)⟶Cu2+(aq)+2e−,Cu2+(aq)+2e−⟶Cu(s).​
(98)
Their sum transfers copper between surfaces. For identical bulk states, this transfer need not have a positive bulk Gibbs free energy change; finite electric current still needs applied drive to overcome losses. Thus "consumes electrical work" does not mean every electrolytic cell stores all that work as chemical Gibbs free energy. Electrolysis can instead redistribute material. The charge-to-amount relation remains ξ=Q/(2F) when only these half-reactions carry the electric current; competing water reactions would change the deposited amount. The electroplating principle and charge accounting are described in 17.7 Electrolysis (§17.7: electroplating and quantitative aspects).
The University of Washington's teaching demonstration makes this material transfer visible with a copper electrode and a stainless-steel electrode in a glass cell containing 0.5molL−1 CuSO4​. The external source connects its positive lead to copper and negative lead to steel; the reported observation is a copper coating on the steel. Reversing the source polarity removes the deposited copper again: the coated surface now supports oxidation and acts as the anode. This polarity reversal changes the drive, unlike swapping the measurement leads in the Daniell cell voltage and load experiment. Coating appearance alone does not measure charge efficiency or exclude competing chemical reactions. See University of Washington, Electroplating Copper on Stainless Steel: apparatus and reversible coating demonstration.
The copper cathode in this driven example is negative, while the copper cathode of a discharging Daniell cell is positive: both support exactly the same reduction half-reaction. Likewise, an anode need not lose material if its conducting surface is absent from its net half-reaction. Neither terminal sign nor a universal mass-change rule defines an anode or cathode.

Half-reaction

Words: 52
Electrochemistry OurBigBook.com
A half-reaction is a balanced chemical equation for either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox chemical reaction, explicitly including exchanged Electrons. Match the electron counts before adding the two half-reactions; the net equation then contains no transferred Electrons. A half-reaction is bookkeeping, not necessarily an elementary reaction. See Florida State University, lab background: separate electrode reactions and Daniell cell.

Salt bridge

Words: 160
Electrochemistry OurBigBook.com
A salt bridge is an ionic connection between electrolyte compartments that limits bulk mixing while permitting electric charge transport. Its mobile ions compensate changes caused by the electrode half-reactions, keeping the bulk chemical solutions approximately electrically neutral during sustained electric current. It does not conduct Electrons like the external wire, and its ions need not be consumed at either electrode. The ionic return path and compensating ion flows are explained in Purdue University, Electrochemical Reactions: salt bridge and charge balance.
In a discharging Daniell cell, anions moving toward the anode compartment and cations moving toward the cathode compartment both contribute to the internal conventional current from anode toward cathode. This charge-balance role is compatible with a negative anode: terminal signs do not imply that the whole anode chemical solution is negatively charged. The simple compensating-inventory example in Daniell cell does not fix all individual ion fluxes; diffusion and the cell's other mobile ions can contribute. A real bridge also introduces electrical resistance and may introduce a junction electric potential difference, so its presence does not guarantee an exact thermodynamic cell reading. See IUPAC Gold Book: salt bridge and liquid-junction potential.

Electrolyte

Words: 581 Articles: 3
Electrochemistry OurBigBook.com
An electrolyte is a conducting medium in which mobile ions carry electric current, according to IUPAC Gold Book: electrolyte. In introductory chemistry, a substance that yields ions when dissolved in water is also called an electrolyte. Both usages point to the same mechanism: an electric field gives mobile cations and anions directed drift velocities.
Mobility matters as much as the presence of electric charge. In a simple ideal model of solid sodium chloride, ions are confined to their sites and do not carry a sustained transport electric current. Molten sodium chloride has mobile ions; dissolved sodium chloride gives mobile Na+ and Cl− ions in water. Real solids can have some ionic transport through imperfections; the immobile-solid picture is an introductory limit, rather than a claim that all solids are perfect insulators.
A strong electrolyte yields essentially all ions from the dissolved substance, whereas a weak electrolyte yields only a fraction under the specified conditions. Dissolved sodium chloride is a strong electrolyte. Sucrose is a nonelectrolyte: it dissolves as neutral molecules, so dissolving something does not automatically create mobile ions. Water's own small population of hydronium and hydroxide remains possible. See 11.2 Electrolytes (§11.2: strong, weak, and nonelectrolytes) and Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §11.4, Table 11.3: sucrose and sodium chloride.
Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte and a weak acid. In water, some neutral acetic acid molecules transfer a proton to water, producing hydronium and the negatively charged partner:
CH3​COOH+H2​O⇌CH3​COO−+H3​O+.
(99)
Both sides have net electric charge zero. At chemical equilibrium, neutral acetic acid coexists with these ions; the fraction converted depends on the conditions. Electrolyte strength describes this extent of ion production, while concentration describes how much substance is present per specified quantity of chemical solution. A dilute strong electrolyte can contain fewer ions per volume than a concentrated weak electrolyte. Neither the words strong and weak nor a conductivity comparison alone specifies concentration.
Now specify an electrolytic cell with a positive anode on the left, a negative cathode on the right, and an approximately uniform electric field pointing right in the bulk electrolyte. With a steady external source and neglecting diffusion and convection, positive cations drift right toward the negative cathode; negative anions drift left toward the positive anode. Yet both populations contribute a rightward conventional current! For number densities n+​,n−​ and drift velocities v+​,v−​, the transport current density is
J=n+​(+e)v+​+n−​(−e)v−​.
(100)
The product of electric charge and velocity determines conventional current: for the anion, both the charge and its rightward velocity component are negative, making its rightward contribution positive. This is the same sign rule used for Electron conventional current. It follows directly from the existing charge carrier formula.
For an independent numerical example, stipulate n+​=n−​=1025m−3, v+,x​=2×10−4ms−1, and v−,x​=−3×10−4ms−1. With the exact elementary charge e=1.602176634×10−19C, the contributions are
J+,x​=320.4353268Am−2,J−,x​=480.6529902Am−2,Jx​=801.088317Am−2.
(101)
Equal number densities of singly charged cations and anions give zero bulk charge density, while their motion gives nonzero current density. This is why a neutral electrolyte can conduct. These numbers are chosen toy inputs, not measurements of sodium chloride; maintaining sustained cell electric current also requires suitable electrode reactions. Blocking electrodes can instead lead to charge accumulation and decay of the electric current.
An electrolyte connects the microscopic motion of ions to observable electrical conductivity. A counterion-only model keeps just the mobile counterions needed to oppose a fixed electric charge; Poisson-Boltzmann equations use ideal Boltzmann distributions to model their equilibrium distributions, rather than the drift example above.

Strong electrolyte

Words: 18
Electrolyte OurBigBook.com
A strong electrolyte yields essentially all ions from its dissolved substance in the specified solvent and conditions. Strength does not specify concentration.

Weak electrolyte

Words: 19
Electrolyte OurBigBook.com
A weak electrolyte yields only a fraction of ions from its dissolved substance under the specified conditions, as illustrated by acetic acid in water.

Nonelectrolyte

Electrolyte OurBigBook.com
A nonelectrolyte supplies neutral molecules rather than ions on dissolving in the specified solvent, as illustrated by sucrose in water.

Chemical reaction

Words: 10k Articles: 70
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
A chemical reaction interconverts chemical species, as defined by the [ref]. The consumed species are reactants; the formed species are reaction products. In ordinary chemical reactions, chemical atoms are rearranged while each chemical element's total atom count is conserved. For a complete chemical equation, net electric charge is conserved too.
For example, the balanced chemical equation
2H2​+O2​⟶2H2​O
(102)
describes conversion of molecular hydrogen and molecular oxygen into water. Both sides contain four hydrogen chemical atoms and two oxygen chemical atoms. Three reactant molecules become two reaction product molecules: atom counts are conserved, but molecule counts need not be. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, balancing chemical equations.
The coefficients describe net consumption and formation, without asserting that three molecules collide in one step. A balanced chemical equation supplies quantitative constraints; it does not determine how quickly the chemical reaction occurs, or whether chemical equilibrium prevents complete conversion. Those questions need further information. Keeping these roles distinct makes stoichiometry useful even when the microscopic details are complicated.

Precipitation (chemistry)

Words: 31
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Precipitation is formation of a solid from a solution. A newly formed solid can create a surface for heterogeneous catalysis; observing it does not establish the composition or catalytic role of that surface.

Redox

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
A redox chemical reaction couples oxidation and reduction. In the electrode examples here, oxidation releases Electrons and reduction accepts them. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §4.2: oxidation-reduction reactions.

Oxidation

Words: 719 Articles: 4
Redox OurBigBook.com
In the electrochemistry examples here, oxidation is loss of Electrons by a chemical species; it occurs at the anode.
Oxidation state (OS)
Words: 704 Articles: 3
Oxidation OurBigBook.com
An oxidation state is an Electron-bookkeeping assignment to a chemical atom: its electric charge number after the ionic approximation of bonds. It helps identify oxidation and reduction and determine stoichiometry, even for covalent bonds without separate charged ions. In water, each hydrogen has oxidation state +1 and oxygen has −2; this does not assert that a water molecule contains two free protons and a free oxide ion.[ref]
Three conventions answer different questions. Formal charge divides each bonding electron pair equally in a chosen Lewis structure. Oxidation state uses the ionic approximation of bonds. Partial atomic charge instead partitions the actual electron density and depends on that partition. In the ordinary water Lewis structure, every formal charge is zero although the oxidation states are not. Neither bookkeeping convention supplies numerical partial atomic charges.
Ionic approximation of bonds (OSi​=vi​−Niassigned​)
Words: 255
Oxidation state OurBigBook.com
For the routine examples here, assign all bonding Electrons between different chemical elements to the more electronegative partner; divide bonding Electrons between identical chemical elements equally. Retain each lone pair on its original chemical atom. Subtract the assigned valence electron count Niassigned​ from the neutral chemical atom's valence electron count vi​. The IUPAC convention uses Allen electronegativity, based on free-chemical atom valence electron energies. Close electronegativity comparisons and some reversibly bound chemical compounds require care beyond this simple rule.[ref]
The examples explain exceptions to memorized rules:
  • Water, H−O−H: oxygen receives both O–H bond pairs plus its two lone pairs, giving eight assigned valence electrons and 6−8=−2. Each hydrogen receives none, giving 1−0=+1.
  • Hydrogen peroxide, H−O−O−H: each oxygen receives its O–H bond pair, one Electron from O–O, and four Electrons in lone pairs. Thus each has 6−7=−1, while each hydrogen remains +1. The O–O connection is why the usual −2 oxygen shortcut fails.
  • Molecular oxygen, O2​: equal splitting of the O–O bonding Electrons leaves each oxygen assigned six valence electrons, so each has oxidation state zero.
  • Sodium hydride, NaH: hydrogen is more electronegative than sodium. The formula unit is assigned sodium +1 and hydrogen −1, consistent with the hydrogen anion. The usual +1 hydrogen shortcut fails here.
These drawings record allocations, not molecular geometry or a physical process of breaking the chemical bonds. In particular, the O–O line in the molecular oxygen panel only marks the connection; it does not assert a complete Lewis structure or spin state.
Oxidation state sum rule (∑i​OSi​=z)
Words: 111
Oxidation state OurBigBook.com
Sum oxidation states over all chemical atoms of the specified molecule, ion or formula unit, including multiplicities:
∑i​OSi​=z,q=ze.
(103)
Here q is the net electric charge and e the positive elementary charge. For a neutral entity the sum is zero; for an ion it equals its signed electric charge number z. The reason is simple: the allocation assigns every valence electron exactly once, so the sum is the neutral Electron budget minus the actual Electron count.
For water, 2(+1)+(−2)=0; for hydrogen peroxide, 2(+1)+2(−1)=0. In permanganate, MnO4−​, assigning each oxygen −2 gives x+4(−2)=−1, so manganese has oxidation state +7. This is not a free Mn7+ ion: the entire permanganate anion has net electric charge −e. The sum rule supplies a constraint; without additional assignments it cannot determine every individual oxidation state.
Acidic permanganate-iron balance
Words: 225
Oxidation state OurBigBook.com
An increase in oxidation state records oxidation; a decrease records reduction. Thus Fe2+→Fe3+ raises the iron oxidation state by one, while MnO4−​→Mn2+ lowers the manganese oxidation state from +7 to +2. Five iron ions supply the five-Electron inventory required per permanganate ion.
In an acidic chemical solution, the complete half-reactions are
Fe2+MnO4−​+8H++5e−​⟶Fe3++e−,⟶Mn2++4H2​O.​
(104)
First balance oxygen with four water molecules, then hydrogen with eight protons, and finally electric charge with five Electrons. Multiply the iron half-reaction by five and add; the exchanged Electrons cancel:
MnO4−​+8H++5Fe2+⟶Mn2++4H2​O+5Fe3+.​
(105)
Both sides contain one manganese, four oxygen, eight hydrogen and five iron chemical atoms, with net electric charge +17e. The H+ notation represents the acidic aqueous proton inventory; it does not imply bare protons moving independently of water. These half-reactions and their sum are the acidic balance used in the documented permanganate-iron titration.[ref]
The coefficients predict amounts consumed, not a collision of five ions or an elementary reaction. Bulk chemical solution also contains compensating counterions, which are omitted from this net chemical equation. The hydrogen and oxygen oxidation states are unchanged; balancing their inventories remains essential even though they do not account for the exchanged Electrons.

A redox titration adds a measured amount of substance of one reactant to determine another through a known redox chemical equation. The burette reading becomes an amount through concentration; the balanced chemical equation supplies the amount ratio. A colour endpoint additionally needs a chemical explanation, as in the permanganate-iron titration.
Permanganate-iron titration
Words: 294
Redox titration OurBigBook.com
A proposed modern teaching measurement puts a pipette-measured portion of an iron Fe2+ chemical solution in a conical flask, acidifies with excess dilute sulfuric acid, and adds standardized potassium permanganate from a clamped burette while swirling. The documented endpoint principle is that added purple permanganate is consumed until the first small excess leaves a pale purple colour; no separate colour indicator is required. Insufficient acidity can produce brown manganese dioxide, invalidating the assumed five-Electron half-reaction.[ref]
Record initial and final burette readings; their difference is the delivered volume V. The following controls are proposed additions to test the inference. Run a reagent blank with the same water, sulfuric acid and endpoint criterion but no sample, obtaining Vb​. Use a separately established potassium permanganate concentration c, clear the burette tip of air, and repeat sample portions. A known added amount of substance of Fe2+ should increase consumption by one fifth of that amount. A blank estimates reagent demand and the small endpoint excess; it cannot remove an interfering sample reactant.
Assuming complete, selective reaction according to the acidic permanganate-iron balance, the corrected inference is
n(Fe2+)=5c(V−Vb​).
(106)
With c in molL−1, use V and Vb​ in litres. As an original stipulated calculation, not an experimental result, take c=0.02000molL−1, V=12.60mL and Vb​=0.10mL. Then the permanganate consumption is 0.2500mmol and the inferred Fe2+ amount is 1.250mmol. In a 25.00mL sample portion this corresponds to 0.05000molL−1.
The endpoint detects residual permanganate, not the iron identity directly. Other sample reactants that consume permanganate raise the apparent Fe2+ amount; prior oxidation of sample Fe2+ to Fe3+ lowers it. A recovery check probes response to the added iron but does not prove absence of every interference. The readout determines the reacting Fe2+ inventory under the stated conditions, rather than total iron in an arbitrary mixture. No measured titres are asserted here.

Energy coupling (ΔGnet​=ΔG1​+ΔG2​)

Words: 415
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Energy coupling links an endergonic reaction to an exergonic reaction through a reaction mechanism, so that the combined transformation has a favourable change in Gibbs free energy. ATP hydrolysis is a common driving chemical reaction. A shared reaction intermediate, produced in one step and consumed in another, can physically connect the transformations; merely placing two independent chemical reactions in the same chemical solution does not establish energy coupling. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: coupled reactions and activated intermediates.
For a computed example, stipulate an endergonic reaction A⟶B with ΔG1∘′​=+20kJmol−1 under precisely the same biochemical standard state conditions as the quoted ATP hydrolysis value. Assume a reaction mechanism couples one ATP hydrolysis to each A-to-B conversion. The formal sum is
AATP+H2​OA+ATP+H2​O​⟶B,⟶ADP+Pi​,⟶B+ADP+Pi​,​ΔG1∘′​ΔG2∘′​ΔGnet∘′​​=+20kJmol−1,=−30.5kJmol−1,=−10.5kJmol−1.​
(107)
The sum +20+(−30.5)=−10.5 gives an exergonic reaction. The +20 is a chosen teaching value, not a measured property of an identified substance. Outside these reference conditions, add the actual ΔG1​ and ΔG2​, each evaluated using consistent thermodynamic activities; mixing a standard value for one chemical reaction with an unrelated cellular value for the other gives no justified prediction.
Why do the changes in Gibbs free energy add? Gibbs free energy is a state function. Adding consistent reaction changes cancels any shared reaction intermediate and leaves the difference between the combined reactants and combined reaction products. This explains the thermodynamic accounting; it does not construct the reaction mechanism. In many ATP-dependent routes, phosphorylation transfers a phosphate group to a substrate or an enzyme, and subsequent transformation consumes that modified material. The shared material is what connects the steps. Other reaction mechanisms use ATP differently. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: ATP-driven biosynthesis.
The useful achievement is that a common regenerated nucleotide can connect many different processes in metabolism. The net negative change in Gibbs free energy permits the coupled conversion, but supplies no reaction rate: enzymes can lower activation energy barriers without changing the endpoint difference. Energy coupling changes which overall chemical reaction is being considered; catalysis accelerates an available route. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.2: free-energy changes and reaction barriers.
A historical landmark is Fritz Lipmann's [ref]. Its sections on the phosphate cycle, generation and utilization of phosphate-bond energy, and group transfer organized these processes around a reusable chemical carrier. The historical terminology should be read with the modern distinction between net hydrolysis and the cost of breaking a chemical bond.

Chemical kinetics

Words: 8k Articles: 42
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Chemical kinetics studies how quickly chemical reactions proceed and how their reaction rates depend on composition and conditions. It connects a measured change in concentration to a rate law, then uses a rate equation to predict future concentrations. This makes it useful for choosing how long to wait for conversion and for testing a proposed reaction mechanism. Changing temperature, reactant concentrations, or the presence of a catalyst can change reaction rates; see Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §12.2: factors affecting reaction rates.
Chemical equilibrium specifies the eventual balance under given constraints; chemical kinetics determines how rapidly it is approached. At fixed temperature and pressure, a decrease in Gibbs free energy favours conversion but does not guarantee a fast chemical reaction: reaching a transition state can require crossing a substantial barrier. Thus a mixture can change imperceptibly over an observation period without being at chemical equilibrium. The distinction separates which direction is favoured from how long conversion takes. See 12.5 Collision Theory (§12.5: collision theory and reaction barriers) and Chemistry 2e, §16.1: spontaneity and speed.

Activation energy (Ea​)

Words: 2k Articles: 6
Chemical kinetics OurBigBook.com
A small increase in temperature can produce a large increase in a reaction rate. In the simplest Arrhenius equation model, warming from 300 to 310K increases a rate constant with Ea​=80kJmol−1 by about 2.81 times, even though the absolute thermodynamic temperature rises by only about 3.33%. This sensitivity helps explain why cooling can slow unwanted chemical reactions and why a hot process can become difficult to control. The comparison assumes the same rate law and reactant concentrations; the activation energy characterizes k(T), rather than every change in the measured reaction rate.
The physical motivation is the distribution of molecular energies. Warming changes the Boltzmann distribution, increasing the relative population of energetically costly configurations. A transition state can therefore become much more accessible than the modest change in average kinetic energy might suggest. The exponential function in an Arrhenius equation captures such sensitivity in a simple model; it is not a universal formula for the fraction above every barrier in a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.[ref]
Activation energy quantifies how strongly a rate constant depends on thermodynamic temperature. For a positive rate constant k(T), the empirical definition is
Ea​(T)=RT2dTd​lnkref​k(T)​,
(108)
where R is the molar gas constant and kref​>0 is a fixed reference with the same units as k. The ratio is a dimensionless quantity, keeping the natural logarithm meaningful without changing its derivative. Thus Ea​ is a molar energy, commonly in Jmol−1 or kJmol−1. The Arrhenius equation makes Ea​ constant over its assumed range. This rate-based definition, and the need for care when identifying it with a threshold on a potential energy surface, are stated in the activation energy.
In a simple barrier picture, reaching a transition state costs energy relative to the starting reactants. The height of that barrier is different from the difference between the reactants and reaction products. An energetically favourable endpoint can still be reached slowly. An energy profile makes the distinction visible, while an Arrhenius plot tests temperature sensitivity from rate constants. A measured Ea​ need not equal a barrier read from an arbitrarily chosen diagram.
For a computed example, assume a first-order reaction has k(300K)=0.100s−1, constant Ea​=80kJmol−1, and a temperature-independent pre-exponential factor. The Arrhenius equation gives
k(300K)k(310K)​=exp[8.31446261880000​(3001​−3101​)]≈2.81398.
(109)
Hence k(310K)≈0.281398s−1. Its half-life falls from ln2/0.100≈6.93147s to ln2/0.281398≈2.46322s. These are chosen model parameters, not measurements of an identified chemical reaction. The exponent uses kelvin, not unconverted Celsius temperatures, and 80000Jmol−1 must match R in Jmol−1K−1.
A microscopic reaction energy barrier belongs to a specified path on a potential energy surface. An experimental activation energy belongs to a specified rate constant and its temperature dependence. A multi-step reaction mechanism can change which step controls the observed conversion, and a temperature-dependent pre-exponential factor contributes to the observed activation energy. Even the Gibbs energy of activation of transition state theory is a different quantity: it incorporates entropy as well as enthalpy and depends on the standard states. These distinctions prevent a fitted Arrhenius plot from being mistaken for a direct microscopic energy measurement.[ref]
Catalysis illustrates the separation between a path and its endpoints. At the same temperature and with the same reactants, reaction products, and standard states, a regenerated catalyst changes the available reaction mechanism and rate constants, while the overall standard change in Gibbs free energy and the equilibrium constant remain the same:
K=exp(−RTΔr​G∘​).
(110)
For a reversible first-order reaction pair A⇌B, consistency at chemical equilibrium requires kf​/kr​=K. A model that multiplies only kf​ by a catalytic speedup while holding kr​ fixed would change this ratio and misrepresent catalysis. This simple ratio applies to that specified rate law; a multi-step catalytic reaction mechanism needs its own rate equations. A potential-energy profile alone cannot determine K, because its endpoint difference is not generally the standard change in Gibbs free energy.[ref]
Apparent activation energy (Ea,app​(T)=−Rdln(k/kref​)/d(1/T))
Words: 190
Activation energy OurBigBook.com
An apparent activation energy reports the temperature sensitivity of an observed rate constant, without assuming that it equals one microscopic reaction energy barrier. The chain rule converts the empirical activation energy definition into the local slope of an Arrhenius plot:
Ea,app​(T)=−Rd(1/T)dln(k/kref​)​.
(111)
The fixed reference kref​ keeps the natural logarithm dimensionless. A fitted straight-line slope estimates this quantity over the chosen temperature interval; curvature means that one number does not describe every local slope.[ref]
For the explicit model k(T)=A(T)exp[−E0​/(RT)] with constant exponent parameter E0​, differentiation gives
Ea,app​(T)=E0​+RT2dTd​lnA(T∗​)A(T)​,
(112)
where T∗​ is fixed. The second term demonstrates why a microscopic interpretation needs more than a slope. If E0​ were itself allowed to depend on temperature, differentiation would also contribute −TdE0​/dT; simply inserting a variable E0​(T) and naming it the measured activation energy is generally incorrect.
An instructive transition state theory example for an effective first-order reaction is
k(T)=hkB​T​exp(RΔS‡∘​)exp(−RTΔH‡∘​).
(113)
Here kB​ and h are the Boltzmann constant and Planck constant; ΔS‡∘ is the entropy of activation, and ΔH‡∘ the enthalpy of activation. With those two quantities constant over the chosen range and successful passage assumed, direct differentiation gives Ea,app​=ΔH‡∘+RT, while the Gibbs energy of activation is ΔG‡∘=ΔH‡∘−TΔS‡∘. These are three distinguishable quantities. The stated first-order reaction and fixed standard states matter when comparing these formulas with measurements.[ref]
Arrhenius equation (k(T)=Aexp[−Ea​/(RT)])
Words: 1k Articles: 4
Activation energy OurBigBook.com
The Arrhenius equation models the temperature dependence of a rate constant by
k(T)=Aexp(−RTEa​​),A>0,T>0.
(114)
Here A is the pre-exponential factor, Ea​ the activation energy, R the molar gas constant, and T the absolute thermodynamic temperature. In its original form, A and Ea​ are held constant over the range being modeled. It is an empirical relationship, not a universal rule for every reaction mechanism. See the Arrhenius equation.
Eliminating A between two positive temperatures gives the useful prediction
lnk(T1​)k(T2​)​=REa​​(T1​1​−T2​1​).
(115)
For Ea​>0, warming increases k. The logarithmic sensitivity is dln(k/kref​)/dT=Ea​/(RT2), so there is no universal doubling per ten degrees. The same 10K rise from 300 to 310K gives a factor 1.67749 for Ea​=40kJmol−1, versus 2.81398 for 80kJmol−1.
The useful simplification is that a strong change in reaction rate becomes a straight-line relation after changing variables. Measurements at several temperatures can estimate the slope and test whether one pair of constants describes the chosen range. Curvature can indicate a failure of that approximation; fitting a line does not uniquely establish a microscopic reaction mechanism.
Svante Arrhenius's 1889 paper on sucrose conversion through catalysis by a chemical acid compared the strong observed temperature dependence with the much smaller increase in collision frequency. He discussed van't Hoff's earlier temperature relations and proposed a small population of hypothetical active sucrose, replenished from ordinary sucrose, to interpret the dependence. The inspected translated excerpt derives an inverse-temperature relation in its equations (6)–(7) and then applies it to the reaction rate. That historical hypothesis is distinct from a modern transition state description. See the On the Reaction Velocity of the Inversion of Cane Sugar by Acids. The excerpt omits parts of the original paper; it does not provide a complete original apparatus description or dataset.
The pre-exponential factor must have the same units as the rate constant, since the exponential function supplies a dimensionless quantity. For a rate law v=k[A]m, both A and k have units (molL−1)1−ms−1. Thus a first-order reaction uses s−1, whereas a second-order reaction uses Lmol−1s−1. Calling A a frequency factor does not give it frequency units for every order of reaction. Its value includes the physical and geometrical factors allowed by the chosen reaction mechanism; equal activation energies need not mean equal reaction rates.
To read the blue Arrhenius plot, define the dimensionless quantity X=1000K/T and y=ln[k/k(300K)]. Its numerical slope is mX​=−60000/(1000R)≈−7.21634, giving Ea​=−(1000K)RmX​=60kJmol−1. The slope against 1/T, by contrast, is −7216.34K. The orange tangent at 300K gives Ea,app​≈64.9887kJmol−1; its finite-interval slope between 280 and 340K gives about 65.1227kJmol−1. The distinction between a local derivative and a fitted interval matters even with perfectly noise-free synthetic evaluations.
Two measured positive rate constants give a two-point estimate
Ea,fit​=R1/T1​−1/T2​ln[k(T2​)/k(T1​)]​.
(116)
Several temperatures let linear regression test the constant-parameter approximation: inspect the regression residuals, keep the same rate law and composition convention, and account for uncertainty in both k and T. A straight line over a short range supports a useful local approximation; it does not uniquely identify a reaction mechanism. A fixed change of units or of kref​ shifts the intercept without changing the inferred activation energy.[ref]

The pre-exponential factor multiplies the exponential function in the Arrhenius equation. It has the same units as the rate constant, so for a first-order reaction both have units s−1. Its physical interpretation depends on the reaction mechanism; an assumed constant A should not be identified with a universal collision frequency. Comparing activation energies alone does not rank absolute rate constants when the pre-exponential factors differ. See the pre-exponential factor.

lnkref​k(T)​=lnkref​A​−REa​​T1​.

The slope is −Ea​/R and the intercept is ln(A/kref​). Changing the reference units shifts the intercept but leaves the slope unchanged. If the horizontal coordinate is displayed in 10−3K−1, its numerical slope must be rescaled before multiplying by −R. A temperature-dependent pre-exponential factor or activation energy can make the plot curved.

Using the dimensionless quantity T/T∗​ leaves A∗​ with the same units as k; in the equivalent convention BTnexp[−E0​/(RT)], B instead has units of k multiplied by K−n. The power exponent n here is not an order of reaction. The IUPAC definition uses that equivalent BTn convention.[ref]

dTdln(k/kref​)​=Tn​+RT2E0​​,Ea,app​(T)=E0​+nRT.

Conductometric determination of activation energy
Words: 378
Arrhenius equation OurBigBook.com
A concrete laboratory route to an Arrhenius plot is to infer a rate constant at each controlled temperature from a changing electrical conductivity. The Technical University of Munich's Activation Energy of a First-Order Reaction supplies a teaching protocol, rather than a published set of measured rate constants.
The manual follows tertiary amylbromide conversion, which produces conducting ions. A measuring cell connects to a thermostat; an immersed electrical conductivity probe also measures solution temperature, and a magnetic stirrer mixes it. Use 80mL of 80% by volume ethanol in water, equilibrate, then add 0.5mL of tertiary amylbromide. Record the baseline before addition and set time zero at addition. Repeat with fresh mixtures at 25, 30, and 35∘C, each within ±0.5∘C; record for 30 minutes at the first two temperatures and until completion at the last. Clean the cell between runs and keep the added volume fixed. The completed 35∘C mixture supplies endpoint electrical conductivity measurements at the other temperatures: one endpoint reading cannot be used unchanged at every temperature.[ref]
To see what is inferred from the readout, let σ0​, σ(t), and σ∞​ be the baseline, current, and completed-mixture electrical conductivities at the same temperature. Assume their baseline-subtracted changes are proportional to converted concentration. Combining that measurement model with a first-order reaction gives
f(t)=σ∞​−σ0​σ∞​−σ(t)​=c0​c(t)​=e−kt,−lnf(t)=kt.
(120)
Thus the electrical conductivity increases toward an endpoint, while the remaining reactant fraction decreases. Fit −lnf against time to obtain k; then fit ln(k/kref​) against 1/T in kelvin to estimate an apparent activation energy. This baseline-aware derivation states the measurement assumptions explicitly; it does not infer a rate constant from the steepness of a raw conductivity trace alone.
The controls distinguish a faster chemical reaction from a larger instrumental response. Measure the actual solution temperature, retain the same solvent composition and initial reactant concentration, and compare endpoint and baseline at that temperature. As further diagnostic checks, repeat runs and inspect regression residuals for departure from a first-order reaction. These checks follow from the model: electrical conductivity also depends on how ions move, a baseline drift can mimic conversion, and a mixing delay can distort early points. Near completion, a small endpoint error produces a large relative error in f and its natural logarithm. A successful fit supports an apparent rate model for this solvent and interval; it does not directly image a transition state or identify a unique reaction mechanism. No measured k or Ea​ is supplied here.

A reaction intermediate is formed in one step of a reaction mechanism and consumed in a later step, cancelling from the net chemical equation. A reaction intermediate can connect the transformations in energy coupling; it is distinct from a transition state. See the IUPAC Gold Book: intermediate.

A reaction coordinate parametrizes changes in molecular configuration along a chemical reaction path. It can involve a bond length, a bond angle, or a combination of geometric changes. The precise choice matters when interpreting an energy profile. See the IUPAC Gold Book: reaction coordinate.

Different paths can share endpoints but cross different barriers. See the IUPAC Gold Book: potential-energy reaction surface.

A potential-energy profile describes a path through configurations, while a free-energy description also accounts for the relevant thermodynamic conditions.
For the two chosen profiles, the reaction energy barriers from the reactants are 80 and 50kJmol−1. From the reaction products, the same maxima are 100 and 70kJmol−1 higher. Both paths have endpoint difference −20kJmol−1. The barrier is measured from the relevant starting endpoint, not from an arbitrary zero of potential energy.
The appeal of the diagram is that it separates two useful questions: which endpoint is lower, and which path is easier to traverse? Catalysis changes the route through transition states while retaining the endpoint thermodynamics of the same overall chemical reaction. A real catalytic route may have several steps and reaction intermediates; the two simple curves do not specify such a reaction mechanism. The plotted potential-energy difference alone is not an equilibrium constant or a calculated rate constant. See Chemistry 2e, 12.7: alternative reaction routes and catalysis.

For an elementary reaction, a suitable reaction coordinate parametrizes the path; a multi-step reaction mechanism needs the coordinates of its successive steps. See the IUPAC Gold Book: potential-energy profile.

An elementary reaction is a single step in a reaction mechanism. The law of mass action models its directional reaction rate using reactant concentrations raised to the step's stoichiometric multiplicities. Applying that rule requires evidence that the step is elementary; a net chemical equation alone supplies no such evidence.

Solvent entities involved only through solvation are excluded. Molecularity describes a microscopic event; order of reaction describes the concentration dependence of a rate law. Assigning molecularity to a net multi-step chemical equation is therefore inappropriate.[ref]

Chemical kinetics OurBigBook.com
Catalysis accelerates a chemical reaction by providing an alternative reaction mechanism with a more accessible barrier through its transition states. A catalyst participates in the route and is regenerated. At fixed temperature, catalysis changes how quickly chemical equilibrium is reached without changing the equilibrium constant; it does not make an unfavourable overall change in Gibbs free energy favourable. [ref][ref]
In his 1909 lecture, Wilhelm Ostwald recalled the introduction of the term catalysis by Jöns Jacob Berzelius and emphasized measurable acceleration rather than merely naming an unexplained force. He also discussed reaction intermediates and participation of the catalyst in the steps whose sum gives the net chemical reaction. This is a participant's retrospective account, not evidence that every catalytic reaction mechanism is the same.[ref]

A catalytic cycle follows the changing forms of a catalyst through a reaction mechanism until its starting form is regenerated. The schematic binding cycle in catalyst illustrates the bookkeeping: C is consumed and recovered, whereas AC is a reaction intermediate formed and consumed. Cancelling both gives the net A-to-B chemical equation. Regeneration concerns the completed cycle; it does not imply that C avoids forming chemical bonds or exchanging Electrons. An alternative reaction mechanism may have more elementary reactions than the uncatalysed route and still be faster.[ref]
For that reversible binding cycle, ideal thermodynamic activities give step equilibrium constants K1​=aAC​/(aA​aC​) and K2​=aB​aC​/aAC​. Their product is K1​K2​=aB​/aA​=K: the same cancellations occur in the equilibrium bookkeeping. Choose consistent standard states for the species. A proposed cycle with K1​K2​=K for the same net conversion at the same temperature would contradict its specified thermodynamics. This statement concerns free-species thermodynamic activities. Appreciable binding in AC can change how the conserved total amount is partitioned among free A, free B and bound AC. An assay counting bound and free material together therefore needs that additional balance; unchanged aB​/aA​ does not by itself guarantee identical analytical totals when the amount of C changes.

The net standard reaction change in Gibbs free energy measures the difference between endpoints. Changing the climb can strongly change a rate constant while leaving that endpoint difference intact. For two illustrative single-barrier routes with common endpoint levels GA∘​ and GB∘​,
ΔGf‡∘​=GTS∘​−GA∘​,ΔGr‡∘​=GTS∘​−GB∘​,ΔGf‡∘​−ΔGr‡∘​=Δr​G∘.

Lowering the common transition state level lowers both directional Gibbs energies of activation; it does not lower just the forward climb. The usual statement that a catalyst lowers an activation energy describes a kinetic route, not a change in the net Gibbs free energy. An activation energy inferred from an Arrhenius plot is also distinct from a Gibbs energy of activation at one temperature.
With a common prefactor in transition state theory, subtracting the directional barriers yields

Catalytic selectivity
Words: 159
Catalysis OurBigBook.com
Catalytic selectivity concerns which reaction products form when competing reaction mechanisms are available. Faster conversion is valuable when a process would otherwise be impractically slow; a suitable catalyst can also favour a useful product within the available time. In an illustrative pair of irreversible first-order reactions A to B and A to D, the initial fraction of converted A going to B is kB​/(kB​+kD​). Multiplying both rate constants by the same factor changes speed but leaves this fraction unchanged; changing their relative values changes the kinetic product split. This is a finite-time kinetic illustration, not a new equilibrium constant.
A catalyst need not accelerate every competing chemical reaction equally. Enzymes, for example, can distinguish substrates through their active sites.[ref] If every relevant reversible channel eventually equilibrates in a closed system, its final chemical equilibrium still obeys the endpoint thermodynamics. Selective acceleration, product removal, or external driving can make an observed product distribution depend on time and operating conditions. A claim of improved yield must specify those conditions.

Catalyst deactivation is loss of catalytic activity during use. Regeneration in an ideal catalytic cycle does not rule out a separate damaging chemical reaction, blocking of a surface, or physical loss of catalyst from the apparatus. A route can also be slowed by diffusion to the surface or by accumulation of a reaction intermediate. Such effects limit the usefulness of a low schematic reaction energy barrier: measured throughput depends on the whole reaction mechanism and on transport. Demonstrating regeneration requires more evidence than observing a faster first run. For a recovered solid catalyst, a useful further comparison is a second run with fresh reactants, matched recovered amount, and the same mixing and temperature, alongside a fresh-solid run and a blank. Loss during recovery or residual reactants can otherwise imitate catalyst deactivation or apparent reuse. This is a proposed control, not an observation reported for the catalysed peroxide comparison.

A simple motivating comparison is visible gas evolution from hydrogen peroxide, whose net chemical equation is

The products are water and oxygen. The Royal Society of Chemistry's teaching resource uses small test tubes and droppers, hydrogen peroxide labelled 5–10 volumes, solutions of metal salts including copper(II) sulfate, and approximately 1molL−1 sodium hydroxide. Its qualitative procedure tests additions singly and in pairs to tubes containing about 1cm depth of hydrogen peroxide. It reports the expected classroom result that the additions individually are not effective under those conditions, whereas the solids produced by mixing metal-salt solution with sodium hydroxide give effective heterogeneous catalysis. This is the resource's expected observation, not a newly measured ranking.[ref]
A focused adaptation compares four matched tubes: no addition, copper(II) sulfate alone, sodium hydroxide alone, and the pair. Use equal initial hydrogen peroxide amounts, identical tubes and the same starting temperature. Record stock concentrations and added volumes; add water to the other tubes to match the total added liquid. Additions can first be checked without hydrogen peroxide to distinguish precipitation from gas evolution. Start a timer at contact, mix consistently, and observe gas evolution over the same interval. These matching controls are proposed improvements to the qualitative resource, not claimed details of its original trials. Follow its supervised chemical-handling requirements; the stated strengths describe its teaching protocol rather than an unrestricted recipe.
The immediate readout is relative bubbling, together with whether a solid appears. More vigorous bubbling in the paired tube supports faster conversion under the comparison conditions; it does not identify the solid's exact composition or establish a unique reaction mechanism. Bubble counts are not a calibrated reaction rate: bubble sizes, gas retention and warming can differ. For a quantitative extension, use a freely moving gas syringe to record collected volume V(t) and compare early slopes dV/dt at matched temperature and pressure; check for leaks and repeat runs. This extension is a measurement proposal, not source-reported gas traces.
The paired treatment also changes pH and produces a surface, so the four tubes alone cannot assign the whole effect to one microscopic catalytic step. A filtered-liquid comparison and a separated, washed-solid comparison would help distinguish dissolved and solid contributions, although washing itself can change the active material. More gas at one time establishes neither a changed equilibrium constant nor indefinite catalyst reuse. The open gas-evolution experiment is especially unsuitable as a demonstration that two closed mixtures reach the same chemical equilibrium: the escaping oxygen changes the constraints. The reversible model above supplies that separate explanation. No numerical experimental rate constants, barrier heights or gas volumes are asserted here.

A catalyst makes a chemical reaction proceed faster by participating in an alternative reaction mechanism and being regenerated. This makes repeated conversion possible: the same catalyst can help many successive reactants become reaction products. An enzyme is a biological catalyst. The overall standard change in Gibbs free energy is unchanged; see the IUPAC Gold Book: catalyst.
Regeneration does not mean that the catalyst sits unchanged throughout every step. For example, a schematic reaction mechanism can temporarily bind A to a catalyst C in a reaction intermediate AC:
A+CACnet:A​⇌AC,⇌B+C,⇌B.​
(128)
Adding the steps cancels both the reaction intermediate AC and the catalyst C from the net chemical equation. AC is produced and later consumed; C is used and later recovered. These letters describe possible roles, not a measured reaction mechanism. The alternative route is useful only if its chemical kinetics permits faster conversion. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §12.7: catalysts and alternative mechanisms.
For a worked barrier example, consider an idealized reversible A-to-B conversion at fixed temperature T=300K. Stipulate standard molar Gibbs free energy levels GA∘​=0 and GB∘​=−20kJmol−1, with effective transition state levels 80 without a catalyst and 50kJmol−1 with a catalyst. Use the same standard states and the same zero for both routes; the catalytic route includes the regenerated C at both endpoints. Unlike the separate potential-energy profile example, this illustration uses Gibbs free energy at one specified temperature.
The Gibbs energy of activation is measured from the starting endpoint in the chosen direction. Thus the four barriers are
ΔGf,uncat‡∘​ΔGr,uncat‡∘​​=80−0=80,=80−(−20)=100,​ΔGf,cat‡∘​ΔGr,cat‡∘​​=50−0=50,=50−(−20)=70,​all in kJmol−1.

Both directional barriers fall by 30kJmol−1. The endpoint difference stays Δr​G∘=−20kJmol−1.
To turn those barriers into rate constants, use the Eyring form of transition state theory for this effective first-order reaction pair, with a common prefactor and unit probability of successful passage:

These Gibbs energies of activation are not the empirical activation energy Ea​ of the Arrhenius equation. With the stipulated value R=8.314462618Jmol−1K−1, the speedup is

The exponent is a dimensionless quantity: convert 30kJmol−1 to 30000Jmol−1 before dividing by RT. The exponential function explains why a modest barrier reduction can have a dramatic kinetic effect. This number follows from the chosen free-energy barriers and common prefactor; it is not a universal catalytic multiplier or a prediction across temperatures.
Assume ideal thermodynamic activities with a common concentration standard state, and directional rate laws Jf​=kf​[A] and Jr​=kr​[B]. At chemical equilibrium, equal reaction rates give K=[B]/[A]=kf​/kr​ for this model. The barriers give

A transition state describes configurations at the barrier between reactants and reaction products in an elementary reaction. It is a crossing region, rather than a stable substance that accumulates in a bottle. The IUPAC definition characterizes these configurations by equal probabilities of proceeding toward reactants or reaction products: [ref]. Lowering the barrier relative to the starting configuration can increase a reaction rate, even when the overall change in Gibbs free energy is unchanged.

The disappearance rate of a reactant A is its positive net loss of concentration per unit time, vA​=−d[A]/dt. Rate law

Reaction rate OurBigBook.com
A rate law specifies how a reaction rate depends on concentrations under stated conditions. A common form is
v=k[A]α[B]β,
(135)
where k is a rate constant and the exponents are partial orders of reaction. Determine them experimentally, or derive them from a justified reaction mechanism. Do not infer α=a and β=b from the net chemical equation: its coefficients describe consumption ratios, whereas the exponents describe sensitivity to concentration. See IUPAC Gold Book: rate law and Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §12.3: rate laws.
A rate law becomes a prediction of time evolution when combined with stoichiometry in a rate equation, for example d[A]/dt=−av. Agreement with a measured rate law is useful evidence for a reaction mechanism, but several routes can give the same dependence.

Rate law OurBigBook.com
An integrated rate law relates concentration to elapsed time after solving a rate equation with an initial condition. Its validity retains the assumptions of the underlying rate law, including fixed rate constants and appropriate stoichiometry. The second-order reaction reciprocal-concentration relation is one example; a different rate equation generally requires a different integrated rate law.[ref]

For example, doubling [A] at fixed [B] multiplies v by 2α: factors of one, two, and four correspond to partial orders of reaction zero, one, and two. These exponents can also be fractional or negative. A single constant order of reaction need not describe a rate law that is not a power form. See IUPAC Gold Book: order of reaction.
For a simple irreversible conversion A⟶B with rate equation −d[A]/dt=k[A]n, initial concentration A0​>0, and fixed k>0, compare zero-order reactions, first-order reactions, and second-order reactions using the dimensionless quantities
X=A0​[A]​,τ=kA0n−1​t,dτdX​=−Xn.

The common τ axis compares curve shapes after each model's own time rescaling, rather than equal laboratory times for an identical numerical k. A first-order reaction has a reaction rate proportional to one reactant concentration in the simple single-species case. For an irreversible A⟶B in a closed system at fixed volume, take [A](0)=A0​, [B](0)=0, and constant rate constant k>0. Its rate equation and solution are

A short check is enough: differentiating A0​e−kt gives −kA0​e−kt, and the two concentrations sum to A0​, as required by the one-to-one stoichiometry. Thus the same exponential decay describes both remaining reactant and decreasing reaction rate. Fixed k means a fixed fractional loss per unit time, not a fixed absolute consumption rate.

t1/2​=kln2​=0.2ln2​s≈3.4657s.
(139)
At each successive half-life, half the remaining reactant is consumed; t1/2​ is independent of A0​ for this first-order reaction. At t=10s, the calculated values are [A]≈0.135335molL−1, [B]≈0.864665molL−1, and v≈0.027067molL−1s−1. These are model predictions for chosen parameters, rather than experimental measurements.
The left panel tracks the two concentrations; the right tracks their instantaneous conversion reaction rate. Their different vertical units matter: v=k[A], so the numerical curves need not have the same height. This gives a practical way to translate a measured concentration into a forecast of both conversion and waiting time.
