Its units are s−1, distinct from the second-order reaction rate constant k2​. For one-to-one stoichiometry, the maximum fractional depletion of B is [A]0​/[B]0​; an original 100:1 initial excess bounds its change by 1%. A twofold excess permits 50% depletion and does not provide the same control.[ref]

Rate constant (k)

Words: 114
Chemical kinetics OurBigBook.com
A rate constant is the coefficient in a specified rate law, held fixed under specified conditions. It can describe an empirical overall chemical reaction, as well as an elementary reaction. Fixed temperature matters: changing temperature can change k, even for the same chemical reaction. See IUPAC Gold Book: order of reaction and rate constants and IUPAC Gold Book: rate coefficient.
For v=k[A]n, dimensional consistency requires
units(k)=(molL−1)1−ns−1.
(148)
A zero-order reaction therefore uses molL−1s−1; a first-order reaction uses s−1; a second-order reaction uses Lmol−1s−1. Comparing bare numerical values of k across different orders of reaction is meaningless without their units and concentrations. Even for the same order of reaction, state whether k multiplies the normalized reaction rate v or a particular reactant disappearance rate: a stoichiometric coefficient can change that convention.

Protonation

Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com

Chemical equation

Words: 336
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
A chemical equation represents a chemical reaction using chemical formulas, with reactants on the left and reaction products on the right. A balanced chemical equation has the same number of chemical atoms of each chemical element on both sides. For molecular hydrogen and molecular oxygen forming water,
2H2​+O2​⟶2H2​O.
(149)
The coefficients 2,1,2 give the relative numbers of molecules; the coefficient 1 is normally omitted. Count hydrogen as 2×2=4 on the left and 2×2=4 on the right, and oxygen as 1×2=2 on the left and 2×1=2 on the right. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §4.1: writing and balancing chemical equations.
To balance the initial expression H2​+O2​⟶H2​O, first put 2 before water to match the two oxygen chemical atoms. This creates four hydrogen chemical atoms on the right, so put 2 before molecular hydrogen. Changing a coefficient multiplies the entire chemical formula. Changing a subscript changes composition and usually the chemical substance: 2H2​O is two water molecules, whereas H2​O2​ is one hydrogen peroxide molecule. Never balance a chemical equation by changing its subscripts.
The bookkeeping follows from conservation of the atomic nuclei in ordinary, non-nuclear chemical reactions; chemical bonds and the distribution of Electrons can change. For a chemical equation involving ions, total electric charge must also match. For example, the existing self-ionization of water equation has zero total electric charge on each side, since the +1 of hydronium cancels the −1 of hydroxide. See 2.6 Ionic and Molecular Compounds (§2.6: nuclei and ions).
The same 2:1:2 ratio relates changes in amount of substance: two moles of molecular hydrogen consumed per mole of molecular oxygen correspond to two moles of water formed. A mole is a defined unit, not one molecule; the little whole-number picture is an abstract counting model, not a claim that a macroscopic sample contains just five molecules. See molecular count and amount of substance for the exact conversion and BIPM, SI base unit: mole for the definition.
This is why a balanced chemical equation is useful: stoichiometry turns the same atom accounting into relations between measurable quantities. It does not determine reaction rate, the final conversion set by chemical equilibrium, or the actual yield of recovered reaction products. The limiting reagent gives an upper bound under the specified chemical reaction.

A chemical species on which a reagent or catalyst acts in a chemical reaction. An enzyme acts on a biochemical substrate, a particular instance of this broader reaction role.

Thermal dissociation

Words: 49
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Thermal dissociation is temperature-driven breaking of a molecule into simpler fragments. The chemical equilibrium abundance depends on pressure as well as temperature: reactions increasing particle number are generally favored at low pressure. In an exoplanet atmosphere, reduced water on a very hot dayside does not by itself establish a low planetary oxygen abundance.

Stoichiometry (νi​)

Words: 520 Articles: 3
Chemical reaction OurBigBook.com
Stoichiometry relates the quantities consumed and formed in a chemical reaction. Its coefficients are ratios of entity counts, or equivalently of amount of substance, rather than ratios of masses. For the water chemical equation, consuming two molecular hydrogen molecules per molecular oxygen molecule gives the same 2:1 ratio as consuming two moles of molecular hydrogen per mole of molecular oxygen. Multiplying every entity count by the same factor preserves the ratio. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, reaction stoichiometry.
Coefficients and subscripts do different jobs. The coefficient in 2H2​O counts two water molecules; the subscript says that each contains two hydrogen chemical atoms. Changing coefficients scales quantities. Changing a subscript changes the specified chemical substance.
This distinction catches a common counting error: one mole of water molecules contains two moles of hydrogen chemical atoms and one mole of oxygen chemical atoms. Always specify what is counted.
Stoichiometry records reactant and product multiplicities in a chemical reaction or a chemical reaction network. The change caused by one reaction is its stoichiometric vector; multiplying by the reaction rate gives its contribution to the concentration equations. For two identical reactants the rate-constant convention absorbs any combinatorial factor.

Molecular count and amount of substance (N=nNA​)

Words: 67
Stoichiometry OurBigBook.com
The molecular count N is a dimensionless integer; the amount of substance n has unit mole, symbol mol. They satisfy
N=nNA​,NA​=6.02214076×1023mol−1.
(150)
The Avogadro constant is exact by the modern definition of the mole: see BIPM, SI base unit: mole. Thus two water molecules correspond to 2/NA​ moles, whereas two moles of water contain 1.204428152×1024 molecules. A mole is a unit for counting specified entities, which may also be chemical atoms, ions or Electrons.

Extent of reaction (ξ)

Words: 65
Stoichiometry OurBigBook.com
For a closed system with one specified chemical reaction, the extent of reaction ξ records progress from ξ=0 through ni​=ni,0​+νi​ξ. Here ni​ is the amount of substance of species i, and the signed stoichiometric vector has negative entries for reactants and positive entries for reaction products. For the water chemical equation in the order H2​,O2​,H2​O, it is (−2,−1,2). The normalization of ξ depends on the chosen coefficients. See IUPAC Gold Book, extent of reaction.

Limiting reagent

Words: 198
Stoichiometry OurBigBook.com
The limiting reagent is the reactant exhausted first if the specified chemical reaction proceeds to the maximum conversion permitted by stoichiometry. With initial values of amount of substance ni,0​ for the reactants and positive consumption coefficients ai​, the largest forward extent of reaction is ξmax​=mini​(ni,0​/ai​). Compare these quotients, rather than simply choosing the smallest initial quantity. This calculation predicts the maximum reaction product quantity and identifies which reactant supply must increase to raise it. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, limiting reactants.
Start with 3mol of molecular hydrogen, 1mol of molecular oxygen and no water. Assume complete conversion by the displayed chemical reaction, without competing reactions. Then
ξmax​=min(23mol​,11mol​)=1mol.
(151)
The molecular oxygen is the limiting reagent. Consumption of 2mol of molecular hydrogen and 1mol of molecular oxygen forms 2mol of water, leaving 1mol of molecular hydrogen. Initially there are 1.806642228×1024 molecular hydrogen molecules and 6.02214076×1023 molecular oxygen molecules; after conversion there are 1.204428152×1024 water molecules and 6.02214076×1023 leftover molecular hydrogen molecules.
As a check, the initial inventory has 6mol of hydrogen chemical atoms and 2mol of oxygen chemical atoms. The final water contains 4mol of hydrogen chemical atoms, and leftover molecular hydrogen supplies the remaining 2mol. The atom totals balance even though the total amount of substance of molecules falls from four to three moles.

Acid-base chemistry

Words: 5k Articles: 32
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
Acid-base chemistry studies how chemical acids and chemical bases exchange protons or electron pairs. Here the focus is transfer of protons in water: a chemical acid donates a proton, and a chemical base accepts it. The resulting chemical equilibrium determines pH, while a buffer solution can resist changes in pH. This connects microscopic chemical reactions with a compact, measurable description of a chemical solution.
The important distinction is between how much chemical acid is present and how readily it transfers a proton. A weak acid and a strong acid at the same total concentration need not have the same pH. Conversely, two buffer solutions can have the same pH while containing very different total quantities of their chemical acids and chemical bases.

Isoelectric point (pI)

Words: 144
Acid-base chemistry OurBigBook.com
The isoelectric point is the pH at which a specified molecule's mean net electric charge is zero. Different protonation states can still carry nonzero electric charges; their contributions cancel in the average. For the two-step glycine speciation model, this gives pI=(pKa1​+pKa2​)/2. Additional ionizable amino acid side chains require their own chemical equilibrium calculations; averaging every pKa is not a general rule. [ref]
Below its isoelectric point, free glycine has positive mean electric charge and an electric field drives it toward the negative electrode; above its isoelectric point, the mean electric charge is negative and the direction reverses. At its isoelectric point the charge-driven contribution vanishes. Diffusion and bulk movement of the chemical solution can still move the sample. Gel electrophoresis applies this charge dependence to separation, although protein size, shape and interactions also affect migration. The pKa values of free glycine do not determine a protein's isoelectric point: its free N-terminus, C-terminus and ionizable amino acid side chains supply a different inventory. [ref]

Acid (chemistry)

Words: 1k Articles: 16
Acid-base chemistry OurBigBook.com
A chemical acid can donate a proton, or accept an electron pair to form a covalent bond. The pH and buffer solution examples below use the former meaning. See IUPAC Gold Book, acid.

Strong acid

Words: 54 Articles: 1
Acid (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
In water, a strong acid transfers its available proton essentially completely to water under the dilute conditions considered here. For the pH example, each initial chemical acid unit supplies one hydronium ion. “Strong” describes this conversion, rather than a high concentration. See 14.3 Relative Strengths of Acids and Bases.
Hydrochloric acid (HCl(aq))
Words: 19
Strong acid OurBigBook.com
Hydrochloric acid is an aqueous chemical solution of hydrogen chloride. The glycine titration model treats its dissociation into hydronium and chloride as complete, retaining both ions in the electric charge balance.

Weak acid

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Acid (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
A weak acid establishes a chemical equilibrium between its proton-donating form and its conjugate base in water. For a neutral monoprotic acid HA, the aqueous chemical equation is
HA(aq)+H2​O(l)⇌H3​O+(aq)+A−(aq).
(152)
Water accepts a proton to become hydronium; A− is the conjugate base. The double arrow denotes reversible exchange at chemical equilibrium, not equal populations. The acid dissociation constant and composition determine the hydronium concentration; substituting total chemical acid concentration into the pH formula is generally incorrect.
“Weak” describes the tendency to transfer a proton in a specified solvent, rather than how much chemical acid was dissolved. A weak acid can be concentrated, and a strong acid can be dilute. Even the same weak acid can have a large weak acid dissociation fraction after sufficient dilution, while its acid dissociation constant stays fixed at the same temperature and standard state conventions.[ref]
Monoprotic acid
Words: 26
Weak acid OurBigBook.com
A monoprotic acid supplies one proton per acid unit in the acid-base chemistry model under consideration. Acetic acid is an example. Several successive proton transfers require several acid dissociation constants and a larger set of chemical species.
Weak acid dissociation fraction (α=[A−]/CT​)
Words: 169
Weak acid OurBigBook.com
For a monoprotic acid with analytical concentration CT​=[HA]+[A−], define the dimensionless weak acid dissociation fraction
α=CT​[A−]​,1−α=CT​[HA]​.
(153)
This counts acid units in the conjugate base form. Identifying it with [H3​O+]/CT​ additionally requires negligible self-ionization of water and no other sources of electric charge. In the ideal dilute chemical solution model, with h=[H3​O+]/c∘, the acid dissociation constant gives α=Ka​/(Ka​+h). Thus lowering hydronium thermodynamic activity favors the conjugate base.
The diagram uses stipulated dimensionless acid dissociation constant Ka​=10−5 and self-ionization of water ion product Kw​=10−14 at fixed temperature; these are model inputs, not measurements of a named substance. It solves the weak acid mass and charge balances. At CT​=0.010molL−1, the calculated weak acid dissociation fraction is about 3.11% and pH about 3.51; at CT​=10−4molL−1, they are about 27.0% and 4.57. More acid units are dissociated as a fraction of the total, yet fewer hydronium ions occur per volume.
At extreme dilution, self-ionization of water makes h approach Kw​​, so pH approaches 7 for the chosen model. The limiting weak acid dissociation fraction is Ka​/(Ka​+Kw​​)≈0.9901, rather than exactly one. The calculation assumes pure added water, a neutral monoprotic acid, and no competing chemical reactions; actual contamination becomes increasingly important as CT​ falls.
Weak acid mass and charge balances
Words: 273 Articles: 1
Weak acid OurBigBook.com
Consider only neutral HA added to pure water, at fixed temperature, with ideal dilute thermodynamic activities, water thermodynamic activity approximated by one, and no added salts or other chemical species. Normalize every concentration by c∘=1molL−1:
c=CT​/c∘,h=[H3​O+]/c∘,x=[A−]/c∘,y=[HA]/c∘,o=[OH−]/c∘.
(154)
Conservation of acid units and zero net electric charge, respectively, require
x+y=c,h=x+o.
(155)
The second equation balances positive hydronium against negative conjugate base and hydroxide. It would need all additional ions if salts or a chemical base were added. Together with acid dissociation constant Ka​=hx/y and the self-ionization of water relation Kw​=ho, these give
x=Ka​+hKa​c​,y=Ka​+hhc​,o=hKw​​,h−hKw​​−Ka​+hKa​c​=0.
(156)
This is exact within the stated ideal model, including depletion and self-ionization of water. Multiplication by h(Ka​+h) yields the cubic equation
h3+Ka​h2−(Kw​+Ka​c)h−Ka​Kw​=0.
(157)
For positive Ka​,Kw​,c, the unmultiplied left-hand side increases strictly from negative to positive values as h increases from zero to infinity; its derivative is 1+Kw​/h2+Ka​c/(Ka​+h)2>0. There is therefore exactly one positive root of a polynomial. A bisection method can find it without choosing an unphysical root of a polynomial.
If Kw​/h2≪1, neglect hydroxide, so h≈x and the quadratic equation retaining acid depletion gives
c−xx2​=Ka​,x=2Ka2​+4Ka​c​−Ka​​=Ka2​+4Ka​c​+Ka​2Ka​c​.
(158)
The last form avoids subtracting nearly equal numbers. If also x/c≪1, neglect depletion to obtain
h≈x≈Ka​c​,[H3​O+]≈Ka​c∘CT​​.
(159)
Check both conditions after computing: x/c measures the fraction lost from the initial undissociated weak acid inventory, while Kw​/h2 measures the omitted hydroxide contribution to electric charge balance. A 5% depletion criterion is a chosen tolerance, not a universal boundary. Keeping depletion does not cure the neglect of self-ionization of water. These weak acid mass and charge balances also explain why the square root estimate cannot be extended to arbitrarily dilute chemical solutions.
Analytical concentration (CT​)
Words: 32
Weak acid mass and charge balances OurBigBook.com
An analytical concentration records the total conserved inventory of a specified component per volume of chemical solution, summed over its relevant chemical species. Here CT​=[HA]+[A−]; it is not generally the chemical equilibrium concentration [HA] of the undissociated weak acid.
Weak acid dissociation measurement
Words: 524 Articles: 6
Weak acid OurBigBook.com
A pH measurement becomes evidence for a weak acid chemical equilibrium when paired with a known analytical concentration and a calibrated glass electrode. For the pure-weak acid model, measured pH estimates h=10−pH only in the ideal thermodynamic activity approximation. Then o=Kw​/h, x=h−o, y=c−x, and Ka​=hx/y. Require 0<x<c; values outside that range signal inconsistent measurements or an inadequate model. Repeating this reconstruction across a dilution series tests whether one acid dissociation constant describes the data, rather than merely fitting one point.
The Analytical Sciences Digital Library's Potentiometric Titration of an Unknown Weak Monoprotic Acid provides a complementary acid-base titration experiment. Its apparatus includes a glass electrode and meter, a stirring magnet, a volumetric flask, pipettes, and a burette containing standardized sodium hydroxide. Prepare an aqueous acid stock of known analytical concentration, transfer a measured portion, and stir gently with the glass electrode clear of the magnet. Record added volume and stable pH after each addition; use a preliminary run to locate the steep region and smaller additions there on a fresh portion. The readout is the pH versus added volume curve, not a visual count of dissociated molecules.
Calibrate with fresh standard buffer solutions bracketing the pH range being interpreted. Use their assigned values at the actual temperature; a pair near pH 4 and 7 can cover the midpoint of many weak acid examples, but does not cover an entire alkaline endpoint region. Rinse between standards and samples to limit carryover, keep the sensing bulb and reference electrode junction immersed, and wait for a stable reading. These instrument practices are documented in HI5221 & HI5222 Instruction Manual: pH and mV and ISE and Temperature Bench Meters by Hanna Instruments (pp. 45–47, 49–50 and 73–74: calibration, measurement, rinsing and electrode conditioning).
Locate the acid-base titration equivalence region from the steepest change of pH with added volume. For one-to-one neutralization, standardized sodium hydroxide concentration times equivalence volume estimates the initial amount of substance of acid. Half that volume gives approximately equal [HA] and [A−] only when subsequent chemical equilibrium redistribution is small. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation then gives pH≈pKa​. Unequal activity coefficients or appreciable hydronium or hydroxide inventories can shift this estimate. The full chemical equilibrium curve supplies a stronger consistency check than its midpoint alone.
Useful controls for this model test are a fresh independently prepared acid portion, a water blank, a check standard after measurement to detect instrument drift, and fixed recorded temperature. A blank diagnoses contamination but should not be subtracted directly from pH, which is a logarithm. Keep exposure to atmospheric carbon dioxide comparable, especially at high dilution, and record any background salt that changes ionic strength. These are experimental-design controls suggested by the model's assumptions. The observed curve and its uncertainty determine whether the model is adequate; the diagrams here contain no experimental readouts. An aqueous acid dissociation constant cannot be inferred unchanged from a sample requiring a different solvent mixture, and a nearly neutral dilute sample makes the difference h−Kw​/h particularly sensitive to pH error.

Acid dissociation constant (Ka​)

Words: 260 Articles: 1
Acid (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
The acid dissociation constant quantifies the chemical equilibrium for loss of one proton from a chemical acid. In water, write the actual proton transfer as HA+H2​O⇌H3​O++A−. Its full dimensionless equilibrium constant is
Krxn​=aHA​aH2​O​aH3​O+​aA−​​.
(160)
The usual aqueous acid dissociation constant uses the solvent convention with water thermodynamic activity approximated by one:
Ka​=aHA​aH+​aA−​​,pKa​=−log10​Ka​.
(161)
Here hydrated hydrogen ions are understood; H+ is shorthand, not an isolated bare proton in the chemical solution. All thermodynamic activities and Ka​ are dimensionless quantities, using consistent standard states. If water thermodynamic activity differs appreciably from one, retain it in the full equilibrium constant instead of silently mixing conventions.
With activity coefficients γi​ and reference concentration c∘=1molL−1, put ai​=γi​[i]/c∘ for each solute. Then
Ka​=γHA​γH+​γA−​​c∘[HA][H+][A−]​≈c∘[HA][H+][A−]​.
(162)
The last expression is the dilute ideal concentration approximation, not the definition in a nonideal chemical solution. Omitting c∘ instead produces a quotient with units of concentration; its numerical value depends on the chosen units. Do not take a logarithm of that dimensional quotient. Conditional concentration quotients can change with ionic strength even at fixed temperature, whereas the thermodynamic acid dissociation constant retains the activity coefficient corrections. The acid dissociation constant entry distinguishes these conventions.
At the same temperature, solvent and standard states, a larger acid dissociation constant, equivalently a smaller pKa, indicates a stronger tendency to donate a proton. It does not specify an analytical concentration, a pH, or a reaction rate. Composition and the weak acid mass and charge balances are needed to predict pH; chemical kinetics addresses how quickly the chemical equilibrium is approached.
pKa (pKa​=−log10​Ka​)
Words: 45
Acid dissociation constant OurBigBook.com
The pKa is the negative base-ten logarithm of the dimensionless acid dissociation constant. A lower pKa means a larger acid dissociation constant and a stronger tendency to donate a proton under the same standard state, solvent, and temperature conventions. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation places equal weak acid and conjugate base thermodynamic activities at pH equal to pKa. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.

Base (chemistry)

Words: 428 Articles: 4
Acid-base chemistry OurBigBook.com
A chemical base can accept a proton, using an available electron pair to form a covalent bond; more generally it can donate an electron pair to form a covalent bond with another species. See IUPAC Gold Book, base.

Conjugate base

Words: 398 Articles: 3
Base (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
A conjugate base is what remains after a chemical acid donates one proton. In the conjugate acid-base pair HA/A−, HA is the conjugate acid of A−; accepting a proton reverses the conversion. For example, acetic acid CH3​COOH loses a proton to give its conjugate base CH3​COO−. Partners differ by one proton and one unit of electric charge; they need not always be neutral and negative. Hydronium/water and water/hydroxide are also conjugate acid-base pairs.
At a prescribed pH, the ideal dilute acid dissociation constant determines the partition of a monoprotic acid inventory between its chemical species:
αA−​=Ka​+10−pHKa​​,αHA​=Ka​+10−pH10−pH​.
(163)
These dimensionless fractions sum to one. They are the weak acid dissociation fraction and its complement when the only acid-bearing chemical species are HA and A−. Equal fractions occur at pH=pKa​ in this ideal approximation. For nonideal chemical solutions, equality of thermodynamic activities need not mean equality of concentrations.
For stipulated pKa 5, the conjugate base fractions at pH 4, 5 and 6 are 1/11, 1/2 and 10/11. Here an external reservoir sets pH; its ions must supply the additional electric charge balance. The diagram omits those ions and water populations. It does not represent three pure HA samples at identical analytical concentration with freely chosen pH. In the latter experiment, the weak acid mass and charge balances determine pH as well as the partition.
Conjugate acid
Words: 27
Conjugate base OurBigBook.com
The conjugate acid of a chemical base is the chemical species formed when it accepts one proton. This is a relationship between partners, rather than a claim that the partner is a strong acid.
Conjugate acid-base pair
Words: 23
Conjugate base OurBigBook.com
A conjugate acid-base pair consists of two chemical species related by transfer of one proton. The conjugate acid has one more proton and one more positive unit of electric charge than the conjugate base.
Base dissociation constant (Kb​)
Words: 158
Conjugate base OurBigBook.com
For the conjugate base A− accepting a proton from water,
A−+H2​O⇌HA+OH−,Kb​=aA−​aHA​aOH−​​.
(164)
This base dissociation constant uses the same water thermodynamic activity approximation and standard state conventions as the acid dissociation constant. Multiplying the two relations cancels the partner thermodynamic activities:
Ka​Kb​=aH+​aOH−​=Kw​,pKa​+pKb​=pKw​,pKb​=−log10​Kb​,pKw​=−log10​Kw​.
(165)
Here Kw​ is the aqueous ion product associated with self-ionization of water. At fixed temperature, a larger acid dissociation constant gives a smaller base dissociation constant for its own conjugate base; this reciprocal rule compares matching conjugate acid-base pairs. A weak acid does not necessarily have a conjugate base that reacts almost completely with water. For example, stipulated Ka​=10−5 and Kw​=10−14 give Kb​=10−9.[ref]
The value of Kw​ changes with temperature; 10−14 is the familiar approximate value near 25∘C, not a universal constant. If water is retained explicitly in both full equilibrium constants, their product instead equals aH3​O+​aOH−​/aH2​O2​, the full equilibrium constant for 2H2​O⇌H3​O++OH−. The acid dissociation constant, base dissociation constant and self-ionization of water convention must agree.

pH (pH=−log10​aH+​)

Words: 325
Acid-base chemistry OurBigBook.com
The pH of a chemical solution is the negative base-ten logarithm of its hydrogen ion thermodynamic activity:
pH=−log10​aH+​,aH+​=10−pH.
(166)
The thermodynamic activity is a dimensionless quantity, so the logarithm has a dimensionless argument. The definition uses thermodynamic activity, rather than total chemical acid concentration. Single-ion thermodynamic activities require a convention; practical pH measurements are tied to calibrated standards. See IUPAC Gold Book, pH.
In a dilute ideal chemical solution in water, a useful approximation is
aH+​≈c∘[H+]​,c∘=1molL−1,pH≈−log10​(1molL−1[H+]​).
(167)
Square brackets denote concentration in moles per litre. In water, [H+] is shorthand for the hydronium concentration, often written [H3​O+]; it does not describe isolated bare protons. Departures from ideal behavior need activity coefficients. The concentration formula approximates the thermodynamic activity definition.
For an ideal strong acid supplying one proton per initial unit, stipulate a total concentration of 0.001molL−1 and negligible self-ionization of water. Then [H+]≈10−3molL−1, so
pH≈−log10​(10−3)=3.
(168)
Reducing that concentration tenfold by dilution gives 10−4molL−1 and pH 4, under the same assumptions. More generally, dividing the hydrogen ion thermodynamic activity by ten raises pH by one. This is why the scale compresses an enormous range: equal steps of pH represent multiplicative changes, rather than equal differences in concentration. These are model calculations, rather than measured samples.
Neutrality depends on temperature. In the dilute ideal water model, define the dimensionless ion product Kw​=([H+]/c∘)([OH−]/c∘) and pKw​=−log10​Kw​. Equal hydronium and hydroxide concentrations imply
pHneutral​=2pKw​​.
(169)
At 25∘C, the textbook approximation Kw​≈10−14 gives neutral pH 7. Since Kw​ varies with temperature, neutrality need not mean pH 7. Nor is pH restricted to 0–14: the activity definition permits negative pH when aH+​>1, and pH above 14 when aH+​<10−14. High concentrations can invalidate the dilute ideal approximation. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, pH and pOH.
S. P. L. Sørensen introduced pH at the Carlsberg Laboratory in 1909, as recorded in the Carlsberg Foundation historical timeline.

Buffer solution

Words: 2k Articles: 6
Acid-base chemistry OurBigBook.com
A buffer solution contains appreciable quantities of a weak acid and its conjugate base, and resists changes in pH caused by small quantities of added chemical acid or chemical base. The conjugate base accepts added protons; the weak acid supplies protons when a chemical base consumes them. Consuming most of either partner undermines the buffering action. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, buffers.
For a separate toy calculation, stipulate pKa 5 for a weak acid HA; this is an input, not measured material data. Initially 1L of buffer solution contains 0.10mol of HA and 0.10mol of its conjugate base A−. In the ideal concentration approximation, the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives initial pH 5. Add 0.010mol of hydroxide with negligible volume change. The dominant neutralization has one-to-one stoichiometry:
HA+OH−⟶A−+H2​O.
(170)
Each mole of consumed hydroxide removes one mole of weak acid and forms one mole of conjugate base and water. Thus the inventories after neutralization are
nHA​≈(0.10−0.01)mol=0.09mol,nA−​≈(0.10+0.01)mol=0.11mol.
(171)
The shared volume cancels from the concentration ratio. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation therefore predicts
pH≈5+log10​(0.090.11​)=5+log10​(911​)=5.0871501757….
(172)
This small increase illustrates how conversion between abundant partners absorbs added chemical base. The calculation neglects the tiny free hydronium and hydroxide inventories, changes during re-establishment of chemical equilibrium, self-ionization of water, and activity coefficient corrections. The displayed inventories approximate the final chemical species distribution; they are not an exact solution of all chemical equilibrium conditions.
A buffer solution has a finite buffer capacity: its weak acid inventory supplies protection against added chemical base, and its conjugate base inventory supplies protection against added chemical acid. Here an addition approaching 0.10mol of hydroxide uses up the available HA in the dominant stoichiometry calculation. Close to that limit, the neglected chemical equilibrium contributions matter; once HA is exhausted, inserting a zero denominator into the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation cannot predict the actual pH. Excess hydroxide and the remaining chemical species require a fresh chemical equilibrium calculation. This is why a buffer solution stabilizes conditions for chemical reactions over a finite range of additions. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, buffer capacity and added base.
For the pair HA/A−, rearranging the acid dissociation constant gives the activity relation
pH=pKa​+log10​(aHA​aA−​​).
(173)
With thermodynamic activity of water approximated by one and ideal dilute thermodynamic activities for both partners, this yields the familiar Henderson-Hasselbalch equation:
pH≈pKa​+log10​([HA][A−]​).
(174)
The concentrations are at chemical equilibrium; using initial values requires negligible equilibration changes. Below, also neglect self-ionization of water and competing chemical reactions.
Stipulate pKa​=4.76 for an illustrative weak acid, without identifying it with a measured substance. A conjugate base to weak acid concentration ratio of two gives
pH≈4.76+log10​2=5.061029995…≈5.06103.
(175)
Equal concentrations give a ratio of one, whose logarithm is zero, hence pH 4.76. Multiplying the ratio by ten raises pH by one: ratios 0.1, 1, and 10 give pH values 3.76, 4.76, and 5.76. The ratio controls the ideal prediction, while the absolute quantities control how much added chemical acid or chemical base the buffer solution can accommodate.

Henderson-Hasselbalch equation (pH≈pKa​+log10​([A−]/[HA]))

Words: 399
Buffer solution OurBigBook.com
The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation estimates buffer solution pH using a weak acid's acid dissociation constant and the conjugate base to weak acid concentration ratio.
Its activity form is an exact rearrangement of the chosen chemical equilibrium relation. Write the acid dissociation step as HA⇌H++A−, with hydrated hydrogen ions understood in water and the solvent convention incorporated into the acid dissociation constant. For consistent standard states,
Ka​=aHA​aH+​aA−​​,pKa​=−log10​Ka​,pH=pKa​+log10​(aHA​aA−​​).
(176)
Here each ai​ is a dimensionless thermodynamic activity at chemical equilibrium. Exactness refers to this specified acid dissociation constant relation and the chosen single-ion thermodynamic activity convention, not to identifying the ratio with quantities initially mixed. If water is instead written explicitly as a reactant, its thermodynamic activity must be treated consistently. See Hippler and Metcalfe, Using activities to correct the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation (2020), equations 3–4.
For a toy weak acid with stipulated pKa 5, use the ideal dilute concentration approximation and put r=[A−]/[HA]. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation becomes pH≈5+log10​r:
r=0.1 ⇒ pH≈4,r=1 ⇒ pH≈5,r=10 ⇒ pH≈6.
(177)
More conjugate base relative to weak acid means higher pH. Each tenfold increase in the ratio contributes exactly one to the calculated pH. The stipulated pKa is not a tabulated value for an identified substance.
The distinction between thermodynamic activity and concentration is explicit when ai​=γi​[i]/c∘, where γi​ is an activity coefficient and c∘ is the reference concentration:
pH=pKa​+log10​([HA][A−]​)+log10​(γHA​γA−​​).
(178)
Neglecting the final term gives the usual approximate Henderson-Hasselbalch equation. It is justified when the ratio of activity coefficients is sufficiently close to one, as in a suitable dilute ideal approximation. Ionic strength, including contributions from other dissolved ions, affects activity coefficients; a nominally dilute weak acid alone does not establish that all corrections are small. The ratio must use chemical equilibrium concentrations. Replacing these by prepared amounts or post-neutralization inventories is a further approximation, suitable only when subsequent redistribution is small. See Hippler and Metcalfe, concentration, activity, and analytical-concentration approximations.
The short derivation is to solve the acid dissociation constant relation for aH+​, take a negative base-ten logarithm, and use the definitions of pH and pKa. Its useful beauty is that a chemical equilibrium becomes a simple rule about a ratio: select a weak acid with pKa near the desired pH, then adjust the partner ratio. Scaling both partner concentrations equally leaves the ideal pH prediction unchanged, while changing buffer capacity. In practical buffer solutions, temperature, ionic strength, and the available inventories still matter.

Buffer capacity (β)

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Buffer solution OurBigBook.com
Buffer capacity measures resistance to a change in pH: how much additional chemical acid or chemical base a chemical solution accommodates per small change in pH. Its differential form is a local derivative, rather than the total inventory available before a buffer solution is exhausted. Two buffer solutions can have identical pH and very different buffer capacities.
Choose a constant volume V and fixed temperature. Let nB​ count added moles of fully dissociated, monovalent chemical base supplying hydroxide, and nA​ added moles of fully dissociated, monovalent strong acid supplying hydrogen ions. Neither addition supplies the weak acid component itself. The signed addition is b=(nB​−nA​)/V, with units molL−1, and
β=dpHdb​=V1​dpHdnB​​=−V1​dpHdnA​​.
(179)
The last two forms describe separate base-only and acid-only additions. The buffer capacity is positive for the stable chemical equilibrium model below and is reported in molL−1 per unit of pH. Since pH is dimensionless, the dimensional unit is just molL−1; stating “per pH” makes the measurement convention clear. Here constant volume is an idealization, realized approximately by small additions of concentrated reagent.
For a sufficiently small addition, ΔpH≈Δb/β. A large buffer capacity means a small local change of pH for a given addition. Over a finite interval, use the changing buffer capacity instead:
Δb=∫pH0​pH1​​β(p)dp.
(180)
This integral gives a finite dose in molL−1; it need not equal the initial buffer capacity times the eventual change in pH.
Buffer capacity of a monoprotic acid
Words: 229
Buffer capacity OurBigBook.com
Assume an ideal dilute aqueous chemical solution with just one monoprotic acid pair HA/A−, self-ionization of water, and other ions that balance electric charge without undergoing further chemical reactions. Hold the analytical concentration C=[HA]+[A−] constant. Keep the acid dissociation constant Ka​ and the self-ionization of water constant Kw​ dimensionless, consistently with pH:
c∘=1molL−1,H=10−pH=c∘[H+]​,Kw​=(c∘)2[H+][OH−]​.
(181)
Thus H denotes normalized hydrogen ion concentration, not a dimensional concentration. The chemical equilibrium and conserved analytical concentration give
[A−]=Ka​+HCKa​​,[OH−]=Hc∘Kw​​,[H+]=c∘H.
(182)
Adding chemical base converts weak acid to conjugate base, increases free hydroxide, and decreases free hydrogen ion concentration. Balancing electric charge, including the added reagent's accompanying ions, gives the signed dose relative to any initial chemical equilibrium at p0​:
b(p)−b(p0​)=Q(p)−Q(p0​),Q(p)=[A−]+[OH−]−[H+].
(183)
Differentiate with respect to pH, using dH/dp=−(ln10)H. The result is
β=(ln10)((Ka​+H)2CKa​H​+c∘H+Hc∘Kw​​).​
(184)
The first term is the monoprotic acid pair's contribution, βpair​; the remaining terms are the free hydrogen ion and hydroxide contributions, βwater​. Each has units molL−1 per pH. Equivalently, with dimensional Hc​=[H+], Ka,c​=c∘Ka​ and Kw,c​=(c∘)2Kw​, the expression is (ln10)(CKa,c​Hc​/(Ka,c​+Hc​)2+Hc​+Kw,c​/Hc​). Mixing the dimensional and dimensionless conventions would give incorrect units.
For r=Ka​/H=10pH−pKa​,
βpair​=(ln10)C(1+r)2r​≤4ln10​C,
(185)
because (1+r)2−4r=(1−r)2≥0. Equality occurs at r=1: equal weak acid and conjugate base concentrations, or pH equal to pKa. This is the exact maximum of the pair contribution in this model. The full buffer capacity need not have its maximum there: free hydrogen ions and hydroxide make it grow toward the acidic and alkaline extremes. When these contributions are small, the central peak lies close to pKa.
Buffer capacity and concentration
Words: 197
Buffer capacity OurBigBook.com
Stipulate pKa 5 and Kw​=10−14; these are model inputs, not measurements of an identified substance. At pH 5 the pair contribution is 0.575646…C. For analytical concentrations C=0.010 and 0.100molL−1, respectively, it is
βpair​=0.00575646…and0.0575646…molL−1 per pH.
(186)
The free hydrogen ion and hydroxide contribution is the same at this pH, βwater​=(ln10)(10−5+10−9)molL−1=0.0000230282…molL−1 per pH. The full buffer capacities are therefore approximately 0.00577949 and 0.0575877molL−1 per pH. Identical pH fixes the free hydrogen ion thermodynamic activity; it does not fix the inventory of weak acid and conjugate base available for neutralization.
At one unit of pH on either side of pKa, r=10 or 0.1, giving βpair​/βpair,max​=40/121≈0.331. The partners still form a buffer solution, but its local resistance is only about one third of the maximum for that analytical concentration. At fixed pH, the pair contribution scales exactly with C; the full buffer capacity contains the additional C-independent water contribution. Consequently, extreme dilution does not justify dropping self-ionization of water.
Finite titrant response of a buffer
Words: 203
Buffer capacity OurBigBook.com
Prepare the same ideal monoprotic acid model at initial pH 5, with appropriate accompanying ions to balance electric charge. To predict the new pH after a finite signed addition Δb, solve Q(pH1​)−Q(5)=Δb using the chemical equilibrium expression above. For Δb=0.002molL−1 of added chemical base, the calculated final pH is 5.366798 at C=0.010molL−1, but 5.034749 at C=0.100molL−1. The initial local approximation gives changes of about 0.34605 and 0.034730, respectively; its accuracy decreases as the partner balance changes appreciably.
For the dilute example, additions beyond approximately 0.005molL−1 in either direction exceed the initial inventory of one partner. The full chemical equilibrium calculation still produces a finite pH; an inventory-only Henderson-Hasselbalch equation calculation would attempt to use a negative partner quantity. At +0.006molL−1 the dilute example reaches pH 10.99564, whereas the concentrated example reaches only 5.104698. This demonstrates a finite operating range, not an abrupt cessation of all buffer capacity.
Buffer capacity measurement
Words: 473
Buffer capacity OurBigBook.com
A proposed modern measurement extends the weak acid dissociation measurement by estimating the local slope of an acid-base titration. Transfer a measured sample with a pipette into a stirred vessel; clamp a combination glass electrode/reference electrode clear of the stirring magnet and place a temperature probe nearby. A calibrated burette delivers a chemical base of independently standardized concentration cT​, such as sodium hydroxide. Record the initial sample volume V0​, cumulative delivered volume v, stable pH, and temperature after each small addition. Use a separate fresh portion for an acidward series. These are proposed measurement conditions, not reported experimental results.
For the instrument calibration, use fresh standard buffer solutions bracketing the measured pH range, with values appropriate to the actual temperature. The Hanna manual specifies separate rinse and calibration portions, gentle stirring, and approximately 4cm immersion of the probe tip. It calls for stable readings; the sensing bulb and reference electrode junction must remain immersed. Rinse between standards and samples and avoid carrying rinse water into the measured portion.[ref]
The readout pairs each added amount of substance with the measured pH. With negligible added volume, neighboring readings give the finite difference estimate
β≈V0​(pHi+1​−pHi​)cT​(vi+1​−vi​)​,
(187)
assigned to the interval's midpoint. High buffer capacity appears as a small change of pH for a measured reagent dose. Choose increments small enough to resolve changing buffer capacity, but large enough that the change of pH exceeds measurement noise. Repeat with a fresh portion and different increment sizes; remeasure a standard afterward to check drift. A water blank can reveal contamination, but its pH must not be subtracted from the sample pH. These controls are proposed tests of the measurement and model assumptions.
If additions appreciably increase volume, even the analytical concentration changes: C(v)=C0​V0​/(V0​+v). Merely dividing the added moles by the current volume does not restore the constant-volume derivative. One alternative is explicitly to report a changing-volume convention. For c(v)=cT​v/(V0​+v), define
βV​=​dpHdc​​=(V0​+v)2cT​V0​​​dpHdv​​.
(188)
This definition includes the reagent's changing concentration and differs from the constant-volume buffer capacity defined above.[ref]
To compare with the constant-volume theory, fit the changing-volume chemical equilibrium model instead of treating the observed slope as β. In the same ideal monoprotic acid system, define S0​=[A−]0​+[OH−]0​−[H+]0​. For baseward additions, the electric charge balance at each reading is
V0​+vS0​V0​+cT​v​=Ka​+HC(v)Ka​​+c∘(HKw​​−H).
(189)
Use a minus sign before cT​v for the corresponding acidward series. From the model parameters, evaluate the constant-volume buffer capacity at the chosen analytical concentration and pH. The fit also tests whether one acid dissociation constant describes the observations.
Limitations include incomplete mixing, slow glass electrode response, uncertain reagent concentration, and changes in temperature or ionic strength. Dissolved atmospheric carbon dioxide introduces an additional chemical acid system; comparable exposure and freshly prepared samples help distinguish it from the intended monoprotic acid response. Additional reacting chemical species and nonideal activity coefficients invalidate the simple formula. Especially when pH increments are tiny, measurement noise can dominate the inferred derivative; reporting the dose, pH interval, volume convention, and repeatability is part of reporting a meaningful buffer capacity.

Acid-base chemistry OurBigBook.com
A neutralization is a chemical reaction between a chemical acid and a chemical base. In the buffer solution example, hydroxide takes a proton from the weak acid to form water and the conjugate base. The stoichiometry updates the partner inventories before the approximate chemical equilibrium calculation. The name does not require the resulting pH to be 7.

Solution (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
The concentration-based ionic strength is Ic​=21​∑i​ci​zi2​, where ci​ is each dissolved ion's concentration and zi​ its signed electric charge number. It has the same units as ci​; some formulas instead use the dimensionless ratio Ic​/c∘. All dissolved ions contribute, including those that balance the electric charge of a buffer solution's conjugate base. Ionic strength helps describe the interactions represented by activity coefficients. See Hippler and Metcalfe, activity coefficients and dimensionless ionic strength.

Dilution lowers a solute's concentration by adding solvent. When the amount of substance of that solute is conserved and c denotes its amount per volume of chemical solution, c1​V1​=c2​V2​. Size-exclusion chromatography separates dissolved molecules using porous columns. Elution depends on molecular size in the chosen solvent; calibration supplies an estimate of molar mass. Absorption associated with stretching or bending motions of chemical bonds helps identify groups and their environments. Peak positions are commonly reported as reciprocal wavelength, in cm−1; a lower value means lower frequency. [ref]

Chemistry OurBigBook.com
Stereochemistry studies the spatial arrangement of chemical atoms in molecules. A Fischer projection records this information at successive stereocenters, whereas a molecular formula only counts chemical atoms. See McMurry: representing carbohydrate stereochemistry.

Stereochemistry OurBigBook.com
Chirality means that a molecule cannot be superposed on its mirror image. A carbon attached to four different groups is a common source of chirality; the definition concerns the whole molecule, rather than requiring this particular structural feature.

Enantiomer

Chirality (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
Enantiomers are a pair of nonsuperposable mirror-image molecules. The D and L configurations of alanine are an example; glycine has no such pair because its amino acid alpha carbon carries two identical hydrogen chemical atoms. [ref]

Stereocenter

Stereochemistry OurBigBook.com
At a stereocenter, exchanging two attached groups produces a different spatial configuration. The open-chain ribose and glucose examples have carbon stereocenters bearing four different groups; C2 of deoxyribose has two identical hydrogen substituents and is not a stereocenter. See Moss, Basic Terminology of Stereochemistry, IUPAC Recommendations 1996: stereogenic units.

Fischer projection

Words: 100
Stereochemistry OurBigBook.com
In a Fischer projection, each cross represents a carbon position: horizontal chemical bonds point toward the viewer and vertical chemical bonds point away. For the open-chain aldehyde sugars illustrated here, place CHO at the top and CH2​OH at the bottom. This is a convention for stereochemistry, not a measured molecular shape. See Moss, IUPAC Recommendations 1996: Fischer projection.
In these Fischer projections, D specifies that the hydroxy group at the lowest stereocenter lies on the right: C4 for ribose and deoxyribose, C5 for glucose. D does not specify every other stereocenter, and it does not specify the direction of rotation of polarized light. See McMurry: the meaning of D and L.

Chemical substance OurBigBook.com
A zwitterion has opposite formal electric charges in different regions of a molecule, with zero net electric charge. Phosphatidylcholine provides a membrane-related example. This is stronger than merely having chemical polarity through fractional partial atomic charges. See IUPAC Gold Book: zwitterions.

Lipid

Words: 794 Articles: 6
Chemical substance OurBigBook.com
Lipids are a chemically diverse family of chemical substances, conventionally associated with biological origin and solubility in nonpolar solvents. They include triglycerides, phospholipids, and cholesterol. The name does not specify one molecular formula, one repeating monomer, or one kind of polymer. Some lipids have both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions rather than being uniformly nonpolar. See IUPAC Gold Book: lipids.
Structure explains the different jobs. A triglyceride has three fatty acid-derived acyl groups attached to glycerol and serves as an energy store. A typical glycerophospholipid instead combines two such chains with a phosphate-containing head, making it an amphiphile suited to a lipid bilayer. Cholesterol has a different structure and also contributes to cell membrane properties. Thus a lipid is a chemical building material, while a lipid bilayer is an organization of many molecules. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 3.3: lipid structures and functions.

Triglyceride

Words: 25
Lipid OurBigBook.com
A triglyceride contains glycerol joined to three fatty acid-derived acyl groups through ester linkages. Compare the three chains with the two-chain, phosphate-headed glycerophospholipid illustrated below. See Biology 2e: fats and oils.

Cholesterol

Words: 30
Lipid OurBigBook.com
Cholesterol is a lipid with four fused rings and a small hydrophilic region. It helps regulate the fluidity of animal cell membranes; it is structurally distinct from a phospholipid. See Biology 2e: cholesterol.

Phospholipid

Words: 615 Articles: 3
Lipid OurBigBook.com
Phospholipids are lipids containing a phosphate group as part of their structure linked by covalent bonds. The familiar membrane-forming phospholipids are amphiphilic: a hydrophilic head region with chemical polarity coexists with a hydrophobic, largely nonpolar hydrocarbon region. These descriptions refer to different parts of the same molecule, not to two separate substances. See IUPAC Gold Book: phospholipids and IUPAC Gold Book: amphiphilic.
A typical two-chain glycerophospholipid provides a useful example: a glycerol scaffold carries two fatty acid-derived acyl groups through ester linkages, plus a phosphate-containing head region. Phosphatidylcholine is one example. This scaffold describes an important subclass, rather than all phospholipids: sphingomyelin has a different backbone, and even glycerophospholipids need not all have two acyl groups. See IUPAC–IUB, Nomenclature of Lipids (1976), Lip-1.5 and Lip-2.1–2.6.
Polar does not mean negatively charged overall. At near-neutral pH, phosphatidylcholine is zwitterionic: its phosphate region carries negative electric charge and its choline region positive electric charge, with zero net electric charge for the molecule. Counting those opposite charges gives (−1)+(+1)=0; it does not remove their local interactions with water. See Lodish et al., Molecular Cell Biology: membrane lipids.
In a lipid bilayer, two membrane leaflets orient their hydrophilic heads toward the water on either side and their hydrophobic chains toward the shared interior. The hydrophobic effect helps explain this organization through the free energy of the water and lipids together. It is not a special repulsive chemical bond between chains and water. Which organization is favored also depends on molecular geometry, temperature, concentration, and the surrounding chemical solution; a phospholipid label alone does not guarantee a lipid bilayer. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: the lipid bilayer.
This organization supplies a flexible barrier for compartments. A fluid lipid bilayer allows lipids to undergo diffusion within each membrane leaflet; barrier function therefore coexists with motion of molecules, as in the fluid mosaic model. It is not completely impermeable: small nonpolar molecules such as molecular oxygen and carbon dioxide cross much more readily than ions. In a cell membrane, ion channels and other membrane transport proteins provide selective routes; the existing membrane transport article explains their driving forces. See Alberts et al.: principles of membrane transport.
In 1925, E. Gorter and F. Grendel extracted lipids from red blood cells and compared the surface area of a one-molecule-thick film on water with the estimated total surface area of the red blood cells. Their table gave ratios near two, supporting a two-layer covering; they also proposed heads facing the aqueous surroundings on both sides. The inference depends on recovering the relevant lipids, estimating the red blood cell surface area correctly, and comparing compatible packing in the film and the cell membrane. It was indirect evidence, not an image of the lipid bilayer. The paper itself notes possible losses during evaporation. See Gorter and Grendel, On Bimolecular Layers of Lipoids on the Chromocytes of the Blood, Journal of Experimental Medicine 41 (1925), 439–443.

Carbohydrate

Words: 1k Articles: 13
Chemical substance OurBigBook.com
Carbohydrates are a family of chemical substances encompassing monosaccharides, combinations of monosaccharides, and their derivatives. Glucose is a small carbohydrate; cellulose is a long-chain polysaccharide. Deoxyribose illustrates why composition alone does not define the family: replacing a hydroxy group in ribose by hydrogen still leaves a carbohydrate. See IUPAC Gold Book: carbohydrates.
Many familiar monosaccharides have a molecular formula of the form Cn​H2n​On​, equivalently Cn​(H2​O)n​. This explains the historical name, “hydrate of carbon”, but does not mean the molecule consists of carbon mixed with intact water molecules. Nor is it a universal formula: deoxyribose has C5​H10​O4​. The family is defined through chemical structure and relationships, not that ratio. See IUPAC's definition and origin of the name carbohydrate.
The useful surprise is the variety of roles obtainable from related building blocks. Glucose participates in metabolism, ribose forms part of RNA, and linked glucose units make structural cellulose in a plant cell wall. Understanding carbohydrates therefore connects cellular energy, molecular information, and material structure. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: the chemical components of a cell.

Sucrose (C12​H22​O11​)

Words: 11
Carbohydrate OurBigBook.com
Sucrose dissolves in water as neutral molecules; it is a nonelectrolyte in this solvent.

Sugar

Words: 899 Articles: 7
Carbohydrate OurBigBook.com
In chemical usage, sugars commonly means small carbohydrates, including single-unit monosaccharides and two-unit disaccharides. Glucose, ribose, and deoxyribose are monosaccharides. Cellulose is instead a polysaccharide assembled from many glucose units. The distinction counts chemically linked units; it does not classify every carbohydrate by sweetness or biological role. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 3.2: carbohydrates.
A useful first description of a monosaccharide asks how many carbon chemical atoms it contains and what its open-chain structure is. Ribose is an aldopentose, a five-carbon aldehyde sugar; glucose is an aldohexose, with six carbon chemical atoms. A Fischer projection then records the stereochemistry, information missing from the molecular formula. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, 25.1: carbohydrate classification.
Ribose (C5​H10​O5​)
Words: 248
Sugar OurBigBook.com
Ribose is a monosaccharide with molecular formula C5​H10​O5​. Its biologically familiar form is D-ribose, an aldopentose whose open-chain Fischer projection has CHO at the top, CH2​OH at the bottom, and hydroxy groups on the right at C2, C3, and C4. The opposite horizontal substituents are hydrogen. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, 25.3: D-ribose and D-glucose configurations.
Read the drawing by counting groups: CHO contributes CHO, three CHOH groups contribute C3​H6​O3​, and CH2​OH contributes CH3​O. Their sum is C5​H10​O5​. The count checks composition; the right/right/right pattern additionally specifies the stereochemistry of D-ribose.
In RNA, ribose occurs as a ring within each nucleotide, joining a nucleobase to the phosphate-linked backbone. Its C2 position retains a hydroxy group, unlike deoxyribose in DNA. In a nucleotide, the sugar positions carry primes, so this is C2′. See Alberts et al.: nucleotide sugars in RNA and DNA. Free ribose in water is also predominantly cyclic, with several ring forms in chemical equilibrium and very little open-chain form; the Fischer projection is valuable for comparing configurations, not for estimating their abundances. See Mason et al., The Conformation of a Ribose Derivative in Aqueous Solution: A Neutron Scattering and Molecular Dynamics Study (2013), introduction.
Deoxyribose (C5​H10​O4​)
Words: 203
Sugar OurBigBook.com
In the usual DNA context, deoxyribose means 2-deoxy-D-ribose, a five-carbon monosaccharide with molecular formula C5​H10​O4​. Relative to D-ribose, the hydroxy group at C2 is replaced by hydrogen. The locant 2 matters: it identifies which position loses its oxygen. See Favre and Powell, IUPAC Blue Book, P-102.5.3: deoxy sugars and IUPAC: nucleic acids and their component sugars.
The paired Fischer projections in ribose make the change concrete. C2 has hydrogen on both sides, while C3 and C4 retain their hydroxy groups on the right. C2 is therefore not a stereocenter: exchanging its two identical hydrogen substituents cannot produce a distinct configuration. The unchanged C3 and C4 still carry stereochemical information.
Replacing OH by H removes one oxygen but leaves the total hydrogen count unchanged: the hydrogen belonging to the removed hydroxy group is replaced by a hydrogen bonded directly to carbon. Thus C5​H10​O5​ becomes C5​H10​O4​. This comparison describes structures, rather than a complete chemical reaction or its mechanism.
In DNA, deoxyribose is incorporated as a ring in each nucleotide, with phosphate connections building the backbone. Its C2′ bears hydrogen where RNA's ribose bears a hydroxy group. This small local difference lets the sugar structure identify the two kinds of nucleic acid; the nucleobases supply their sequence information. See Alberts et al.: nucleotides as the subunits of DNA and RNA.
Glucose (C6​H12​O6​)
Words: 266
Sugar OurBigBook.com
Glucose is a monosaccharide with molecular formula C6​H12​O6​. Its familiar biological form, D-glucose, is an aldohexose. In the open-chain Fischer projection, CHO is at the top and CH2​OH at the bottom; the hydroxy groups at C2, C3, C4, and C5 point right, left, right, right. This full pattern distinguishes D-glucose from other six-carbon aldehyde sugars. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, 25.4: configurations of the aldoses.
The molecular formula can be checked directly: one CHO group, four CHOH groups, and one CH2​OH group give six carbon, twelve hydrogen, and six oxygen chemical atoms. All four interior carbon positions are stereocenters in this open-chain structure. Neither their orientations nor the arrangement of chemical bonds can be recovered from the molecular formula alone.
In water, glucose exists mainly in six-membered rings in chemical equilibrium with a small amount of open-chain glucose. Ring closure connects the hydroxy group at C5 to the aldehyde carbon at C1; the ring contains five carbon chemical atoms and one oxygen, with C6 outside it. No chemical atoms are lost, so the molecular formula remains C6​H12​O6​. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, 25.5: cyclic structures of monosaccharides.
Glucose is useful both as a substrate in cellular metabolism and as a building block of polysaccharides. Cellulose chains assembled from glucose units help support plant cell walls. The same small sugar thus connects chemical fuel to a structural material; its role depends on how it is transformed or linked. See Cooper, The Cell: A Molecular Approach, the molecular composition of cells.

Chemical formula

Words: 444 Articles: 2
Chemical substance OurBigBook.com
A chemical formula uses symbols of chemical elements and numerical subscripts to record composition. In the molecular formula H2​O of water, the subscript 2 counts two hydrogen chemical atoms, and the omitted subscript after O means one oxygen chemical atom. A molecular formula describes one molecule; a chemical formula need not describe a discrete molecule.
Read a preceding coefficient separately from the subscripts. One H2​O contains two hydrogen and one oxygen chemical atom; 2H2​O contains four hydrogen and two oxygen chemical atoms distributed between two water molecules. In H2​O2​, the second subscript instead puts two oxygen chemical atoms into each hydrogen peroxide molecule. Thus 2H2​O=H2​O2​: the coefficient scales the whole chemical formula, while a subscript specifies its composition. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §2.4: chemical formulas.
For crystalline NaCl, the chemical formula specifies a 1:1 ratio of sodium ions Na+ to chlorine ions Cl−. Its formula unit is the accounting entity; the ordinary crystal is an extended arrangement of ions, rather than a collection of discrete NaCl molecules. Specifying the entity matters when assigning an amount of substance. See formula unit and 2.6 Ionic and Molecular Compounds (§2.6: ionic and molecular compounds).
A molecular formula gives an atom inventory, not the full arrangement of chemical bonds or the molecular geometry. For example, C6​H12​O6​ counts six carbon, twelve hydrogen, and six oxygen chemical atoms in a glucose molecule, but does not specify the pattern shown by its Fischer projection. Different structures can share a molecular formula. This compact inventory is useful for chemical equation accounting precisely because it leaves the structural detail to other representations.
The choice of letters has an early explanation in Jöns Jacob Berzelius, Essay on the Cause of Chemical Proportions (1813–1814), §III, transcribed by Carmen Giunta: letters made chemical signs easier to write and print, and formulas compressed information about composition. His numerical notation differed from modern subscripts; the lasting idea was to make proportions readable in ordinary text.

Cohen et al., IUPAC Green Book, 3rd ed., §2.10.1(iii)(b), p. 51 defines a formula unit as a specified group of chemical atoms, rather than a unit of measurement. An amount of substance of one mole of NaCl formula units therefore corresponds to one mole of each kind of ion.

Amino acid
Words: 1k Articles: 9
Carboxylic acid OurBigBook.com
An amino acid combines carboxylic acid and amine functionality in the same molecule; the name alone does not specify their separation. An alpha-amino acid has its amino nitrogen attached to the carbon immediately adjacent to the carboxyl carbon, the amino acid alpha carbon. For example, H2​N−CH2​−COOH is glycine, whereas H2​N−CH2​−CH2​−COOH has an extra intervening carbon and is not an alpha-amino acid. These chemical formulas describe connectivity, not the predominant protonation state in water.
Most common proteinogenic amino acids share the skeleton H2​N−CH(R)−COOH, with R the amino acid side chain. In glycine, R is hydrogen; in alanine, R=CH3​. Proline is a useful exception to the displayed primary-amine skeleton: its amino nitrogen is part of a ring and has a second carbon substituent. The shared backbone permits assembly into polypeptides, while different amino acid side chains give the resulting proteins diverse chemistry. [ref]
In a chemical solution, protonation changes the electric charges without changing this backbone. Free glycine near neutral pH is predominantly H3​N+−CH2​−COO−, a zwitterion. Its positive and negative groups are joined within one molecule; zero net electric charge does not mean absence of local electric charges, nor does it mean the uncharged drawing H2​N−CH2​−COOH predominates. Glycine protonation explains how lowering or raising pH changes the balance. [ref]
Building a protein joins the carboxyl carbon of one amino acid to the amino nitrogen of another through a peptide bond, an amide linkage. The formal net condensation loses the elements of water; cellular translation uses activated substrates at a ribosome, rather than simply mixing free amino acids in water. Incorporated units are amino acid residues. The interior amide groups no longer have the same acid/base behavior as the two free terminal groups of glycine, so its free-molecule glycine titration cannot be copied independently at every chain position. [ref]
Chirality distinguishes most common proteinogenic amino acids from glycine. The other nineteen members of the conventional twenty have a stereocenter at their amino acid alpha carbon; ordinary translation incorporates their L forms. Glycine's two identical hydrogen substituents make it achiral. Thus being an amino acid, or even an alpha-amino acid, does not by itself imply chirality. [ref]

Glycine protonation

Alpha-amino acid OurBigBook.com
The three principal aqueous glycine forms differ by loss of one proton at each step:
H3​N+−CH2​−COOH+H2​OH3​N+−CH2​−COO−+H2​O​⇌H3​N+−CH2​−COO−+H3​O+,⇌H2​N−CH2​−COO−+H3​O+.​
(190)
Call these glycine forms G+, G0 and G−, respectively: a cation, a zwitterion and an anion, with net electric charges +e, 0 and −e, where e is the elementary charge. G0 specifically denotes the zwitterion, not an uncharged amino/carboxyl drawing. The first dissociation removes the carboxyl proton; the second removes a proton from the positively charged nitrogen. The chemical equilibrium changes are reversible, not three permanently separate kinds of glycine. [ref]
For all calculations and both diagrams here, explicitly stipulate the pKa values pKa1​=2.35 and pKa2​=9.78. These are illustrative model inputs, not measurements from the glycine titration experiment or a claim of universal constants. Actual acid dissociation constants depend on temperature and on the convention used for thermodynamic activity; apparent concentration-based values also depend on ionic strength. For comparison, the inspected textbook tabulates 2.34 and 9.60 for glycine, which would give a different isoelectric point. [ref]
Glycine speciation model
Words: 149
Glycine protonation OurBigBook.com
In an ideal aqueous chemical solution, set h=[H3​O+]/c∘=10−pH, with c∘=1molL−1, and approximate activity coefficients by one. Put K1​=10−2.35 and K2​=10−9.78 for the stipulated dimensionless acid dissociation constants. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives the adjacent-state ratios
[G+][G0]​=hK1​​,[G0][G−]​=hK2​​.
(191)
With analytical concentration CT​=[G+]+[G0]+[G−], normalization gives the three fractions and mean electric charge in units of the elementary charge:
D=h2+K1​h+K1​K2​,α+​=Dh2​,α0​=DK1​h​,α−​=DK1​K2​​,zˉ=α+​−α−​.
(192)
All three fractions are nonnegative and sum to one. At pH 7, the model gives about 99.832% zwitterion, 0.00224% cation and 0.1657% anion; zˉ≈−0.00163. Predominantly zwitterionic therefore need not mean exactly at the isoelectric point.
Setting zˉ=0 requires h2=K1​K2​. Taking the logarithm yields
pI=2pKa1​+pKa2​​=22.35+9.78​=6.065.
(193)
At this model isoelectric point, α+​=α−​≈0.0001927 and α0​≈0.9996146: about 0.0193% of each charged form remains. At either pKa, the relevant adjacent fractions are equal, but the third fraction is not mathematically zero. This three-state model neglects the minor uncharged form H2​N−CH2​−COOH; macroscopic pKa values alone do not determine its fraction separately from the zwitterion.
Glycine titration
Words: 596 Articles: 1
Glycine protonation OurBigBook.com
Adding sodium hydroxide to acidified glycine successively removes its two titratable protons. Two broad buffer solution regions appear around the two pKa values, separated by a steep pH rise near the isoelectric point. This is useful evidence for two separated acid-base chemistry steps even though the changing chemical species are invisible. In the approximation that added hydroxide only changes glycine protonation, b=1−zˉ is the added base amount of substance per initial amount of substance of glycine. Then b≈0.5, 1 and 1.5 correspond to pKa1​, pI and pKa2​; endpoints are not exactly pure chemical species. [ref]
For the solid-curve model, start with nG​=0.00200mol of glycine in V0​=0.0200L and exactly nG​ of fully dissociated hydrochloric acid; this fixes the chloride inventory, but does not force every glycine molecule to remain G+. Let the sodium hydroxide concentration be CB​=0.100molL−1 and b=nNaOH​/nG​. Assume volume is additive and no other ions are present; stipulate Kw​=10−14 for self-ionization of water at a temperature of 25∘C. Then
V=V0​+CB​bnG​​,CT​=VnG​​,[Na+]=bCT​,[Cl−]=CT​.
(194)
Balancing all positive and negative electric charges requires
c∘(h−hKw​​)+CT​(b+zˉ−1)=0.
(195)
Solving this equation gives the solid curve. It remains finite at b=0 and beyond b=2, where ignoring free hydronium and hydroxide would fail. At the first pKa, the full model gives b≈0.436, rather than 0.5: appreciable free hydronium makes that half-equivalent shortcut inaccurate. At the second pKa, b≈1.502. Known acid inventory, dilution, and thermodynamic activity assumptions are therefore part of any quantitative interpretation, not optional corrections inferred from the curve's shape.
Glycine titration experiment
Words: 325
Glycine titration OurBigBook.com
The Amrita Virtual Lab procedure uses 0.1molL−1 glycine, hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, two burettes, a pH meter, beaker and stirrer. A pipette transfers 20mL of glycine into a 100mL beaker. Calibrate the meter with standard buffer solutions at pH 4, 7 and 10, then record the starting pH. Add hydrochloric acid in 0.3mL increments, recording pH after each addition until 1.6. Rinse the electrode in distilled water, take a separate fresh 20mL portion, and add sodium hydroxide in 0.3mL increments until pH 12.5. Its observed readout is paired added volume and pH, plotted as an acid-base titration curve; it does not measure each glycine form directly. [ref]
These are two titrations from the starting glycine chemical solution, rather than the single acidified-sample protocol assumed by the solid curve in glycine titration. Retain each portion's initial volume and the signed added acid/base amount of substance; do not concatenate raw burette readings and assume the result begins at b=0. For this procedure's 0.00200mol of glycine, each 0.3mL addition supplies 0.000030mol of acid or base, a 0.015 increment relative to the glycine inventory. This calculated resolution is not a reported measurement.
Useful additional controls are a fresh repeat portion, independently checked acid/base concentrations, a water blank, and a calibration-check buffer solution after the run. Stir without striking the glass electrode, keep its sensing region immersed and wait for stable readings; record temperature and background salts. Reduce addition size near a steep pH change. These are suggested controls for testing the model, beyond the published steps. A water blank can reveal contamination but must not be subtracted directly from pH, which is a logarithm.
The standards at pH 4, 7 and 10 do not bracket either endpoint of this protocol. Extreme readings therefore require independently checked instrument performance, and alkaline samples are sensitive to atmospheric carbon dioxide uptake. Electrode drift, incomplete mixing, volume error, dilution and changing ionic strength can shift apparent pKa values. A titration constrains the acid/base model; it cannot establish chirality or separate every microscopic protonation form. The two original diagrams show calculated predictions to compare with measured points, not reconstructed experimental data.

Chemical element

Words: 2k Articles: 62
Chemical substance OurBigBook.com
A chemical element is an identity shared by all chemical atoms whose atomic nuclei contain the same number of protons. That number is its atomic number, Z: six means carbon, eleven means sodium. The identity survives differences in neutron count, which distinguish isotopes, and differences in Electron count, which distinguish neutral chemical atoms from ions. See the IUPAC Gold Book, chemical element.
The same name can also denote a pure chemical substance containing only that chemical element. These two uses answer different questions. Molecular oxygen, O2​, is a chemical substance made entirely of oxygen; water, H2​O, is a chemical compound containing both hydrogen and oxygen. A water molecule contains three chemical atoms but only two chemical elements. Joining chemical atoms through chemical bonds changes their arrangement without changing their atomic numbers.
This distinction makes stoichiometry possible: ordinary chemical reactions rearrange chemical atoms, so one can count each chemical element before and after a transformation. Changing the proton count instead changes the chemical element and requires a nuclear reaction. The periodic table organizes these identities into a useful map, while atomic number bookkeeping keeps identity, isotope, and electric charge separate.

Periodic table

Words: 438 Articles: 2
Chemical element OurBigBook.com
The periodic table arranges chemical elements in increasing atomic number, across successive periodic table periods. Its columns are periodic groups, numbered 1–18. The layout places recurring outer electron configurations above one another, making similarities in chemical bonds and chemical reactions easier to recognize. Ordering is by proton count, not by mass; the mass number of a particular isotope does not determine its box. See the official IUPAC periodic table and numbering conventions.
For the first eighteen neutral chemical atoms in their ground states, a compact description counts Electrons in successive electron shells. Thus carbon has (2,4), meaning two Electrons in the first electron shell and four in the second; the sum 2+4=6 agrees with its atomic number. Sodium has (2,8,1), whose sum is 11. These are occupancy counts, not circular trajectories of Electrons.
Reading each row from left to right gives:
  • Periodic table period 1: hydrogen (1) and helium (2).
  • Periodic table period 2: lithium (2,1), beryllium (2,2), boron (2,3), carbon (2,4), nitrogen (2,5), oxygen (2,6), fluorine (2,7), and neon (2,8).
  • Periodic table period 3: sodium (2,8,1), magnesium (2,8,2), aluminium (2,8,3), silicon (2,8,4), phosphorus (2,8,5), sulfur (2,8,6), chlorine (2,8,7), and argon (2,8,8).
The counting outline is short: the occupied electron subshells in this range are 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, and 3p, filled in that order for these neutral ground states. Each s electron subshell holds up to two Electrons and each p electron subshell up to six, giving 2, 2+6=8, and 2+6=8 along these three rows. This 2,8,8 summary applies only through argon; it is not a general rule that each electron shell fills completely before the next begins, nor a claim that the third electron shell can hold only eight Electrons. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, electronic structure and electron configurations.
The recurring outer counts make the arrangement useful. Lithium and sodium each have one valence electron, whereas fluorine and chlorine each have seven valence electrons. Such similarities help anticipate chemical reactions, without making all properties identical throughout a periodic group. Helium is an instructive exception to an eight-Electron shortcut: its two Electrons complete the first electron shell, so it belongs above neon and argon in periodic group 18. Hydrogen shares column 1 with lithium and sodium but has its own distinct chemistry. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, periodic-table organization.

Atomic number (Z)

Words: 371
Chemical element OurBigBook.com
The atomic number Z is the number of protons in an atomic nucleus, and fixes the chemical element. It is a count, with no units. An atomic nucleus with six protons is always carbon, regardless of how many neutrons accompany them or how many Electrons surround it. See the IUPAC Gold Book, atomic number.
Three independent bookkeeping questions become easy once their symbols are kept separate. Let N count neutrons, ne​ count Electrons, A be the mass number, and Q be the net electric charge. A proton carries electric charge +e and an Electron carries −e, where e is the positive elementary charge; a neutron carries zero net electric charge. Hence
A=Z+N,N=A−Z,Q=(Z−ne​)e,ne​=Z−Q/e.
(196)
The reasoning is just counting: add protons and neutrons for A, and subtract negative Electron contributions from positive proton contributions for Q. A neutral chemical atom has Q=0, so ne​=Z. For a positively charged ion, fewer Electrons remain. Notation ZA​X gives the mass number at upper left and atomic number at lower left, with X standing for the chemical element; a right superscript such as + specifies the electric charge in units of e. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, atomic structure and symbolism.
For neutral carbon-12, 612​C, the atomic number gives six protons, the subtraction N=12−6=6 gives six neutrons, and neutrality gives six Electrons. Neutral carbon-13, 613​C, instead has N=13−6=7 neutrons, with the same six protons and six Electrons. Thus these two isotopes occupy the same carbon box in the periodic table.
For neutral sodium of mass number 23, 1123​Na, the counts are eleven protons, 23−11=12 neutrons, and eleven Electrons. Removing one Electron gives the ion 1123​Na+: Q/e=1, so ne​=11−1=10. Both its atomic number and its twelve neutrons stay unchanged. This is ionization, not conversion into the chemical element neon, even though a neutral neon chemical atom also has ten Electrons.
This bookkeeping is useful whenever a symbol must be translated into a physical inventory. Mass number answers how many protons plus neutrons there are; electric charge answers the imbalance between protons and Electrons; atomic number alone answers which chemical element it is. Keeping those questions distinct prevents an isotope or an ion from being mistaken for a different chemical element.
