Isotope (ZA​X)

Words: 760 Articles: 8
Chemical element OurBigBook.com
Isotopes of a chemical element have the same atomic number Z, hence the same number of protons, but different neutron numbers N and therefore different mass numbers A=Z+N. For example, every neon atomic nucleus contains ten protons: neon-20, neon-21, and neon-22 contain ten, eleven, and twelve neutrons, respectively. They occupy one chemical element box in the periodic table, rather than three boxes.
Three labels answer different questions. The chemical element fixes Z; the isotope specifies which neutron number accompanies that Z; the ion label specifies the net electric charge. Neutral 1022​Ne and the ion 1022​Ne+ both contain ten protons and twelve neutrons; they contain ten and nine Electrons, respectively. Ordinary ionization changes the Electron count, leaving the isotope unchanged. Changing the neutron number can change nuclear binding energy and the possibility of radioactive decay. Isotopic abundances can help distinguish material sources, while radioactive decay can additionally supply chronological information.
A mass spectrum makes the distinction experimentally visible: a single chemical element can give separate ion peaks at different mass-to-charge ratios. Its bulk atomic weight is a weighted mean governed by isotopic abundances, rather than the location of one compulsory peak. The historical mass spectrograph experiment and the synthetic neon mass spectrum below illustrate these complementary observations.
Mass number (A=Z+N)

Isotope OurBigBook.com
The mass number A is the total number of nucleons, namely protons plus neutrons, in an atomic nucleus:
A=Z+N,N=A−Z.
(197)
It is an exact positive integer with no units, rather than a measured mass. Carbon-12 has A=12 because its atomic nucleus contains six protons and six neutrons. No improvement in a mass measurement can turn that count into 11.999 or 12.001.[ref]
The left superscript in 1022​Ne denotes mass number 22, not an atomic mass of exactly 22u. For neon-22, the displayed reference atomic mass is about 21.991385114u. Even a weighted mean of mass numbers, such as 20.1877 for the illustrative neon population below, is a population average, not the mass number of an individual atomic nucleus.[ref]
Neutron number (N=A−Z)
Words: 16
Mass number OurBigBook.com
The number of neutrons in an atomic nucleus. Two isotopes of the same chemical element differ in neutron number while sharing an atomic number.
Atomic mass (ma​)
Words: 293 Articles: 4
Isotope OurBigBook.com
The rest mass of a chemical atom in its ground state, a physical quantity expressed in SI mass units or the unified atomic mass unit. Here mi​ means the atomic mass of a neutral chemical atom of isotope i, not the mass of its bare atomic nucleus and not a population average.[ref]
Atomic mass includes Electrons and depends on nuclear binding energy; it is not just mass number times a universal nucleon mass. The atomic mass of neutral carbon-12 in its ground state is exactly 12u by definition of the unified atomic mass unit. That exactness establishes the reference scale, rather than making the atomic masses of all isotopes exact integers in the same unit.
Dalton (unit, Da=u)
Words: 46
Atomic mass OurBigBook.com
The unified atomic mass unit and dalton are names for the same mass unit:
1u=1Da=12ma​(12C)​,
(198)
where the carbon-12 chemical atom is free, at rest, and in its nuclear and electronic ground state. Its conversion to SI mass units is determined experimentally. See The International System of Units (SI), ninth edition, SI Brochure (Table 8, footnote (f), printed p. 146: dalton and unified atomic mass unit).
Nuclear mass defect (Δm=Zmp​+Nmn​−Mnuc​)
Words: 90
Atomic mass OurBigBook.com
The mass deficit of a bound atomic nucleus relative to its separated protons and neutrons. If their rest masses are mp​ and mn​, the atomic nucleus has rest mass Mnuc​, and the positive nuclear binding energy is B, then
Δm=Zmp​+Nmn​−Mnuc​=c2B​,
(199)
with c the speed of light. Releasing energy when the nucleons bind reduces the rest mass of the bound system without changing the exact count A=Z+N. A neutral atomic mass also includes Z Electron rest masses, reduced by the energy required to separate those bound Electrons. Consequently A−ma​/u is not the definition of the nuclear mass defect: the reference unit and constituent rest masses must also be accounted for.
Relative atomic mass (Ar​=mˉ/u)
Words: 80 Articles: 1
Atomic mass OurBigBook.com
For a chemical element in a specified population, its relative atomic mass or atomic weight is the dimensionless ratio Ar​=mˉ/u, with mˉ the mean neutral atomic mass weighted by isotopic abundance. For the illustrative neon population, Ar​≈20.1800, whereas mˉ≈20.1800u has mass units.[ref]
Standard atomic weight (Ar∘​)
Words: 42
Relative atomic mass OurBigBook.com
A recommended atomic weight applicable to normal materials, rather than the result for every possible enriched sample. The tabulated neon value 20.1797(6) and the arithmetic result above need not agree in every last displayed digit. Some chemical elements have intervals of standard atomic weight because their isotopic abundances vary across normal materials.[ref]
Isotopic abundance (fi​)
Words: 162
Isotope OurBigBook.com
An isotopic abundance is an atom fraction within a specified population of one chemical element.[ref] If ni​ counts its chemical atoms of isotope i, use
fi​=∑j​nj​ni​​,fi​≥0,∑i​fi​=1.
(200)
The denominator includes every isotope of that chemical element included in the stated population, not every chemical atom of every chemical element in the sample. Thus an oxygen atom fraction among all chemical elements is a different quantity.
For an illustrative neutral neon population, take the displayed central isotopic abundances f20​=0.9048, f21​=0.0027, and f22​=0.0925 from the reference table, so 0.9048+0.0027+0.0925=1. Its mean atomic mass is the weighted arithmetic mean
mˉ​=i∑​fi​mi​=(0.9048×19.9924401762+0.0027×20.993846685+0.0925×21.991385114)u=20.18004638052026u≈20.1800u.​
(201)
These are rounded reference inputs with uncertainties, not exact universal isotopic abundances; the long decimal shows their arithmetic result, not measurement precision.[ref]
The population convention matters. If instead wi​ is the fraction of total neutral-atom mass supplied by isotope i, then wi​=fi​mi​/mˉ and
mˉ=(∑i​mi​wi​​)−1.
(202)
This is a weighted harmonic mean in the mass fractions. Using ∑i​wi​mi​ with those mass fractions would answer a different question. The conversion follows directly by counting chemical atoms and adding their masses.

Snowflake OurBigBook.com
An exposed tip receives vapour more efficiently than a sheltered surface and can amplify its lead, producing crystal dendrites and side branches. The planar thermal solidification mechanism is an analogy, not a complete vapour-growth model. The hexagonal ice crystal anisotropy selects six preferred directions; an isotropic linear instability alone does not select six arms.

Steady state (chemistry)

Words: 40
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
A steady state has time-independent concentrations because formation and removal rates balance for the species considered. Nonzero reaction fluxes can continue, so a steady state need not be chemical equilibrium. A quasi-steady-state approximation imposes this balance approximately for a fast intermediate while slower species evolve.

Chemistry OurBigBook.com

Chemical polarity

Words: 94 Articles: 2
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
Chemical polarity concerns unequal distribution of electron density in a chemical bond or molecule. A polar molecule has a permanent electric dipole moment; the effects of individual bonds must be combined with their spatial arrangement. In a symmetric linear carbon dioxide molecule, opposing bond-dipole contributions cancel. In water, its bent molecular geometry prevents that cancellation, giving a permanent electric dipole moment.[ref]

Polar molecule

Words: 24
Chemical polarity OurBigBook.com
A polar molecule has a nonzero permanent electric dipole moment because of its internal electric charge distribution. It can still have zero total electric charge. Water is polar; a nonpolar molecule has no permanent electric dipole moment.

Nonpolar molecule

Words: 19
Chemical polarity OurBigBook.com
A nonpolar molecule has no permanent electric dipole moment. This distinguishes its charge distribution from the separated partial charges of a polar molecule.

Hydrophilicity

Words: 59
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
Hydrophilicity describes affinity for water. Regions with chemical polarity or electric charge can interact favorably with water, including through hydrogen bonds where suitable groups are present. Hydrophilic regions of membrane-forming phospholipids face the water on either side of a lipid bilayer. Such affinity does not mean forming covalent bonds with every neighboring substance, nor does it require a net negative electric charge. See Alberts et al.: the chemical components of a cell.

Amphiphile

Words: 45
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
An amphiphile is a molecule containing distinct hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions. Amphiphilic and amphipathic describe this combination. Membrane-forming phospholipids are examples; their two regions give different parts of one molecule different affinities for water. The word describes a structure, not a guarantee of a particular aggregate shape. See IUPAC Gold Book: amphiphilic.

Hydrophobicity

Words: 159 Articles: 1
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
Hydrophobicity describes unfavorable mixing with water, as illustrated by long hydrocarbon regions. The hydrophobic regions of membrane-forming phospholipids face the interior of a lipid bilayer. This organization is explained by the hydrophobic effect, rather than by imagining that chains actively repel water. See IUPAC Gold Book: hydrophobic interaction.

Hydrophobic effect

Words: 116
Hydrophobicity OurBigBook.com
The hydrophobic effect is the solvent-mediated tendency of nonpolar regions to associate in water. Exposing a hydrocarbon region changes how surrounding water molecules can arrange and interact; reducing that exposure can lower the total free energy. Both water and lipids enter the accounting. The effect is not an additional covalent bond between chains. See IUPAC Gold Book: hydrophobic interaction.
At fixed temperature and pressure, compare two candidate organizations by the change in Gibbs free energy, ΔG=ΔH−TΔS, where H is enthalpy, T is absolute temperature, and S is entropy. An organization with lower G is favored in this comparison. Reducing exposed hydrocarbon area is one contribution; changes in chain packing and the entropy of the lipids also matter. This explains why hydrophobicity alone cannot predict every aggregate shape. See 16.4 Free Energy.

Absorbance (A)

Words: 109 Articles: 1
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
Absorbance is the dimensionless quantity A=log10​(P0​/P), where P0​ and P are reference and transmitted radiant powers at the chosen wavelength. For example, A=1 means one tenth of the reference power is transmitted. Under the Beer-Lambert law, absorbance can determine an absorbing species' concentration; attenuation by cloudiness or unrelated colored solutes needs separate controls. [ref]

Beer-Lambert law (A=εlc)

Words: 54
Absorbance OurBigBook.com
The Beer-Lambert law relates absorbance A to an absorbing species' concentration c and path length l by A=εlc in a homogeneous medium using sufficiently narrow-band light. The coefficient ε depends on the species, wavelength and chemical solution conditions. This makes Ellman's reagent useful for quantitative thiol assays once its released colored species has been calibrated. [ref]

Chemistry OurBigBook.com

Hess's law

Words: 56
Thermochemistry OurBigBook.com
Hess's law states that compatible chemical reaction enthalpies add when their equations add. Reversing a chemical reaction reverses its enthalpy change; multiplying the entire chemical reaction equation by a factor multiplies that change by the same factor. The reason is that enthalpy is a state function: intermediate states cancel from the differences. A cycle supplies one independent balance relation; it cannot determine two unknown inputs without further information.

Standard enthalpy of formation (ΔHf∘​)

Words: 43
Thermochemistry OurBigBook.com
The standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change for forming one mole of a specified chemical substance from its chemical elements in their reference states at the stated temperature. For sodium chloride at 298.15K, those reactant states are solid sodium and diatomic gaseous chlorine. Standard state specifies conditions; it does not by itself select a temperature.

Enthalpy of atomization (ΔHat∘​)

Words: 37
Thermochemistry OurBigBook.com
An enthalpy of atomization is the enthalpy change for making one mole of separated gaseous chemical atoms from a specified starting chemical substance. For sodium, the relevant step is sublimation to monatomic gas; for diatomic chlorine, it is half the compatible molar bond-dissociation energy expressed as an enthalpy.

Enthalpy change of solution (ΔHsol​)

Words: 25
Thermochemistry OurBigBook.com
An enthalpy of solution is an enthalpy difference for dissolution into a specified solvent at stated temperature and final concentration. Keep a measured finite-dilution value distinct from an infinite-dilution reference value.

Mass spectrometry

Words: 653 Articles: 4
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
Mass spectrometry separates and detects ions according to mass-to-charge ratio. It can distinguish isotopes which belong to the same chemical element but have different atomic masses. The instrument measures ions: interpreting the result as a neutral atomic mass requires accounting for Electron removal and its ionization energy. For a singly positive ion in its ground state, m+​=ma​−me​+I/c2, where me​ is the Electron rest mass, I is the ionization energy, and c is the speed of light.
For a simple illustrative analyzer, positive ions of mass m and electric charge q=ze gain kinetic energy qV=mv2/2 across an electric potential difference V before entering a transverse uniform magnetic field B. The Lorentz force supplies centripetal acceleration, so
qvB=rmv2​,qm​=2VB2r2​.
(203)
At fixed V and B, the measured bending radius r separates mass-to-charge ratios, not masses independently of electric charge. This ideal model assumes negligible initial kinetic energy and speeds small compared with the speed of light; the historical focusing mass spectrograph used the geometry described below.

Mass spectrograph

Words: 244
Mass spectrometry OurBigBook.com
A mass spectrometry instrument with a photographic readout. In the 1919 apparatus described in Chapter V: The Mass-Spectrograph, a gas discharge produced positive ions. Two narrow slits formed a ribbon beam in a vacuum; plates applied an electric field to spread it, an aperture selected part of it, and a magnetic field bent it oppositely. Focusing reduced the spread caused by differing ion speeds, concentrating a given mass-to-charge ratio into a line on a photographic plate.
The observed quantity was line displacement from a fiducial spot. Known reference lines calibrated displacement against mass-to-charge ratio; repeated exposures with changed magnetic field tested the calibration. Evacuation limited collisions. Comparing line shapes with narrow and wide apertures helped distinguish geometric broadening from photographic spreading. Finite slit widths, plate response, and overlapping molecular or multiply charged ions limited interpretation. See Chapter V: The Mass-Spectrograph (§§33–40: apparatus and photographic procedure; §§43 and 45–46: calibration, aperture comparisons, and accuracy).
In Mass spectra and isotopes by Francis William Aston (Nobel lecture, 12 December 1922), the reported neon lines at 20 and 22 have companions at 10 and 11 from doubly charged ions. That paired pattern and comparison with reference lines support different atomic masses within one chemical element, rather than an atomic mass concentrated at the bulk average. The lecture also describes an earlier failed separation by distillation and partial separation by diffusion, showing why the focused mass spectrum supplied stronger evidence. These numbers used a historical oxygen-based reference scale. The lecture's whole-number rule was an empirical approximation at its stated accuracy, not the modern exact definition A=Z+N.[ref]

Mass-to-charge ratio (m/q)

Words: 50
Mass spectrometry OurBigBook.com
The ratio of an ion's mass to its electric charge; in SI it has units kg/C. A convenient numerical mass spectrum coordinate is x=(m/u)/z, with q=ze and positive integer z here. This x is dimensionless. Doubling z at fixed mass halves x, so the electric charge state must be identified before assigning an isotope.

Mass spectrum

Words: 156
Mass spectrometry OurBigBook.com
A mass spectrum displays detected signal against mass-to-charge ratio. Peak positions identify candidate ions; peak areas give isotopic abundances only after the response and overlapping contributions have been accounted for.
Broadening can hide a weak component without changing its area in this ideal model. An actual mass spectrum can also contain molecular ions, different electric charge states, background, and unequal detection responses. A missing visible peak therefore cannot by itself prove the absence of an isotope. Conversely, a fractional atomic weight is a property of a population: there is no requirement for an ion peak at the weighted mean.

Mass resolution (R=x/Δx)

Words: 79
Mass spectrometry OurBigBook.com
Mass resolving power compares a peak coordinate x with a stated width or separation criterion Δx. With Δx taken as full width at half maximum, a Gaussian function of standard deviation σ has
Δx=22log2​σ,R=Δxx​.
(204)
At the neon-20 coordinate in the synthetic mass spectrum, σ=0.04 gives Δx≈0.0942 and R≈212, while σ=0.70 gives Δx≈1.648 and R≈12.1. The width criterion and relative peak areas both matter when judging whether a small neighboring isotope can be distinguished. Mass resolution also differs from the accuracy of a calibrated peak position.
